Elsternwick|Prep|How We Express Ourselve.d: Students photograph a classroom toy, draw a mouth on it and record the toy telling one part of a story. This explores “ways stories are shared” by turning a still object into a speaking character. Each student makes a short talking-character video to show the class. The simple photo, mouth line and voice-recording features keep the task manageable for Prep students.

In pairs, students choose characters and a setting, then move the puppets while recording an imagined beginning, middle and end. This supports “imagining stories together” as children agree on what happens and take turns speaking. Each pair produces a short puppet show that can be played to the class. The drag-and-move puppets and built-in voice recording allow students to act out their story in one simple tool.

Students choose a character and background, then use simple picture blocks to make the character move and speak through a familiar story event. This explores the central idea that “stories are shared in different ways” by presenting a story as a small animation. Each student creates and presents one animated story scene with movement and a speech bubble. ScratchJr’s snap-together movement and speech blocks make the coding suitable for Prep students with teacher modelling.

Small groups record voices and everyday sound effects to create an audio version of a short class story. This connects with “connecting with stories” as students consider how voices, music and sounds help listeners imagine what is happening. Each group produces a brief audio story that classmates can hear without seeing any pictures. GarageBand’s voice recorder, simple sound library and play button are the main features used.

Students use playdough figures or classroom blocks to make a simple story, moving the characters a little before taking each photo. This explores “ways stories are shared” by turning a sequence of still pictures into a moving story. Pairs create a short stop-motion film with a clear event, such as a character finding a lost object. The app’s large camera button, frame-by-frame capture and playback feature make the process clear and achievable for Prep.

Elsternwick|Prep|How We Organise Ourselv.d: As a class, students use Google Maps to explore the Elsternwick community and look for places such as the library, shops, parks and emergency services. This supports the line of inquiry, “My communities,” by helping students notice the places and people that make up their local area. Pairs take turns presenting a short Street View walkthrough and explaining who might work or help at each place. The teacher uses the search and Street View features while students direct where to look.

Students use Book Creator to make a class book called “Everyone Has a Role in Our Community.” Each child creates one page about a familiar community member, adding a drawing or photo and recording a sentence about how that person contributes. This directly explores the central idea that everyone has a role to play in the community. The simple page, drawing, photo and voice-recording features allow the finished book to be read and listened to together.

Students build a simple floor route showing connections in their community, with stops representing places such as home, school, the library and the park. They place Indi’s coloured tiles to make the car move, turn and stop at each location, then test and adjust the route if it does not work. This connects directly to the line of inquiry, “Connections in my community,” by showing how people travel between community places. Groups present their completed route and explain the role of each stop, using Indi’s colour-sensing movement as the main feature.

Students use Seesaw to create a short “How I Contribute” post about a job they do at school or at home. They take a photo or make a drawing, then record their voice explaining the role and why it helps their community. This supports the line of inquiry, “Contributing to the local community,” and reinforces that everyone has a role to play. Seesaw’s drawing, photo and voice-recording tools produce a shareable class collection of everyday contributions.

Students use ScratchJr to code a short scene showing two community members working together, such as a librarian helping a family or a crossing supervisor helping children. They choose characters and a setting, then connect simple movement and speech blocks to show what each person does. This explores the line of inquiry, “Connections in my community,” by showing how one role can support another. Pairs test and debug their sequence before presenting the finished animation to the class.

Elsternwick|Prep|How the World Works.d: Students use Tablet Magnifiers to closely examine leaves, feathers, bark or classroom objects as part of observing my world. They follow a simple scientific process by looking first, noticing details and then comparing what they found. Each pair captures a small set of magnified images and presents one surprising observation to the class. The tool’s everyday zoom and image-capture features make tiny patterns, edges and textures easy for Prep students to see and share.

Students use Seek by iNaturalist during a supervised garden walk to observe and identify plants, insects and other living things. This directly supports the line of inquiry observing my world, as students look carefully before drawing conclusions about what lives in the school grounds. Pairs create a saved collection of several identified living things and share one identification with the class. Seek’s built-in camera recognition gives students immediate suggestions without requiring them to type or publish publicly.

Students investigate how scientists follow a method by predicting, testing and correcting a Beebot route across a simple floor grid. In pairs, they choose a destination, enter movement commands, watch what happens and debug the sequence if the Beebot misses its target. Each pair presents a successful route and explains one change they made after observing a test. The Beebot’s forward, backward, turn, clear and go buttons make the testing process concrete and manageable for Prep students.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to record a simple change, such as an ice cube melting or a wet paper shape drying, for the How the World Works unit. They take pictures at regular points, observe what changes and draw a conclusion from the finished sequence. The class ends up with a short stop-motion science record that can be replayed and discussed. The app’s frame-by-frame camera and playback features let students see a slow change happen quickly.

Students use Book Creator to make a class science book showing how scientists follow a method to discover new things. Small groups photograph stages of a simple sink-or-float test, then add a spoken prediction, the result and a conclusion on separate pages. Their finished book provides a concrete record that can be read and replayed for classmates or families. Book Creator’s built-in camera, voice recording and page-making features allow Prep students to document the scientific process with minimal typing.

Elsternwick|Year 1|How We Express Oursel.d: Students use ChatterPix Kids to photograph a classroom object, draw on a mouth and record it speaking as a chosen emotion. They explain what the character is feeling, what clues show the emotion and what might help, supporting the line of inquiry about recognising our own and others' emotions. Each student makes a short talking character to play for a partner or the class. The simple photo, mouth-drawing and voice-recording features make this manageable for Year 1 students.

Students code two characters in ScratchJr to show an everyday situation involving emotions, such as feeling left out and then being invited to play. They choose facial expressions, backgrounds, speech and simple movements to explore responding to and interpreting our emotions. Each pair makes a short coded scene with a clear beginning, response and ending, then presents it to the class. ScratchJr's picture-based coding blocks, character editor and speech bubbles allow students to build and test the scene without needing to type much.

Students use PicCollage to make an emotions clues poster about one feeling, such as excitement, sadness or worry. They take or select suitable photos, arrange them on the page and add simple labels showing facial, body and situation clues, linking to recognising our own and others' emotions. Each student produces a clear visual poster that can be displayed and used for class discussion. The ready-made layouts, photo tool, stickers and text boxes support a practical Year 1 task.

In small groups, students use Puppet Pals to perform a short story in which characters express the same emotion in different ways. They move the puppets and record dialogue that shows actions such as talking, becoming quiet, asking for help or taking a break, connecting directly to the line of inquiry about different ways we express emotions. Each group records a puppet show and presents it for classmates to interpret the characters' feelings. The character selection, backgrounds, touch movement and built-in voice recording are the key features students use.

Students use Seesaw's drawing canvas to create a picture of a time a character might feel a strong emotion, then record their voice explaining a helpful response. This directly explores the line of inquiry about responding to and interpreting our emotions. Each student publishes a simple illustrated voice reflection that the teacher can replay during a class discussion. The drawing, microphone and playback features let Year 1 students share their thinking without relying on lengthy writing.

Elsternwick|Year 1|How We Organise Ourse.d: Students view the Elsternwick area in Google Maps and use Street View to find local services such as the library, fire station, medical centre and post office. They discuss the line of inquiry about local services and why people need them in the community. Pairs present a short Street View walkthrough, pointing out one service, nearby landmarks and how a person could reach it. The familiar search, zoom and Street View features make the local area easy for Year 1 students to explore with teacher support.

Students create a simple class book about services that help people in the Elsternwick community. Each pair makes one page showing a local service, who works there, what people might need and how the service helps meet that need. The finished book can be read aloud and shared with families or another Year 1 class. Students use Book Creator’s drawing, photo, text and voice-recording features to build their pages.

Students complete a short class survey about which local service they might use in everyday situations, such as borrowing a book, posting a parcel or getting help when someone is hurt. This directly explores why we need local services in our community and how they meet personal needs. The class views the automatic charts and presents simple findings such as which service was chosen most often for each situation. Microsoft Forms’ picture questions, large answer choices and automatic response charts keep the data collection manageable for Year 1.

Students code a short animation showing a community member using a local service, such as visiting a library to borrow a book or calling firefighters in an emergency. Their animation explains how services are established to help meet the needs of people in the community. Students create and present a two-scene story in which a character has a need, travels to the service and receives help. ScratchJr’s character, background, movement and speech blocks let students build and debug the sequence with simple drag-and-drop coding.

Students build a small floor route that connects model locations such as a home, library, medical centre and fire station, then drive Sphero Indi to the service needed in a given situation. This explores local services and introduces how people navigate through a community to get help. Groups test and debug their coloured-tile route, then present a working journey and explain why the destination service is needed. Sphero Indi’s colour tiles and built-in colour sensor allow Year 1 students to control turns, speed and stopping without complex coding.

Elsternwick|Prep|Who We Are.d: In Who We Are, students work with a partner to record a short introduction about something they enjoy doing together. They explain how listening, sharing and kind words help with developing relationships. Each pair creates a Seesaw post with a photo, a simple drawing and a recorded voice message to share with the class. Seesaw’s camera, drawing and voice-recording features make the task manageable for Prep students.

In Who We Are, students create a short puppet scene in which one character wants to join a game and another character responds. They show how those around us impact our behaviours and interactions by acting out both a helpful response and an unhelpful response. Each pair records and presents a simple puppet story with a positive ending. Puppet Pals’ character, background and voice-recording features let students move the puppets while speaking.

In Who We Are, students make a collage showing everyday ways to keep themselves healthy and safe at school. They photograph simple actions such as washing hands, wearing a hat, drinking water or asking a trusted adult for help. Each student adds a few spoken or teacher-supported text labels and shares the finished safety collage with the class. PicCollage’s camera, picture layout and text features keep the task visual and suitable for Prep.

In Who We Are, small groups record a short help-seeking video about a common Prep problem, such as feeling left out, getting hurt or losing something. The video connects to keeping ourselves healthy and safe by showing who students can approach and what they can say. Each group presents a clear beginning, safe response and positive ending in a video of less than one minute. Apple Clips’ simple video recording, trimming and automatic caption features support students to make and replay their message.

In Who We Are, students help build a class board showing the people and actions that support their wellbeing. Each child draws themselves, then adds lines to simple drawings of friends, family members, teachers or other trusted adults and explains how that relationship helps them. The finished board becomes a relationship map that the class can revisit when discussing the central idea that relationships impact our wellbeing. Freeform’s drawing tools, shapes, connecting lines and text boxes allow the class to create the map together on one board.

Elsternwick|Prep|Sharing the Planet.d: In pairs, students use Seek by iNaturalist during a supervised walk to photograph and identify plants, insects and other living things around the school. This directly supports the line of inquiry about the different living things around us. Students build a small collection of identified observations and show one discovery to the class. The live camera identification feature helps them compare what they see with possible species without needing to type or read long descriptions.

Students create a short digital book about how living things share our world and have an important role in nature. Each child draws or photographs one local living thing, then records a simple sentence about its role, such as a bee helping flowers or a worm improving soil. The finished class book can be played on screen and shared with families. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tool and voice-recording button make the task manageable for Prep students.

Students code a Beebot to travel across a simple floor grid showing plants, animals, water, shelter and human spaces. They plan and test a route that visits what one living thing needs while avoiding obstacles, then debug the commands if the Beebot goes to the wrong square. This explores how humans and other living things share space. Each pair presents a working route, using the Beebot’s forward, backward and turn buttons to show their sequence.

Students use ChatterPix Kids to make a local plant or animal explain its role in nature. They take a photo within the app, draw a mouth and record a short message such as, “I am a bird and I spread seeds.” This connects directly to the line of inquiry about the roles living things play in nature. The simple photo, mouth-drawing and voice-recording features produce a short talking-picture clip that students can present to the class.

As a teacher-guided group, students view Google Maps and use Street View to explore places where people, plants and animals share space, such as a local park, beach or wetland. They look closely for trees, gardens, water, paths, roads and buildings, then discuss which living things might use each part of the place. This supports the line of inquiry about how humans and other living things share space. Using the zoom controls and Street View arrows, pairs present a short on-screen tour and point out one helpful feature and one possible challenge for living things.

Elsternwick|Year 1|How the World Works.d: Students use a Beebot to travel across a grid of coloured shapes arranged in repeating patterns. They code, test and debug a route that follows the pattern correctly, linking to the line of inquiry “How patterns can be created, interpreted and extended”. Each pair presents its programmed route and explains which colour or shape should come next. The Beebot’s forward, backward, turn and clear buttons make the movement pattern easy for Year 1 students to control.

Students create short sound patterns connected to patterns and cycles in our lives, such as clap-clap-pause or morning-afternoon-night. They record and repeat these sounds to explore the line of inquiry “Patterns and cycles in our lives”. Each student or pair produces a short audio track and plays it for classmates, who identify and extend the pattern. GarageBand’s simple audio recorder and loop feature allow students to hear the repeated pattern clearly.

Students code a character to move in a repeating pattern, such as jump-turn-jump-turn, as part of learning how patterns can be created and extended. They arrange movement blocks, run the code and debug any part that does not repeat as planned. Each pair makes a short animated pattern and presents it for classmates to interpret and predict what will happen next. ScratchJr’s picture-based coding blocks and repeat block keep the task manageable for Year 1.

Students use virtual bands to build repeating shape patterns, such as triangle-square-triangle-square, while exploring different patterns around us. They copy, extend and explain their designs, directly supporting the line of inquiry “Different patterns around us”. Each student creates a finished digital geoboard pattern to show the class and asks classmates to predict the next shape. Geoboard’s peg grid, coloured bands and clear-board button make it easy to build, change and test ideas.

Students build a growing pattern with everyday classroom objects and photograph one new step at a time in Stop Motion Studio. They play back the frames to see how patterns help us to interpret what comes next in the world around us. Each group publishes a short stop-motion film that shows its pattern growing, then pauses the film so classmates can predict the next frame. The app’s frame-by-frame camera and playback controls let students capture and check each stage without needing another app.

Elsternwick|Year 1|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use Seek by iNaturalist to photograph and identify plants around the school grounds. This directly explores the line of inquiry, Plants all around us. In pairs, they collect a small set of identified plant photos and present one plant they found to the class. The tool’s camera recognition gives students an immediate suggested plant name while the teacher supports safe, careful observation.

Students use Book Creator to make a short class book about products derived from plants, such as paper, fruit, cotton clothing and wooden furniture. This connects directly to the line of inquiry, Products derived from plants, and the central idea that plants are a life sustaining resource. Each student creates one page with a drawing or photo, a simple sentence and a recorded voice explanation. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing pen and audio recording make the finished book easy to read and share together.

Students view Google Maps and use Street View to explore plants in different places, such as a Melbourne street, a farm and a tropical area. This supports the line of inquiry, Plants all around us, by helping students notice where plants grow and how the surroundings differ. The class presents a simple comparison by revisiting each place on the screen and naming the plants or green spaces they can see. Google Maps’ search, zoom and Street View features allow students to explore these places without creating or editing a map.

Students use ScratchJr to code a simple animation showing the interconnectedness of plants with a bee, a flowering plant and a person or animal. They program the bee to move to the flower, then add a second scene showing fruit or seeds that help another living thing. Pairs present their animation and explain how the characters depend on the plant. ScratchJr’s picture backgrounds, character editor and drag-and-drop movement blocks make the sequence manageable for Year 1.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to show how a familiar plant becomes a useful product, such as wheat becoming bread or a tree becoming paper. This directly addresses the line of inquiry, Products derived from plants. Small groups move simple pictures or classroom objects a little at a time, photograph each step and add a short spoken explanation to their finished sequence. The tool’s frame-by-frame camera and playback button turn their steps into a short film they can present to the class.

Elsternwick|Year 1|Where We Are in Place.d: Students use Google Maps to view homes in Elsternwick and compare them with homes in a contrasting place chosen by the teacher. This supports the line of inquiry into different types of homes and helps students notice how homes reflect culture and environment. Using Street View, students look for visible features such as building materials, roof shapes, gardens, balconies and nearby streets. Pairs present two similarities and two differences they noticed using the zoom, map view and Street View features.

Students create a short digital book called “A Home That Suits Its Place” using Book Creator. This connects to the central idea that homes reflect our culture and environment. Each student draws or photographs a home, records a spoken explanation and adds pages showing features that suit the local weather, people and surroundings. They publish and share their book using the drawing, audio recording, camera and page-making features.

Students use ScratchJr to code a character giving a simple tour of a home. This explores the line of inquiry into the characteristics of a home as students include spaces for sleeping, eating, washing and spending time together. They create two or three room backgrounds, then use movement and speech blocks to guide the character from one space to another. The finished project is a short, playable home tour powered by ScratchJr’s backgrounds, characters and block coding.

Students complete a teacher-made Microsoft Forms survey about features found in their homes, such as balconies, gardens, shared walls, solar panels or water tanks. This supports the lines of inquiry into different types of homes and sustainable living spaces. The class views the automatic charts and discusses which features are common, uncommon or helpful for saving energy and water. Students then present one finding from the survey, using the picture questions, multiple-choice responses and automatic graph features.

Students build a small model of a sustainable home with classroom craft materials, then use Stop Motion Studio to show one feature working. This directly explores the importance of sustainable living spaces through examples such as opening curtains for daylight, collecting rainwater or adding shade to keep a home cool. Students move one part of the model a little at a time and capture each change as a frame. They present a short stop-motion film using the app’s camera, frame-by-frame capture and playback features.

Elsternwick|Year 1|Who We Are.d: Students program a Beebot to travel through a simple floor grid showing safe and unsafe places around a school. They test and debug the route so the Beebot stops at safe places, linking to the line of inquiry about safe environments. Each pair presents its finished route and explains how the chosen actions support safety and wellbeing. The activity uses the Beebot’s forward, backward, turn and clear buttons.

Students complete a short picture-based class survey about actions that keep their body and mind healthy, such as sleeping, moving, drinking water and asking for help. The class views the automatic charts and discusses how everyday actions influence wellbeing. Together, students present two findings from the survey and choose one healthy action to practise that week. The activity uses simple multiple-choice questions and the built-in response charts in Microsoft Forms.

Students make a digital poster showing actions that help create a safe classroom environment. They arrange teacher-provided photos, add short labels such as “walk inside” and “pack bags away,” and remove any examples that could cause harm. The finished posters are shared with the class to explain how our actions affect ourselves and others. The activity uses PicCollage’s photo layout, text and sticker features.

In pairs, students create a short puppet scene about a common safety or wellbeing problem, such as someone feeling left out or equipment being left on the floor. They move the characters and record dialogue showing a helpful action and how it affects others. Each pair presents its finished scene, linking it to the central idea that our actions influence safety and wellbeing. The activity uses Puppet Pals’ built-in characters, backgrounds, movement and voice recording.

Students view Street View around the streets near the campus and look for features that help people move safely, such as crossings, footpaths and traffic lights. They compare a safer walking place with one that needs extra care, linking to the line of inquiry about safe environments. Small groups present a live Street View walkthrough and explain the safe actions a child should take at two locations. The activity uses Google Maps’ viewing, zoom and Street View features without students needing to log in or create a map.

Elsternwick|Year 2|How We Express Oursel.d: Students use Sketchbook to create an original artwork for How We Express Ourselves, inspired by the colours, lines and shapes they notice in a teacher-selected artwork. This supports the line of inquiry about understanding and appreciating art as students explain which artistic choices inspired them. They produce a finished digital picture and briefly present the thoughts or ideas it expresses. The simple brushes, colour picker, eraser and layers make it easy for Year 2 students to draw, change and refine their work.

Students use Puppet Pals to perform a short scene for How We Express Ourselves in which two characters share an idea in different ways. This connects with the line of inquiry about expressing thoughts and ideas through voice, character and movement. In pairs, students choose characters and a background, move the puppets and record their own dialogue to make a short puppet show. The built-in characters, backgrounds, puppet movement and voice recording keep the task manageable for Year 2.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to make a short animation showing a simple artwork changing from one form of expression into another, such as a drawing becoming a paper sculpture. This explores the line of inquiry about forms of expression and shows how artistic ideas can inspire imagination and creativity. Small groups move paper shapes or classroom art materials a little at a time, photograph each change and add a title. The frame-by-frame camera and playback feature let students immediately test their sequence and fix any jumps.

Students use PicCollage to create a digital gallery page for How We Express Ourselves using photos of their own classroom artworks. This supports the line of inquiry about understanding and appreciating art as they select details they value and write a short reason for each choice. Each student produces a shareable collage with two or three artwork photos, a title and simple labels describing colour, shape, texture or mood. The photo layout, text and sticker features allow Year 2 students to arrange and decorate their gallery page independently.

Elsternwick|Year 2|How We Express Oursel.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
Elsternwick|Year 2|How We Express Oursel.d: Students use Animating a Character with Adobe Express to make an artwork character speak about what it sees, thinks or imagines in How We Express Ourselves. This connects directly to expressing thoughts and ideas while showing how art can inspire imagination and creativity. Students choose a character and background, then record a short first-person message that becomes a shareable animated video. The character choices and automatic mouth movement from a voice recording make the activity quick and achievable for Year 2 students.

Elsternwick|Year 2|How We Organise Ourse.d: Students survey classmates about items they would need or want at a class marketplace, then enter the answers into a simple Excel table. This directly explores the line of inquiry, needs and wants, and shows how marketplaces reflect the needs and wants of communities. Pairs use the chart feature to turn their tally into a clear column chart. They present the chart and explain which items a class marketplace should offer.

Students use Google Maps to view Elsternwick and another Melbourne shopping area, exploring the streets and shopfronts in Street View. They look for places that meet community needs and wants, such as supermarkets, pharmacies, cafes and toy shops. This connects to the central idea that marketplaces reflect the needs and wants of communities. Small groups present a live Street View walkthrough and explain two similarities and two differences they noticed.

Students code a short ScratchJr animation showing a customer visiting a marketplace to buy one needed item and one wanted item. This supports the line of inquiry, needs and wants, while helping students show how different shops serve a community. They use character movement, speech bubbles and page changes to create the customer’s journey. Students test and debug their code, then play their finished animation for a partner.

Students create a short digital book called Our Community Marketplace, with one page for each stall they think the local community needs. This links to the central idea that marketplaces reflect the needs and wants of communities. They use Book Creator’s drawing, text and voice-recording features to show what each stall sells and explain whether it meets a need or a want. The finished books are shared with classmates as marketplace proposals.

Students follow the design process to make a clear advertisement for a new marketplace stall. They choose a product that meets a community need or want, then use PicCollage’s photos, text, shapes and layout tools to create a stall sign with a name, price and short message. Students show a partner their first design, gather one suggestion and edit the layout to make it easier for customers to understand. They present the finished advertisement and explain the change they made after testing it.

Elsternwick|Year 2|How the World Works.d: Students program a Beebot to move between marked spots, testing how forward movement, turns and obstacles change its motion. This directly explores forces around us and the central idea that forces and motion are all around us. Pairs record successful command sequences on simple paper cards and demonstrate their final route to the class. The Beebot’s arrow buttons and clear button make it easy for Year 2 students to code, test and debug one step at a time.

Students code a character to start, stop, speed up, slow down and change direction while exploring forces and motion. This connects to the line of inquiry into scientific laws of motion by showing how different commands change an object’s movement. Each student creates and presents a short animated motion demonstration with spoken or written labels such as push, pull, fast and slow. ScratchJr’s movement blocks, speed blocks and start triggers provide the simple tools needed to build and debug the animation.

Students use blocks or classroom objects to make a short stop-motion sequence showing a push or pull changing an object’s speed or direction. This investigates forces around us and helps students see motion as a series of small changes. Groups produce a short film with a title and labels identifying the force and its effect. Stop Motion Studio’s frame-by-frame camera and playback feature let students capture, review and improve the movement.

Students test toy cars with gentle and stronger pushes, then enter the distance travelled into a teacher-prepared Microsoft Excel table. This supports the line of inquiry into scientific laws of motion by helping students compare how the size of a push affects movement. As a class, students create a simple column chart and present one pattern they notice in the results. Excel’s cells and chart button turn the collected measurements into a clear, shareable visual.

Students find and record examples of forces and motion in the classroom, such as opening a drawer, rolling a ball or pulling a chair. This directly explores the line of inquiry into forces around us by linking pushes and pulls to familiar actions. Each student publishes a short video or photo-and-voice explanation that names the force and describes how the object moved. Seesaw’s built-in camera, microphone and drawing labels allow students to capture and explain their evidence in one place.

Elsternwick|Year 2|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use Seek by iNaturalist during a schoolyard walk to photograph and identify plants, insects and other living things. This explores Earth’s resources and shows that our school grounds provide habitats for many species. Pairs record their identified species in the app and present one discovery that people should help protect. The tool’s camera identification feature gives students an immediate suggested name without requiring them to type or search.

Students conduct a one-day classroom rubbish audit, then enter the numbers of paper scraps, food scraps, soft plastics and reusable items into Microsoft Excel. This connects directly to how our actions affect the environment and the choices we make each day. As a class, students create and present a simple column chart showing which type of waste was most common and choose one realistic way to reduce it. Excel’s table cells and chart button make the results easy for Year 2 students to organise and see.

Students use ScratchJr to code a short animation about caring for our planet, such as switching off a light, using both sides of paper or placing rubbish in the correct bin. This supports the line of inquiry into ways we can care for our planet. Each pair makes two scenes showing an unhelpful choice followed by a better choice, then presents the animation to the class. ScratchJr’s picture-based coding blocks let students move characters, change scenes and add recorded speech.

Students use Book Creator to make a class book called “Our Earth-Friendly Choices” about taking care of our Earth. Each student creates one page explaining a resource such as water, trees or energy and one choice that helps protect it. The finished book combines drawings, short sentences and recorded voices, and can be read aloud to another Year 2 class. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools and voice-recording button make it manageable for young students.

Students use Minecraft Education to build a small home or school area that shows ways we can care for our planet. They add practical features such as recycling bins, gardens, trees, natural light and places for walking or cycling, linking their build to Earth’s resources and how our actions affect the environment. Pairs then guide classmates through their finished build and explain three choices they included. Minecraft Education’s block-building and in-world sign features allow students to construct and label their ideas clearly.

Elsternwick|Year 2|Who We Are.d: Students use Book Creator to make a class book about developing and maintaining healthy relationships. Each pair creates one page showing an everyday friendship problem and a helpful way to respond, linking directly to the line of inquiry about healthy relationships. They add a drawing, a short sentence and a recorded explanation, then present their page to the class. Book Creator’s simple page templates, drawing tool and audio recording make the task manageable for Year 2.

Students use Puppet Pals to act out short scenes about relationships with friends, family members or classmates. Their scene shows how listening, sharing, including others or solving a disagreement can affect someone’s life, connecting to the central idea that our relationships with others impact our lives. Pairs choose characters and backgrounds, record their voices and present their finished puppet scene. The drag-and-move puppets and built-in voice recording let students focus on practising helpful words and actions.

Students complete a short Microsoft Forms class survey about actions that help them feel safe, included and supported in relationships. The class views the automatic charts and discusses what the results show about the impact of relationships on wellbeing. Students then present one evidence-based class agreement, such as inviting others to join a game or listening when someone speaks. Microsoft Forms’ picture questions, large answer choices and automatic charts make the data collection clear and realistic for Year 2.

Students use PicCollage to create a relationship appreciation poster about someone who has a positive impact on their life. They add a photo or drawing, simple labels and two sentences explaining why the relationship is important, connecting directly to the line of inquiry about the importance of relationships. Students publish their finished collage to share with a partner or during a class gallery walk. PicCollage’s ready-made layouts, text boxes, stickers and image tools support a clear, shareable Year 2 product.

Students use Seesaw to record a weekly reflection about one action they took to develop or maintain a healthy relationship. They draw the situation, add a short caption and record their voice explaining how the action may have affected the other person’s wellbeing. At the end of the unit, students choose one reflection to present as evidence that relationships can impact our lives. Seesaw’s drawing, caption and voice-recording features allow Year 2 students to explain their thinking without needing lengthy writing.

Elsternwick|Year 2|Where We Are in Place.d: Students use Google Maps to explore Elsternwick and visit local landmarks through Street View. They look closely for clues about the connection between landmarks and community identity, such as signs, memorials, buildings and gathering spaces. In pairs, students present a short Street View walkthrough of one place and explain why it may be significant to local people. The everyday map search, zoom and Street View features make the exploration possible without students needing to log in or edit a map.

Students use Book Creator to make a short digital book about landmarks and places of significance. Each student adds two or three pages showing how a chosen place tells a story about our history, supporting the central idea. They include a drawing or photo, a simple written fact and a recorded explanation, then share the finished book with classmates. Book Creator's page templates, drawing tools and voice recording button keep the task manageable for Year 2 students.

Students use ScratchJr to code a character travelling between two landmarks linked to a place they have studied. At each stop, the character shares a short fact through a speech bubble, showing how landmarks and symbols represent our history. Students test and debug their code, then present the finished animated journey to a partner. ScratchJr's movement blocks, backgrounds and speech bubbles provide the simple tools needed for the task.

Students use Minecraft Education to build a small model of a landmark or place of significance from the unit. They choose key shapes, colours and symbols that help show the connection between the landmark and the identity of the people connected to it. Students place signs beside important features and lead classmates through a short tour of their finished model. The familiar block-building and sign features allow Year 2 students to create a clear model without complicated coding.

Students use ChatterPix Kids to make a landmark or historical symbol speak about its story. They photograph their own drawing with the app, add a mouth line and record a short first-person message explaining what the landmark represents. The finished talking picture is shared with the class as part of the line of inquiry into how landmarks and symbols represent our history. The built-in camera, mouth-drawing tool and short voice recorder make this a quick and achievable Year 2 task.

Elsternwick|Year 3|How We Express Oursel.d: Students create one page about a personal or cultural celebration, adding a drawing, short text and recorded explanation. They explain how the celebration connects to the line of inquiry, “The ways personal and cultural events are celebrated.” The pages are combined into a class book called Celebrations in Our Community, which students can read and share with families. Book Creator’s simple page templates, drawing tool and audio recording button make this manageable for Year 3 students.

Students record or arrange a short soundscape that represents a celebration or tradition, such as clapping, bells, voices or a steady drum pattern. They discuss how shared sounds connect people and link their work to the central idea that celebrations and traditions shape the culture of a community. Each pair presents its finished audio piece and explains the choices it made. GarageBand’s voice recorder, built-in loops and simple track controls allow students to record, replay and adjust their work.

Students use Google Maps and Street View to explore two places where community celebrations happen, such as Federation Square, a place of worship or a public square in another country. They compare visible landmarks, decorations, gathering spaces and the way each location supports a community event, connecting to the line of inquiry, “Our appreciation of the diversity of cultures.” In pairs, students present a short live Street View walkthrough and point out three details they noticed. Google Maps’ search, zoom and Street View features are used only for viewing and comparing places, with no student login or saved map required.

Small groups use figures, paper props and Stop Motion Studio to show the sequence of a familiar celebration or tradition, such as preparing food, welcoming guests and sharing a special activity. They connect their sequence to the line of inquiry, “The ways personal and cultural events are celebrated,” while taking care not to copy sacred practices without understanding them. Each group produces a short stop-motion film with a clear beginning, middle and end, then presents what the tradition means to the community. The app’s frame-by-frame camera, playback and simple title features let students film, check and improve their sequence.

Students make a one-page invitation or information poster for a class celebration that respectfully includes traditions contributed by different families. They link their choices to the line of inquiry, “How celebrations shape community identity,” by showing how food, music, symbols or greetings can help people feel included. The finished posters are presented to classmates, who identify the features that welcome the whole community. Canva’s ready-made poster templates, text boxes, shapes and image library help Year 3 students create a clear, shareable design.

Elsternwick|Year 3|How We Organise Ourse.d: Students use National Geographic MapMaker to explore and annotate a map of the local community, marking places where rules or laws apply, such as roads, parks, schools and shops. This connects to the line of inquiry about the differences between rules and laws. Pairs add simple labels explaining one rule or law at each place and who is responsible for enforcing it. The map layers, drawing and annotation features help students create a shareable community rules and laws map.

Students use Microsoft Forms to survey classmates about the rights and responsibilities of citizens in everyday situations, such as using a playground or crossing a road. This directly explores the line of inquiry about the rights and responsibilities of citizens. They write clear multiple-choice questions, collect responses and examine the automatically generated charts. Each group presents one chart and explains what it suggests about the class community.

Students use Canva to create a public information poster about one important community rule or law. Their poster explains the right it protects, the responsibility citizens have and a likely consequence when it is not followed, linking directly to the central idea. Students combine short text, headings, icons and images to make the message clear for other Year 3 students. Canva’s poster templates and drag-and-drop design tools help them produce a polished piece to display or present.

Pairs use Podcasting using Canva to record a short interview about people responsible for enforcing rules and laws. One student acts as a host and the other takes the role of a police officer, council worker, teacher or sports referee, using facts gathered during the unit. They record questions and answers explaining what the person enforces, why it matters and what happens when expectations are not met. Canva’s built-in audio recording and timeline features allow each pair to create and play a two-minute class podcast.

Students use Padlet to sort everyday examples connected to rules, laws, rights and responsibilities in a community. The teacher sets up four columns, and students post a short scenario in the column where they think it belongs, then explain their choice. This helps the class examine the differences between rules and laws and the consequences when they are not met. Padlet’s column layout, post and comment features create a shared sorting board that the class can review and discuss.

Elsternwick|Year 3|Who We Are.d: Students create a short “Who We Are” book showing the people, beliefs, values, interests and routines that help shape their identity. This connects directly to the central idea’s focus on the nature of the self, beliefs and values, and human relationships. Each student publishes a book with drawn or photographed illustrations, short written reflections and a recorded reading of one page. Book Creator’s simple page templates, drawing tool, camera and audio recording make the task manageable for Year 3.

Students complete a class survey about everyday habits that support physical, mental and social health, such as sleep, movement, quiet time and talking with trusted people. This directly explores the central idea’s focus on personal, physical, mental and social health. The class examines the anonymous response charts and records three patterns they notice and one realistic wellbeing goal for the group. Microsoft Forms’ question types and automatic charts power the activity without students needing to calculate results by hand.

In small groups, students make a short stop-motion scene about a common Year 3 relationship problem, such as being left out, disagreeing in a game or needing help. This connects to the central idea’s focus on human relationships and social health. They move simple classroom figures frame by frame to show the problem, a respectful response and a positive outcome, then present the finished film to the class. Stop Motion Studio’s frame-by-frame camera, playback and title features keep the filmmaking process straightforward.

Students design a “Values in Action” poster for the Who We Are unit, choosing one value such as kindness, honesty, fairness or courage. This directly connects to the central idea’s focus on beliefs and values by asking students to show what a value looks and sounds like in daily life. Each student publishes a one-page poster with a clear heading, two practical examples and simple images, then briefly presents it to a partner. Canva’s ready-made poster layouts, text boxes and image library make the design achievable in one or two lessons.

Students build a shared class wall called “People and Practices That Help Us Thrive” as part of the Who We Are unit. This connects to the central idea’s focus on mental, social and spiritual health and human relationships. Each student posts one safe, non-private example of a person, place or routine that helps them feel supported, then adds a thoughtful comment or question to a classmate’s post. Padlet’s simple post cards, image option and commenting feature create a shareable class collection that can support a follow-up discussion.

Elsternwick|Year 3|Sharing the Planet.d: Students create a short digital field guide about plants and animals living in a chosen Victorian ecosystem. Each page explains a structural feature or behaviour that helps one living thing survive, linking directly to the line of inquiry about adaptations and structural features of living things. Students publish a book with labelled pictures, short explanations and a final page showing how the living things depend on one another. Book Creator’s simple page templates, drawing tools, image tool and voice recording make the task manageable for Year 3.

Students survey a small part of the school grounds and enter counts of visible living things such as birds, insects, trees and flowering plants into Microsoft Excel. They use the results to discuss the roles of living things in an ecosystem and consider why some are more common than others. Each group produces a clear table and a column chart, then presents one pattern they noticed in the data. Excel’s cells, simple totals and chart button are the main features used for the task.

In small groups, students build a simple ecosystem in Minecraft Education that includes shelter, food, water and several living things. They then add one realistic environmental change, such as reduced water or removed vegetation, and adapt their design to help the living things survive. This directly explores how adaptation and sustainability support survival in changing environments, as well as actions that benefit or harm ecosystems. Students use Minecraft’s blocks, animals, plants and in-world signs to build and label a model they can guide classmates through.

Students use clay or paper models to show how an animal’s structural feature helps it survive in a changing environment. Their stop-motion sequence might show a bird using its beak to reach food or a camouflaged insect avoiding a predator, connecting directly to the line of inquiry about adaptations and structural features of living things. Each pair produces a short film with a title and simple captions explaining the survival advantage. Stop Motion Studio’s frame-by-frame camera and playback tools let students capture, test and improve the movement.

Students create a one-page campaign poster about an action that would benefit a local ecosystem, such as planting native species, protecting habitat or reducing litter. They explain which living things are helped and how the action supports a healthier ecosystem, directly addressing actions that benefit or harm ecosystems. Each student publishes a poster with a clear heading, two or three facts and a practical action for the school community. Adobe Express’s poster templates, text boxes and built-in image search provide a simple way to arrange and present the message.

Elsternwick|Year 3|Where We Are in Place.d: Students use Google Maps to retrace the route of an explorer connected to the unit Where We Are in Place and Time. They view key locations, measure distances and use Street View to compare the landscapes and settlements the explorer encountered. This supports the line of inquiry about how exploration brings change and new understandings for people, places and society. Pairs finish by presenting a live map walkthrough, using the search, distance and Street View features to explain three important stops.

Students code Sphero BOLT to travel across a simple floor map that represents an exploration route, including a starting point, obstacles and a final destination. They test and debug the speed, direction and timing commands as they consider the challenges that can affect exploration. This connects to the line of inquiry about the factors that motivate exploration and the decisions explorers make along the way. Each group presents its completed coded route and explains one discovery or route change caused by testing.

Students create a short digital field journal about a past exploration studied in Where We Are in Place and Time. They add pages showing the explorer's motivation, key discoveries and ways those discoveries shaped or changed society. This directly explores the central idea that exploration leads to new discoveries that can shape and change society. Using Book Creator's page templates, drawing, image and audio-recording features, students publish a shareable journal with captions and a spoken reflection.

Students build a recorded explanation comparing what people first believed about a place with what they understood after an important exploration or discovery. They arrange teacher-provided images on the canvas, add arrows and labels, and move through the evidence while recording their voices. This addresses the line of inquiry about how people reflect on discoveries from the past to inform change. The finished product is a short narrated presentation powered by Explain Everything's drawing, object-moving and screen-recording features.

Students use Microsoft Forms to collect class opinions about why people explore, with choices such as curiosity, trade, safety, resources and scientific learning. They review the automatic response charts and identify the most common motivations and any surprising patterns. This provides a simple investigation of the line of inquiry about the factors that motivate exploration. The class presents the built-in summary charts and records a shared conclusion about what their data suggests.

Elsternwick|Year 3|How the World Works.d: Students investigate How the World Works by testing which wrapping material keeps an ice cube from melting for the longest time. They enter each group’s measurements into Microsoft Excel and use the results to explore the central idea that humans use their understanding of scientific principles to take action. Using the simple table and chart features, students compare the materials and look for patterns in the class data. They produce a labelled column chart and present a recommendation for keeping something cold.

Students explore How the World Works by coding Sphero BOLT to travel across smooth flooring and carpet using the same speed and movement instructions. They test, observe and debug their code to investigate how friction changes movement, linking to the line of inquiry about the process of learning. The block coding, speed controls and movement commands allow students to run a fair comparison several times. Each group finishes with two saved programs and a short classroom demonstration explaining what they changed and discovered.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to show how heating and cooling can change the way particles move in solids, liquids and gases as part of How the World Works. This connects to the line of inquiry about how science brings about new understandings and changes. They move small classroom objects a little at a time and use the frame-by-frame camera feature to create a clear model of faster, slower, closer and more spread-out particles. Students publish a short labelled animation and present the scientific idea it demonstrates.

Students explore the Elsternwick campus with Seek by iNaturalist to observe and identify plants, insects and other living things connected to How the World Works. They use the app’s camera identification feature and check visible features carefully, mirroring the work of scientists who collect evidence before making a claim. Each pair records several confirmed or partly confirmed identifications in the app and compares what was found in different parts of the campus. They present their saved observation collection and suggest one practical action that could support local living things.

Students investigate the work of scientists in How the World Works by choosing a scientist from a teacher-provided set of reliable facts. They create a one-page profile showing the scientist’s question, how they tested ideas, what they discovered and how that understanding led people to take action. Canva’s poster templates, text boxes, shapes and image library help Year 3 students organise the information clearly. The finished science profile is published as a classroom poster and shared in a short gallery walk.

Elsternwick|Year 4|How We Organise Ourse.d: Students explore how transport, communication and community services connect places as part of the unit How We Organise Ourselves. They use MapMaker’s map layers, markers, lines and measurement tools to trace links between homes, schools, hospitals, shops and transport hubs. This directly explores the line of inquiry about interconnections within and across systems. Each group presents an annotated map showing one local system, the places it connects and what could happen if one connection stopped working.

Students investigate human systems by coding a Micro:bit to act as a pedestrian crossing controller. They use simple blocks to show stop and walk symbols, add timed pauses and test and debug the sequence so that it works reliably. This connects to the central idea that systems connect us by showing how an automated system helps drivers and pedestrians share a community space safely. Each pair presents its working program and explains the purpose of every step in the sequence.

Students collect class data about one everyday system, such as how people travel to school or how lunch orders move through the school. They enter their tally into Excel and use its sorting, totals and chart features to find patterns. This supports the line of inquiry into the influence of systems on communities by helping students see who uses the system and how often. Each group produces a labelled chart and presents one conclusion and one practical suggestion for improving the system.

Students create a short digital book explaining how a familiar human system works, such as rubbish collection, public transport, food delivery or the school library. They use Book Creator’s page templates, drawing, text and voice-recording features to show the people, places and steps involved. This directly addresses the line of inquiry into human systems and highlights how each part depends on other parts. The finished book includes a system diagram, a narrated explanation and a page describing what happens when one part fails.

Students model a delivery system by coding Sphero BOLT to travel between labelled classroom locations representing a warehouse, sorting centre and local address. They use the Sphero coding blocks to set movement, direction, speed, pauses and coloured signals, then test and debug the route. This explores the central idea that systems connect us by showing how an item must move through several linked stages to reach its destination. Each team demonstrates its completed route and explains how changing or removing one stage affects the whole system.

Elsternwick|Year 4|How We Express Oursel.d: Students create a short digital museum about how technology transforms how we create and share ideas. Each page features a communication tool from a different time, with students adding a labelled drawing, a short explanation and a recorded spoken message. This directly explores the evolution of communication tools, and the finished books can be presented to classmates. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools, text boxes and built-in audio recording make the task manageable for Year 4 students.

Elsternwick|Year 4|How We Express Oursel.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
Elsternwick|Year 4|How We Express Oursel.d: Students write and record a short message about how technology expands creative possibilities, then choose a digital character to deliver it. They test how changing the character, background and tone of voice affects the way the same idea is expressed. This connects directly to the impact of technology on expression, and students present their finished animated message to a small group. The tool’s simple voice recording and automatic character animation power the activity without students needing to animate each movement themselves.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to show how technology transforms how we create and share ideas by making a short animation from classroom objects or paper shapes. They plan a clear message, move the objects a little at a time, capture each frame and test the sequence before adding titles or narration. This explores how technology expands creative possibilities, and each group finishes with a shareable 30–60 second animation. The frame capture, onion-skin guide and playback features help Year 4 students film and improve their work independently.

Pairs create a three-minute podcast episode about the evolution of communication tools, comparing an older tool such as a letter or landline with a modern one such as messaging or video calls. Students script, record and edit a host-and-guest conversation, including one benefit and one possible drawback of the newer technology. Their finished episode explains how technology transforms how we create and share ideas and can be played to the class. Canva’s audio recording, timeline editing and podcast templates keep the production simple and contained in one tool.

Students design a simple three-dimensional model of a future communication device that could change how people create and share ideas. They combine basic shapes, add labelled features and explain how their design expands creative possibilities or changes expression. Each student ends with a digital model that they rotate on screen and present to a partner for feedback. Tinkercad’s drag-and-drop shapes, resize handles, grouping and text features make the design task realistic for Year 4.

Elsternwick|Year 4|How the World Works.d: Students use Google Maps to explore a community affected by an earthquake, volcanic eruption or tsunami and compare its location with nearby coastlines, mountains and settlements. This directly supports the line of inquiry into how extreme environments cause natural disasters. Pairs use the world map, satellite view and Street View to identify visible risks and then present a short guided walkthrough to the class. The teacher can provide a small set of locations so the viewing task stays focused and manageable.

Students enter a teacher-provided set of earthquake or volcanic eruption data into Microsoft Excel, including dates, locations and measurements such as magnitude or ash-cloud height. They use the chart feature to look for patterns linked to the causes of geological change over time. Each pair produces a labelled graph and writes two simple observations in nearby cells. The finished spreadsheet gives students a clear, shareable record of how the Earth has changed across different events.

Students code a Micro:bit to use its accelerometer as a simple earthquake warning model. This connects to the impact of natural events on communities by showing how an alert can help people respond quickly to shaking. They test different amounts of movement, debug the trigger level and program the lights or sound to give a clear warning. Each group presents its working warning device and explains what happened during testing.

Students use Minecraft Education to build a small community beside a volcano, coastline or fault zone, then redesign it to reduce the effects of a natural event. This explores the central idea that changes to the Earth impact environments and communities. Using ordinary building blocks, signs and the in-game camera, students add practical features such as higher ground, evacuation routes, barriers and safe meeting places. Each group presents a short tour of its finished community and explains three design choices.

Students use Book Creator to make a short digital guide about how one natural event changes the Earth and affects a community. This directly addresses the line of inquiry into the impact of natural events on communities. They create pages showing the cause, the environmental change, the community impact and sensible preparation or recovery actions. The simple page templates, drawing tools and built-in voice recording let students publish an illustrated, narrated book to share with classmates.

Elsternwick|Year 4|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use National Geographic MapMaker to locate and label several First Nations language groups across Australia using teacher-provided, community-approved information. This directly explores the line of inquiry about the diversity of First Nations people and shows that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples are not one single group. Students create a shareable map with labels, short notes and a legend, while avoiding restricted or culturally sensitive places. The everyday map layers, drawing and annotation features make the task manageable for Year 4.

Students use Book Creator to make a short digital book about how Country, language and community are significant to the lives of First Nations people. Each pair builds pages from teacher-provided First Nations sources, adding key facts, respectful illustrations and recorded explanations. Their finished book presents learning about the importance of Country and includes a page acknowledging the Traditional Owners of a place studied. Book Creator's page templates, drawing tools, text boxes and audio-recording button support the whole task.

Students use GarageBand to record a two-minute radio segment about the importance of community, family and kinship to First Nations people. Working from a teacher-provided case study, they write and record a host introduction, key facts and a closing reflection without pretending to speak as a First Nations person. Each group produces a polished audio segment that can be played to the class. GarageBand's voice recorder, simple track editor and built-in sound effects allow students to record, trim and balance their work.

Students use Google Maps to view several places connected to teacher-selected First Nations communities, including urban, regional and remote settings. They explore the world map, satellite view and available Street View imagery to investigate the diversity of First Nations people and the different features of Country. Pairs then present a live Google Maps walkthrough, identifying visible waterways, landforms, community facilities and distances while explaining that a map cannot show every cultural connection to Country. The search, zoom, distance and Street View features are central to the task, and students do not save pins or create a custom map.

Students use Explain Everything to create a narrated visual explanation of the importance of Country to First Nations people. They place teacher-provided quotes or facts on a canvas, draw links between Country, language, community and responsibility, and record themselves explaining those links in their own words. The finished product is a short playable presentation that uses evidence rather than stereotypes or imagined First Nations experiences. Explain Everything's blank canvas, pen, text and voice-recording features let students build and present the explanation in one place.

Elsternwick|Year 4|Who We Are.d: Students use Book Creator to make a class book called “Leaders Shape Communities”, with each pair creating a page about a local, national or global leader. They identify the leader’s role, responsibilities and actions, linking their research to the line of inquiry about the roles and responsibilities of effective leadership. Each page includes short written sections, an image and a recorded student explanation, and the finished book is shared with the class. The simple page templates, image tools and built-in audio recording make the task manageable for Year 4 students.

Students use Microsoft Forms to collect class opinions about the qualities of influential leaders, such as fairness, courage, listening and honesty. In small groups, they write a short set of multiple-choice and rating questions, then review the automatic charts to see which qualities their classmates value most. Each group presents one finding and explains how it connects to the idea that leaders shape communities. The ready-made question types and automatic response charts do the main work, so students can focus on asking clear questions and interpreting results.

Students use National Geographic MapMaker to locate community organisations where leadership has a clear purpose, such as councils, hospitals, schools, emergency services and charities. They add markers with short notes explaining who leads in each place, what responsibilities they have and how their decisions affect the community. Pairs then present their annotated map and connect it to the line of inquiry about the purpose of leadership in communities. The search, marker and annotation features allow students to build and share a clear visual map without needing advanced mapping skills.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to create a short scene showing a leader helping a group solve an everyday community problem, such as sharing a playground, organising a fundraiser or responding to litter. Their scene must show at least two qualities of influential leaders through visible actions and dialogue, rather than simply naming the qualities. Students build the scene with classroom objects, capture it frame by frame and publish a short stop-motion video with titles or recorded voices. The large capture button, frame timeline and playback feature make it easy to test, adjust and improve the sequence.

Students use Adobe Express to create a one-page “Effective Leader” profile based on a real leader studied during the Who We Are unit. They explain the leader’s purpose, key responsibilities, influential qualities and one example of how that person shaped a community. Students publish a clear visual profile containing a heading, brief text, images and a quotation, then present it to a small group. The ready-made poster templates, text boxes and image tools help Year 4 students produce a polished piece within one or two lessons.

Elsternwick|Year 4|Where We Are in Place.d: Students explore a teacher-selected migration journey connected to the unit topic of human migration, such as travel from Italy to Melbourne after the Second World War. They view the starting place and destination, compare distance and scale, and use Street View to notice differences between the two communities. This directly supports the line of inquiry into migration throughout history and helps students see the size and setting of a real journey. Pairs present a short live map walkthrough, using the search, zoom, distance and Street View features to explain the route and important landmarks.

Students create a short digital book about human migration from the viewpoint of a real or teacher-provided migrant profile. They explain the challenges or opportunities behind the move and show effects on the individual, culture and new community. Each finished book includes written pages, labelled drawings or photos, and a recorded first-person reflection. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools and built-in audio recording make the book manageable for Year 4 students.

Students build and run a class survey using fictional human migration situations, asking which challenges or opportunities might lead people to move. They collect classmates’ choices and examine how the answers connect to the line of inquiry about reasons people migrate. Each group presents the automatic results charts and explains one clear pattern or surprising result. Microsoft Forms’ question templates, response collection and automatic charts power the whole task without students needing to calculate totals by hand.

Students work together to build a class timeline showing examples of human migration throughout history. Each student adds one post with a date, place, brief explanation of why people moved, and an image, then reads and responds to classmates’ posts. The class uses the finished timeline to compare recurring challenges and opportunities across different periods. Padlet’s timeline layout, post boxes, image upload and comment feature make the shared display easy to create and present.

Students design a one-page infographic explaining how one example of human migration affected a community, culture and individual people. They organise their information under simple headings such as reasons for moving, challenges, opportunities and lasting changes. The finished infographic is presented to a small group and published as a clear visual summary of the unit learning. Canva’s ready-made infographic templates, text boxes, icons and image library help students create a polished result within one or two lessons.

Elsternwick|Year 5|How We Express Oursel.d: Students use Canva to create two versions of an advertisement for the same everyday product, with one aimed at younger children and the other at adults. This explores the line of inquiry about the devices used to target audiences through choices such as colour, images, slogans and font size. Each pair publishes a side-by-side advertisement and presents the choices they made for each audience. Canva’s ready-made templates, stock images and simple text tools make the task manageable for Year 5 students.

Students use GarageBand to record a 30-second audio advertisement connected to How We Express Ourselves, choosing a clear target audience such as families, gamers or sports fans. They explore the central idea that people can create or manipulate messages by changing their voice, wording, sound effects and background music. Each group plays its finished advertisement to the class, who identify the intended audience and the persuasive devices they noticed. GarageBand’s voice recorder, music loops and simple editing timeline provide everything needed for the task.

Students use Microsoft Forms to test how different messages influence their classmates. They create a short survey showing pairs of slogans or product descriptions, then ask respondents which option they would choose and why. This directly supports the line of inquiry about how we know we have been influenced, and students present the automatic charts as evidence of which words or claims were most effective. Microsoft Forms’ question choices, image option and automatic response charts keep the data collection simple and clear.

Students use Padlet to build a class message detective board for How We Express Ourselves. The teacher sets up columns such as emotional language, celebrity appeal, special offers and missing information, and students add posts explaining how sample messages target an audience. This supports the critical evaluation of messages, with students commenting on whether each message is fair, exaggerated or misleading. Padlet’s columns, post boxes and comment feature create a shareable class collection that can be reviewed together.

Students use Kahoot to create a short quiz that asks classmates to identify the audience and persuasive device used in different messages. Their questions can include brief slogans, claims or images and should cover ideas such as humour, repetition, fear, popularity and expert opinion. This checks students’ critical evaluation of messages, and each group hosts its finished quiz for the class before discussing any answers that caused disagreement. Kahoot’s quiz builder, image questions and live results make the activity quick to create and easy to present.

Elsternwick|Year 5|How We Organise Ourse.d: Students use Microsoft Forms to survey classmates about what they value in sustainable products, such as reusable packaging, fair prices and recycled materials. This supports the line of inquiry into sustainable business practices by showing how entrepreneurs can gather evidence before developing a product. Students write clear questions, collect responses and study the automatic charts to identify customer preferences. They present a short summary of the survey findings and explain one decision their business would make as a result.

Students use National Geographic MapMaker to trace where the materials for an everyday product, such as a cotton T-shirt or chocolate bar, might come from and where the finished product is sold. This connects directly to how our environment is impacted by the products we create. Using the map’s drawing, marker and information features, students add key locations and notes about transport distances, waste or environmental pressures. They present their completed supply-chain map and suggest one realistic change an entrepreneur could make to reduce the product’s impact.

Students use Adobe Express to create a digital advertisement for a sustainable product or service they have planned. This addresses the central idea that entrepreneurs have a responsibility to develop, market and sell sustainable products and services. Students combine a product image, business name, price, sustainability claim and clear explanation of how the business will give back. They use a ready-made poster or webpage template and present the finished advertisement to classmates as potential customers.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to make a short animation showing the life cycle of a product, from raw materials and production through to sale, use and disposal or reuse. This explores how our environment is impacted by the products we create. Students move simple paper pieces or classroom objects, capture each frame and add titles that identify wasteful and sustainable choices. They publish a short stop-motion film that ends with advice for a more responsible entrepreneur.

Students use Book Creator to build a short digital business proposal for a class enterprise that gives part of its profit, time or products back to the community. This focuses on the line of inquiry about the power of giving back.
