Each proposal includes the product or service, intended customers, sustainable business choices, pricing and a clear giving-back plan. Students use Book Creator’s page templates, text, drawing, image and voice-recording features to make a shareable book, then present it to the class for feedback.

Elsternwick|Year 5|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use Book Creator to make a short guide about a familiar Year 5 conflict, such as disagreement over game rules or shared materials. They explain the type of conflict, its causes and impacts, then show how listening, compromise or mediation could lead to a peaceful solution. Each guide includes a page for each person’s point of view and a final page presenting the agreed solution. The simple page templates, text boxes, drawing tools and audio recording feature help students create a book they can share with classmates.

Small groups use Minecraft Education to build a community where two neighbourhoods must share limited land, water and building materials. Students pause during the build to identify causes of conflict, negotiate fair rules and test whether their solution meets both groups’ needs. They finish with a shared community and use in-game signs or boards to present the agreement that helped them build peacefully. The block-building, shared world and in-game signs make the negotiation visible and practical without requiring advanced coding.

Students use Microsoft Excel to record examples of playground or classroom conflict under headings such as type, likely cause, impact and possible peaceful solution. They sort the examples into categories and create a column chart showing which causes or solutions appear most often. This gives the class simple data for discussing the lines of inquiry about types, causes and impacts of conflict. Excel’s tables, sorting and chart buttons allow students to produce a clear chart and a short written conclusion to present.

Elsternwick|Year 5|Sharing the Planet.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
Elsternwick|Year 5|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use Animating a Character with Adobe Express to create a short message from a fictional peer mediator responding to a Year 5 conflict. In the script, the character briefly names the cause and impact of the conflict, then explains a peaceful resolution using listening, calm language and a fair next step. Students record their voice and publish a short animated clip that can be played to the class. The tool’s character choice, background options and automatic voice animation make the task manageable in one or two lessons.

Students use National Geographic MapMaker to explore a teacher-selected example of conflict connected to shared land, water or natural resources. They examine map layers such as rivers, borders, population or land cover, then add labels and notes showing where competing needs may cause conflict and who could be affected. This directly supports the line of inquiry into the causes and impacts of conflict and helps students consider where cooperation could make a difference. MapMaker’s layers, drawing tools, labels and measurement feature allow each group to publish and present an annotated map with a suggested peaceful solution.

Elsternwick|Year 5|Who We Are.d: Students use Microsoft Forms to create a class survey about everyday choices linked to fairness, honesty, kindness and responsibility. This directly explores how values and beliefs impact choices. They collect anonymous responses, view the automatic charts and present two patterns they notice about how different choices could affect others. The simple question builder and built-in response charts make the task manageable in a few lessons.

Students use Book Creator to make a short digital book about a character facing three realistic choices at school, such as including someone, reporting damage or sharing limited equipment. For each choice, they explain the belief or value involved and show how the action impacts other people, connecting directly to the central idea. Their finished book includes written scenarios, illustrations and recorded narration, then ends with advice about responsible decision-making. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools and audio recording are the main features used.

Students use Adobe Express to design a one-page campaign encouraging responsible decision-making in the classroom or playground. They choose one value, such as respect or fairness, and show how actions based on that value can positively impact others. The finished poster includes a clear message, two practical examples and a short call to action that students present to the class. Adobe Express’s ready-made poster templates, text boxes and image library keep the design process simple.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to create a short animation about an everyday dilemma connected to Who We Are, such as whether to exclude a classmate or take credit for someone else’s work. They move simple paper figures or classroom objects frame by frame to show the choice, its impact on others and a more responsible alternative. This addresses the line of inquiry about how people’s choices and actions impact others. The app’s frame-by-frame camera, playback and voice-recording features allow students to publish a clear one-minute scene.

Students use Explain Everything to map a decision pathway for a realistic Year 5 situation, such as receiving an unkind group message or finding lost property. They add branches showing possible choices, the values behind each choice and the likely impact on different people, directly exploring responsible decision-making. Students record a short spoken explanation while moving through their pathway, then present the finished recording to a partner group. Explain Everything’s digital whiteboard, arrows, movable text and built-in recording are central to the task.

Elsternwick|Year 5|Where We Are in Place.d: Students use National Geographic MapMaker to locate and label key places connected to British colonisation in Australia, including arrival points, early settlements and areas of Aboriginal resistance. This directly explores the line of inquiry about the impact of colonisation by showing how settlement spread across Country. Students create a shareable annotated map with markers, short evidence-based notes and measured distances between locations. The activity uses the tool’s map layers, drawing, marker and distance features.

Students use Book Creator to make a short evidence-based book about one colonisation story, such as the arrival of the First Fleet, the experiences of a named First Nations community or an example of resistance. This connects directly to the line of inquiry about colonisation stories and helps students notice that the same event can be described from different perspectives. Each student publishes a six-page book containing brief text, images, captions, source acknowledgements and a recorded reflection. The activity uses Book Creator’s page templates, image import, audio recording and read-aloud features.

Students enter a small set of teacher-provided data about changes linked to colonisation, such as Aboriginal population estimates, language use or land ownership across selected years. This supports the line of inquiry about the effects of colonisation in the past, present and future. Students build a labelled graph, identify two visible trends and add a short evidence-based statement explaining what the data shows and what it cannot show. The activity relies on Excel’s simple tables, chart button and text boxes.

In small groups, students plan and record a three-minute podcast episode explaining one way colonisation has shaped Australian society. This addresses the central idea that colonisation has shaped society, while requiring students to distinguish historical evidence from personal opinion. Each group records an introduction, two clearly attributed facts, a discussion of a past or present effect and a closing question for listeners. Students use the microphones, headphones and recording controls to produce a clear audio episode that can be played to the class.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to create a short timeline showing how one effect of colonisation developed from the past into the present. This directly explores the line of inquiry about the effects of colonisation in the past, present and future. Using paper maps, dates, labels and carefully worded captions, students photograph each small change and finish with a question about what may happen next. The activity uses the app’s frame-by-frame camera, playback, title and timing features to produce a shareable one-minute animation.

Elsternwick|Year 5|How the World Works.d: Students build a small structure designed to withstand an earthquake, then use the motor to create a simple shaking platform and test it. This directly explores how design processes are used to generate and test solutions to natural hazards. They change one feature at a time, such as the base width or bracing, and record their test results in the project’s coding workspace. The LEGO building pieces, motor and block coding make repeated building, testing and debugging manageable for Year 5 students.

Students build a small flood-ready community with raised homes, safe paths, drainage channels and an emergency meeting place. This connects to the central idea that design processes enable people to respond creatively to challenges in the natural world. They release water from a set starting point, observe where it travels, then rebuild parts of the community that do not work. Minecraft’s building blocks and flowing water allow students to create, test and present a shareable model within one world.

Students enter a teacher-provided set of natural hazard data, such as earthquake strength, cyclone wind speed or flood height, into a spreadsheet. This helps them investigate the nature and impact of natural hazards through the line of inquiry about causation. They sort the data, calculate simple averages and create a column or line chart showing patterns and differences. Excel’s tables, formulas and chart button turn the class data into a clear visual report students can present.

Students code Sphero BOLT to carry a small emergency-supply marker along a floor map from a response centre to a community cut off by a natural hazard. This explores how design processes are used to generate and test solutions, including the practical need for safe and accurate navigation. Teams measure distances, program movement and turns, test the route, then debug their code when the robot hits a blocked road or hazard zone. Sphero’s block coding, movement controls and programmable lights let students demonstrate a working response route.

Students create a one-page public safety guide for a chosen natural hazard, such as a bushfire, flood or earthquake. This addresses the ethical and practical considerations in human responses to natural challenges by asking students to include advice that is accurate, useful and accessible to different community members. Their finished guide combines a clear heading, short safety steps, labelled images and a section explaining why the recommended design response helps. Adobe Express templates, text boxes, icons and image tools make the guide easy to design, revise and publish.

Elsternwick|Year 6|How the World Works.d: Students code the Micro:bit to measure and display light levels in several parts of the classroom at different times of day. They test each location repeatedly and record the readings to explore sustainable energy practices and whether solar panels would work equally well in every position. Each group presents its results and recommends the strongest location for collecting solar energy. The activity uses the Micro:bit’s built-in light sensor, simple coding blocks and LED display.

Students build and test a virtual circuit that converts electrical energy into light, sound or movement. They change one component at a time, such as the battery, resistor, light or motor, and observe how the circuit behaves. This directly explores the central idea that energy may be converted and transformed to support human progress. Students finish with a labelled circuit design and a short written explanation, using Tinkercad’s drag-and-drop circuit parts and simulation button.

Students enter a small set of class-provided data comparing the cost, energy output and carbon emissions of solar, wind, coal and gas. They use formulas to calculate totals or averages, then create charts to investigate the impact of different energy sources on the planet. Each group presents one evidence-based recommendation about which source should supply a fictional town. Excel’s table, formula and chart features make the comparisons clear and shareable.

Students use National Geographic MapMaker to investigate where solar, wind and hydroelectric energy could be produced across Australia. They examine map layers showing features such as sunlight, wind, rivers, population and protected environments, then add labels or annotations to mark suitable locations. This connects to different forms of energy and how they are used, as well as their possible impact on the planet. Students publish or present an annotated energy suitability map, using MapMaker’s layers, drawing and annotation features.

Students create a short digital guide called “Energy Transformations in Everyday Life” using examples such as a toaster, bicycle, speaker and solar light. On each page they explain the starting energy, how it changes form and how the device supports people, linking directly to the central idea about energy conversion and human progress. They include their own diagrams, captions and recorded spoken explanations, then share the finished book with classmates. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools, audio recording and page-turning format support the whole task.

Elsternwick|Year 6|How We Organise Ourse.d: Students build a digital process journal for their student-led exhibition (PYPEX), adding their questions, research notes, decisions and weekly reflections. This directly supports the line of inquiry into approaches to learning by showing how their thinking and organisation develop over time. They finish with a shareable book that includes key evidence, challenges, changes and a final reflection. Book Creator’s simple page templates, text, drawing and voice-recording features make it manageable for Year 6 students.

Students enter and organise survey or observation data connected to their student-led exhibition (PYPEX) inquiry. This supports the line of inquiry into research and presentation skills by asking them to check their data, choose a suitable graph and explain what the results show. They produce a clear data table and one or two charts that can be displayed during the exhibition. Excel’s cells, sorting tools and chart button are the everyday features that power the task.

Students create a research evidence board for their student-led exhibition (PYPEX), with separate posts for useful facts, source details, expert viewpoints and questions that still need answering. This connects directly to the line of inquiry into research and presentation skills because students must organise evidence and distinguish strong information from unsupported claims. They end up with a shareable board that classmates can read and respond to with specific feedback comments. Padlet’s columns, text posts and comment feature keep the work visible and easy to manage.

Students make and record a short rehearsal presentation explaining the central idea, evidence and proposed action from their student-led exhibition (PYPEX) inquiry. This supports the line of inquiry into research and presentation skills by giving them a practical way to practise clear explanations before presenting to an audience. They produce a narrated presentation that can be replayed for self-checking and teacher feedback. Explain Everything’s slide canvas, drawing tools, image import and built-in recording feature allow students to point to evidence while they speak.

Students create a short audience quiz based on the most important learning from their student-led exhibition (PYPEX) inquiry. This connects to the central idea that students develop and present their own units of inquiry because they must decide which ideas an audience should understand and how to check that understanding. They publish and run a five-question quiz at the end of a practice presentation, then use the response results to identify explanations that need improving. Kahoot’s question builder, answer choices and live results screen make the activity quick and practical for Year 6.

Elsternwick|Year 6|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use Google Maps to explore Street View around Elsternwick and compare it with another community near a river, coast or forest. They look for visible examples of how each community interacts with the environment, such as tree cover, transport, waterways, rubbish facilities and protected spaces. This directly explores the central idea that communities interact with the environment in different ways. Using Street View, satellite view and the distance tool, pairs present a short guided comparison of the two places to the class.

Students use Microsoft Forms to create a short survey about community values and local environmental choices, such as reducing waste, protecting trees and using public transport. They collect anonymous responses from classmates and examine the built-in charts to see which actions the group values most. This directly supports the line of inquiry about how community values shape the management of the natural environment. Each group presents one clear finding and one realistic action suggested by its survey data.

Students use Microsoft Excel to record and analyse one week of classroom waste data as part of their study of sustainable practices. They enter daily amounts for landfill, recycling and food scraps, then use simple formulas to calculate totals and compare categories. This connects directly to the line of inquiry about the need for sustainable practices. Using Excel's table and chart features, students produce a clear waste report and set a measurable class target for the following week.

Students use Minecraft Education to build a small sustainable neighbourhood that shows how a community can care for its natural environment. Their model must include practical features such as native planting, shared green space, water collection, low-waste systems and safe walking or cycling routes. This addresses the central idea that communities interact with the environment in different ways and the need for sustainable practices. Using the game's building blocks, signs and camera feature, groups create a walk-through model and present the choices they made.

Students use Adobe Express to create a one-page public awareness poster encouraging environmental stewardship at school or in the Elsternwick community. They choose one achievable action, such as protecting habitat, reducing litter, saving water or cutting single-use packaging, and support it with a clear reason and practical steps. This directly connects to the line of inquiry about taking action for environmental stewardship. Using a poster template, text, icons and images, students publish a polished campaign piece that can be displayed for other classes.

Elsternwick|Year 6|How We Express Oursel.d: Students use Book Creator to keep a digital process journal for the How We Express Ourselves unit, showing how their thinking and planned action change over time. This directly supports the line of inquiry, “How we evidence our process.” They add dated reflections, photographs of work, short audio explanations and examples of feedback they acted on. The simple page, audio-recording and media tools help them create a shareable digital book that clearly shows their learning journey.

Students use Microsoft Forms to find out whether a message about a chosen community issue can provoke others to make meaningful change in the How We Express Ourselves unit. They create a short survey, share it with classmates before and after presenting their message, and compare the responses. This connects directly to the line of inquiry, “How we provoke others to make meaningful change.” The question builder and automatic response charts give each group clear evidence to present about which parts of its message worked.

Students use Minecraft Education to build a small interactive exhibition about an issue they care about for the How We Express Ourselves unit. This explores the central idea, “Thinking beyond ourselves empowers us to act,” by asking visitors to consider how their choices affect other people or the environment. Students construct a simple walk-through space with signs, examples of the problem and realistic actions visitors could take. The block-building tools, signs and in-game presentation mode allow each group to guide classmates through its finished exhibition.

Students use Podcasting using Canva to produce a three-minute episode about an action taken during the How We Express Ourselves unit. They explain what they did, interview a classmate about what changed, and reflect on how the action grew their understanding. This directly addresses the line of inquiry, “How taking action helps us grow our understandings.” Canva’s built-in recording, timeline and audio-editing features help students publish a clear episode with an introduction, interview and closing call to action.

Students use National Geographic MapMaker to map places connected to a local or global issue explored in the How We Express Ourselves unit. They add markers, labels and simple notes showing where the issue is visible, who may be affected and where practical action could happen. This supports the central idea, “Thinking beyond ourselves empowers us to act,” by linking a persuasive message to real people and places. MapMaker’s layers, markers and measurement tools help each group present a shareable evidence map and explain one meaningful change it wants to encourage.

Elsternwick|Year 6|Who We Are.d: Students create a short digital book about how their sense of self has changed from early childhood to Year 6. This directly explores the physical, social, emotional and intellectual changes that occur throughout life. Each page includes a safe personal example, an image or drawing, and a short reflection on what influenced that change. Students use Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools and built-in voice recording to publish a book they can share with classmates or family.

Students build a class survey about influences that shape identity, such as family, friendships, culture, interests, school and important experiences. They write respectful multiple-choice questions and avoid collecting names or private personal details. After classmates respond, students use the automatic charts in Microsoft Forms to identify patterns and discuss how different influences contribute to an evolving sense of self. Each group presents two findings and one question raised by the survey data.

Students design a one-page visual called “Layers of My Identity” to show the interests, relationships, places, values and experiences that help shape who they are. This connects directly to the line of inquiry about influences that shape our identity. They arrange short captions, symbols, shapes and suitable personal or stock images, choosing what they feel comfortable sharing. Canva’s templates, drag-and-drop layout tools and image library help students produce a polished poster for a classroom gallery.

Students record a two-minute audio reflection about one way their sense of self has changed and an influence that contributed to that change. This addresses the central idea that personal changes and influences contribute to our evolving sense of self. They plan a beginning, middle and ending, record their voice, trim mistakes and add a quiet piece of loop music as an introduction. GarageBand’s voice recorder, editing timeline and built-in loops allow students to publish a short audio piece for a class listening session.

Students build a simple three-room virtual exhibition titled “Past, Present and Future Me” to explore developing a sense of self. In each room they place objects, images and short text labels representing an earlier interest or strength, something important now, and a realistic hope for the future. They add a brief recorded explanation showing how changes and influences connect the three rooms. Delightex’s ready-made scenes, object library and voice recording tools let students create and present a walk-through exhibition without needing advanced coding.

Elsternwick|Year 6|Where We Are in Place.d: Students investigate how a teacher-selected significant event shaped Elsternwick or another Melbourne place by viewing landmarks, roads and surrounding areas in Google Maps. They use Street View, map scale and the distance tool to examine how the place is arranged today and identify visible signs of change. This directly explores the central idea that significant events shape a place. Each group presents a short live Street View walkthrough, pointing out three locations and explaining how each connects to the event.

Students use Book Creator to make a short digital book about a significant event that shaped a chosen place. Their pages explain what happened, why it occurred and how the place changed afterwards, linking to all three lines of inquiry. They combine written explanations with drawings, photos supplied by the teacher and a recorded narration. The simple page templates and audio recording button help students publish a clear account that classmates can read and listen to.

Students enter a teacher-provided set of figures connected to a significant event, such as population, building numbers or visitor numbers before and after the event. They use Excel’s table and chart features to look for changes and discuss what the data suggests about the event’s impact on the place. This directly supports the line of inquiry into the impact of significant events. Each pair produces one labelled chart and adds a short conclusion in the spreadsheet explaining the change they found.

Students create a one-minute stop-motion explanation of a significant event that shaped a place, using paper maps, labels and simple classroom objects as props. They arrange and photograph a sequence showing the place before the event, why the event occurred and what changed afterwards. This connects directly to the central idea that significant events shape a place. Stop Motion Studio’s frame-by-frame camera, text and playback features allow students to test, adjust and present a clear cause-and-effect sequence.

Students record a short history podcast episode about a significant event that changed Elsternwick, Melbourne or another studied place. Working in pairs, they script a host-and-expert discussion covering what made the event significant, why it occurred and its lasting impact. This addresses the unit’s three lines of inquiry through a clear spoken explanation. Canva’s audio recording, timeline editing and simple music options allow students to produce and present a polished three-minute episode.

Glen Waverley|Prep|How We Express Oursel.d: Students make one page about an emotion, showing what it can feel like in their face and body and one action that may help them feel better. This explores how our feelings and emotions affect us and the central idea that emotions influence our wellbeing. Each child creates a page with a simple drawing, a short teacher-supported sentence and a voice recording, which are combined into a class emotions book. The easy page templates, drawing pen and audio record button make the task manageable for Prep students.

Students photograph a classroom puppet or their own drawing of a face showing an emotion, then add a moving mouth and record it speaking. The character names its feeling, explains a visible clue and says what it might need from a friend, linking to how feelings and emotions are interpreted. Students make a short talking-face video to present to a partner, who guesses the emotion before hearing the answer. ChatterPix Kids’ simple mouth line and voice-recording features power the activity.

In pairs, students create a short puppet scene about a common Prep situation such as being left out, losing a turn or receiving help. They record the characters showing how emotions and behaviour affect relationships, then include a kinder choice that improves the situation. Each pair presents a short narrated puppet play for the class to discuss. The character selection, movable puppets, backgrounds and record button allow students to act out and capture the scene directly in Puppet Pals.

Students code a character to show two different responses to an emotion such as anger, worry or excitement. One sequence shows behaviour that may hurt a relationship, while the second shows a helpful choice, directly exploring how our emotions and behaviour affect relationships. Students make and present a short animated comparison in which characters move, speak and change expression. ScratchJr’s picture-based movement, speech and start blocks let Prep students build and test the sequences with simple teacher modelling.

Students create a digital painting that expresses one emotion through colour, line and shape rather than drawing a detailed face. This helps the class explore how feelings and emotions are interpreted and supports the central idea that emotions influence our wellbeing. Each child saves a finished emotion artwork and briefly presents which choices show the feeling. The large brushes, colour picker, undo button and simple layers in Brushes Redux make it easy for Prep students to experiment and revise their work.

Glen Waverley|Prep|How We Organise Ourse.d: Students make a simple class book showing how wheat changes from a plant into flour and then bread. This directly explores where food comes from and how food can be changed for different purposes. Each pair creates one page with a drawing or photo, a short label and a recorded sentence, which the class then reads in the correct order. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tool and voice recording button make the task manageable for Prep students.

Students code a Beebot to travel across a floor mat showing a food journey from farm to shop to home. This helps them explore where food comes from and the steps products go through before people use them. In small groups, students press the direction buttons, test the route and fix their code if the Beebot stops at the wrong picture. Each group presents its completed route and explains the food journey as the Beebot moves.

Students record a short video showing how a familiar food changes, such as fruit being cut for a fruit salad or milk being mixed into a smoothie. This connects directly to how food can be changed for different purposes. With an adult handling any cutting, students film three or four safe steps and add spoken explanations and simple text labels. Apple Clips’ large record button, camera, titles and voice recording let each group publish a clear process video.

Students code an animation showing a food product changing through a simple process, such as an apple becoming apple sauce. This supports the central idea that the products people use go through a process of change. Students choose or draw characters, place each stage on a page and use movement and speech blocks to show and explain the sequence. They test and debug their code, then present the finished animation to a partner who checks whether the stages are in a sensible order.

Students complete a teacher-made picture survey about foods they appreciate and the reasons they value them, such as taste, family traditions or helping their bodies grow. This directly supports an appreciation of food. Students tap one picture choice and give a short teacher-scribed or recorded response, then the class views the automatic response charts together. Microsoft Forms’ picture questions, large choice buttons and response summary create a shareable class snapshot of food preferences and appreciation.

Glen Waverley|Prep|Where We Are in Place.d: Students make a short digital book about the people in their family and what makes their family special. This directly explores the lines of inquiry, “The people in your family” and “What makes a family.” On each page, they draw a family member, add a simple label and record one spoken sentence about that person. They share the finished book with a partner or at a family morning. Book Creator’s drawing, text and voice-recording features keep the task manageable for Prep students.

Students use Google Maps to view a place that is important in their family history, such as a grandparent’s town, a previous home or another country. This connects directly to the line of inquiry, “Your family history,” by showing that families can have links to different places. With teacher support, each student finds the place, looks for a nearby landmark and explores it using Street View where available. Students then present a short guided walkthrough on the screen and explain why the place matters to their family. The everyday map search, zoom and Street View features are central to the activity.

Students record a short family sound story about something their family values, such as sharing meals, celebrating together or helping one another. This explores the line of inquiry, “What is important to your family,” and supports the central idea that family histories shape what we value. Each student records two or three spoken sentences and adds one simple sound effect or short music loop. The finished audio story can be played for classmates as part of a listening gallery. GarageBand’s voice recorder, sound effects and ready-made loops power the task.

Students code a simple animated scene showing people in their family doing something important together. This connects to the lines of inquiry, “The people in your family” and “What is important to your family.” They choose or draw characters, place them in a setting and use basic movement and speech blocks to show the family event. Students test and debug their sequence, then present the finished animation and explain the family value it shows. ScratchJr’s character creator and picture-based coding blocks make the activity realistic for Prep.

Students create a simple then-and-now family history page in Seesaw. This directly explores the line of inquiry, “Your family history,” and the central idea that family histories shape who we are. They draw one picture of a family member in the past and one picture of their family now, then record a short voice explanation of what has changed or stayed the same. The completed page is shared in the class journal for families and classmates to view. Seesaw’s drawing canvas, labels and built-in voice recording support students who are still developing their writing.

Glen Waverley|Prep|Who We Are.d: Students use Seesaw to record themselves explaining one classroom routine that helps them become independent, such as unpacking their bag or putting away materials. This directly explores the line of inquiry, “Routines that allow developing independence.” Each student creates a short video demonstration with a simple spoken explanation, which can be shared with classmates and families. The easy video recording and voice features let Prep students show the routine rather than needing to write a long response.

Students build a simple floor route showing how to move safely from the classroom door to places such as the bag area, mat or class library, then program Sphero Indi to follow it. This connects to the organisation of the Junior School and how organised spaces help students learn and work together. In small groups, students place the coloured tiles, test the route and adjust any section where Indi turns the wrong way or stops. They present their working route and explain the safe movement choices, using Indi’s colour-sensing movement as the key feature.

Students use Puppet Pals to act out a short classroom or playground safety situation linked to how we keep shared spaces healthy and safe. They choose characters and a background, then record a scene showing an unsafe choice followed by a safer choice. Each pair produces a short puppet video to present to the class as a safety reminder. The simple character-moving stage and built-in voice recording make the task manageable for Prep students.

Students use ScratchJr to code a character moving through the steps of a familiar school routine, such as arriving, placing a bag away, sitting on the mat and getting ready to learn. This directly supports the line of inquiry, “Routines that allow developing independence.” Students arrange simple movement and speech blocks, run their sequence and debug it if the steps happen in the wrong order. They finish with a short animated routine that they can play and explain to a partner.

Students use PicCollage to make a visual guide called “Healthy and Safe in Our Classroom and Playground.” They take or select teacher-prepared photos of familiar spaces and arrange them with simple labels such as “walk,” “wash hands,” “pack away” and “wear a hat.” This directly explores how to make the classroom and playground healthy and safe. Each pair publishes one clear collage to display, using the photo layout, text and sticker features to make the safety messages easy for other Prep students to understand.

Glen Waverley|Prep|How the World Works.d: Students roll the same ball down a small ramp onto carpet, cardboard and a smooth tabletop, then record each test in slow motion. They compare how the properties of the surface materials influence how the ball moves, linking directly to the central idea. Pairs replay their clips and present which surface made the ball travel fastest, slowest or furthest. The slow-motion recording and frame-by-frame replay features make small changes in movement easier for Prep students to notice.

Students build a short path with Indi’s colour tiles, then add small sections of fabric, foil and cardboard for the car to travel across. They test and debug the path, noticing how different material surfaces influence Indi’s movement. Each group presents its working route and explains where Indi moved smoothly, slowed down or became stuck. Indi’s colour-sensing car and simple coding tiles let Prep students control and test movement without needing to read code.

Students use Tablet Magnifiers to closely examine classroom materials such as wood, plastic, metal, fabric and paper. They explore the line of inquiry about properties of materials by looking for fibres, bumps, shine, holes and smooth surfaces. Each pair saves a small set of close-up images and presents a mystery-material challenge for classmates to identify. The magnification, zoom and image-capture features make tiny material details visible and shareable.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to show how the shape of a material can change the way it moves. They photograph a flat piece of paper sliding, the same paper folded into a simple glider, and the paper scrunched into a ball that rolls. Their finished short animation presents three ways one material can be used and moved, connecting to the lines of inquiry about how objects move and how we use materials. The frame-by-frame camera and instant playback features help students build and check the sequence one small step at a time.

Students use PicCollage to photograph everyday objects made from materials such as plastic, metal, wood, fabric and paper. They sort the photos into groups and add simple labels such as hard, soft, bendy, smooth or rough, exploring the properties of materials. Each pair publishes one picture collage showing which material properties make the objects useful for their jobs. The built-in camera, photo arranging and text-label features support a clear visual explanation that Prep students can share with the class.

Glen Waverley|Prep|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use Seek to scan and identify plants, insects and other living things in the school grounds as part of Sharing the Planet. They discuss how caring for these living things connects to the central idea about our responsibilities when sharing spaces and resources. Each pair saves three identified observations and presents what each living thing needs to survive. Seek’s camera identification feature makes the activity manageable for Prep students who are still learning to read.

Students code a Beebot to travel across a simple habitat mat to reach limited resources such as water, food and shelter. They test routes that avoid trampling plant and animal spaces, linking directly to the central idea about sharing finite resources with other living things. Each group debugs its route and presents one responsible way to reach a resource. The Beebot’s forward, backward and turn buttons let Prep students create and check the route themselves.

Students make a class book about Sharing the Planet, with each child creating one page about a resource such as water, food, trees or safe shelter. Their page explains through a drawing and recorded sentence how people can share or protect that resource, connecting to the central idea about rights and responsibilities. The finished book can be played to the class and shared with families. Book Creator’s drawing, voice recording and page-turning features keep the task simple and accessible for Prep.

Students use toy animals or classroom counters to create a short stop-motion scene about animals sharing a limited water source or habitat. They first show a problem and then move the pieces to show a fairer solution, linking to the central idea about sharing finite resources with living things. Each group makes and presents a short film with a clear beginning, problem and solution. Stop Motion Studio’s frame-by-frame camera and playback button allow students to capture, test and improve the movement.

Students draw or photograph a local animal or plant and use ChatterPix Kids to make it speak about Sharing the Planet. They record a short message explaining what the living thing needs and one responsibility people have when sharing its habitat or resources. Each child produces a talking-picture video that can be presented to the class as part of a gallery of living things. The simple mouth line and voice-recording features let Prep students create the message with minimal teacher help.

Glen Waverley|Year 1|How We Express Ours.d: Students choose characters and backgrounds, then move the digital puppets while recording their own voices to tell a short story. This explores the features and purposes of puppet performances and shows how people use imagination to express stories through performance. Each pair makes a one-minute puppet show to present to the class. The simple character movement and voice-recording features make the performance manageable for Year 1 students.

Students build a simple puppet from classroom craft materials, then take a sequence of photos as they move it across a small stage. This directly explores different materials used to make puppets and how movement helps a puppet communicate a story or idea. Each group produces a short stop-motion puppet performance that can be played for classmates. The frame-by-frame camera and playback buttons let students test their movement and retake unclear sections.

Students photograph three class puppets made from different materials, such as paper, fabric, socks or wooden spoons, and arrange the pictures in a collage. This supports the line of inquiry into different materials used to make puppets by helping students compare how each material looks and moves. Students add short labels or recorded teacher-supported captions explaining the material and what kind of character it could become, then present the finished comparison page. The photo layout, text and sticker features provide a simple way to organise and share their observations.

Students code two on-screen characters to act like puppets by moving, speaking and taking turns in a short scene. This connects to the features and purposes of puppet performances, including characters, movement, voice and a clear message or story. Each pair creates and presents a short coded performance with a beginning, middle and end. The snap-together movement, speech and start blocks allow Year 1 students to build, test and fix the sequence.

Students record a short live puppet performance that shares a familiar story, family tradition or cultural celebration. This links to the inquiry into the types and uses of puppets in different cultures and to the central idea that people express stories, ideas and culture through performance. Each group publishes a brief video with an opening title and a spoken explanation of what its puppet performance communicates. The large record button, simple trimming and built-in title cards make it easy to capture and tidy the performance in one tool.

Glen Waverley|Year 1|How We Organise Our.d: Students use Book Creator to make a class book about How We Organise Ourselves at school. Each pair creates a page showing one community role, what that person does and which need they help meet, linking directly to the line of inquiry about the roles people play in a community. Students draw or add a photo, write a simple sentence and record themselves explaining the role. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools and voice recording make the task manageable for Year 1. The finished book can be read together and shared with families.

Students use Sphero Indi to explore how systems and routines help a community stay organised. Small groups arrange the coloured coding tiles to create a route that delivers Indi between places such as a home, school, shop and hospital. They test the route, move tiles when it does not work and explain how each stop helps meet a community need. Indi’s colour-sensing movement and reusable coding tiles are central to building and debugging the delivery system. Each group presents its working route and describes the roles needed to keep it running.

Students use Seesaw to record a short explanation of one classroom routine that helps people live and learn together. They draw the steps or photograph themselves demonstrating actions such as returning books, packing bags or collecting materials. This connects directly to the line of inquiry about systems and routines that help us stay organised. Seesaw’s drawing, photo and voice-recording features let students label each step and explain why it matters. The finished posts form a practical class library of routines that students can revisit.

Students use Puppet Pals to create a short scene about people working together in a community. They choose characters for roles such as a teacher, librarian, nurse or crossing supervisor, then record dialogue showing how those people meet a shared need. This directly explores the line of inquiry about how communities work together to meet needs. Puppet Pals’ movable characters, backgrounds and built-in voice recording allow Year 1 students to act out the scene without complex editing. Pairs present their finished puppet scene and name the role each character played.

Students use a simple Microsoft Forms survey to collect class data about which school systems help them learn and stay organised. They answer teacher-prepared picture and multiple-choice questions about routines such as lining up, borrowing books, packing away and asking for help. This links directly to the line of inquiry about systems and routines that help us stay organised. Microsoft Forms’ large answer choices and automatic charts make it easy for Year 1 students to respond and see the class results. The class presents the charts together and identifies one routine that is working well and one that could be improved.

Glen Waverley|Year 1|How the World Works.d: Students code a Beebot to move along a simple classroom track using forward, backward and turn commands. They test how changing the sequence changes the Beebot’s movement, linking directly to the line of inquiry about ways objects move. Pairs debug their code and adapt the track or instructions so the Beebot reaches a chosen finish point. They present their successful route using the Beebot’s arrow buttons and clear memory button.

Students use small classroom objects to make a short animation showing different ways objects move, such as rolling, sliding, spinning and bouncing. This directly explores the line of inquiry about ways objects move. They move each object a small amount between photos, then play the finished animation for the class and explain where a push or pull was used. Stop Motion Studio’s frame-by-frame camera and playback tools make the movement visible.

Students test how far the same toy car travels across surfaces such as carpet, cardboard and smooth flooring, exploring the influence different materials have on movement. They count the distance in floor tiles or another simple classroom unit and enter the results into a teacher-prepared Excel table. With teacher support, they create a basic column chart and use it to identify which surface allowed the most or least movement. Excel’s simple cells and chart button turn the class results into a clear, shareable display.

Students build and test a simple ramp for a toy car, then change one part of the design to help the car move further, more slowly or in a straighter line. This addresses the line of inquiry about how designs can be adapted and improved. In Book Creator, they make a two-page before-and-after report with photos, drawings and a recorded explanation of what they changed. The built-in camera, drawing pen and audio recording buttons let Year 1 students publish their design thinking in one place.

Students record short demonstrations of pushes and pulls using safe classroom objects such as balls, blocks and toy cars. They explain how each force starts, stops or changes movement, linking to the central idea that movement is dependent on different forces. Small groups combine their clips into a brief class-ready video with spoken explanations and simple text labels such as push, pull, roll and slide. Apple Clips’ hold-to-record camera, trimming and text tools make the video quick to create and easy to present.

Glen Waverley|Year 1|Sharing the Planet.d: In pairs, students use Seek by iNaturalist in the school garden to photograph and identify safe invertebrates such as ants, butterflies and spiders. They compare where each animal was found, linking to the interdependence of invertebrates and their environment. The app’s camera identification feature helps students check possible species without touching the animals. Each pair presents its saved observations and explains which habitat features, such as leaves, soil or flowers, the invertebrate appeared to need.

Students use Tablet Magnifiers to closely examine classroom specimens or safely collected items such as an empty snail shell, shed insect skin or preserved insect. They look for characteristics of invertebrates, including body sections, legs, wings, shells and patterns. Using the tool’s magnification and photo features, each student records a detailed close-up image of one feature. Students present their image and explain what it shows about that invertebrate.

Students use ScratchJr to code a simple butterfly or beetle life cycle from egg to adult. They create one scene for each stage and use movement and message blocks to make the stages appear in the correct order. This directly explores the life cycles of invertebrates. Each pair presents a short animated life cycle that classmates can watch and check for accurate sequencing.

Small groups use Stop Motion Studio to make a short model showing an invertebrate life cycle, such as a butterfly changing from egg to caterpillar, pupa and adult. They move paper or clay models a small amount between each photo, keeping the stages in the correct order. This supports the line of inquiry into life cycles of invertebrates. The app’s frame-by-frame camera and playback features turn their photos into a short film that the group can present to the class.

Students use Seesaw to explain why invertebrates are essential to living things and the environment. They choose or take a photo of an invertebrate, then use the drawing tools to add arrows showing connections such as a bee visiting a flower or a worm improving soil. Using the built-in voice recording feature, they record a short explanation of how the invertebrate and its environment depend on each other. The finished photo, arrows and narration form a shareable learning post for classmates and families.

Glen Waverley|Year 1|Where We Are in Pla.d: Students create a simple class book about ways children’s lives have changed over time, with pages on school, toys, clothing and travel. Each pair makes a then-and-now page using pictures, short labels and a recorded sentence explaining one change. The finished book directly explores the line of inquiry about ways in which children’s lives have changed over time and can be read together or shared with families. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools and audio recording button make the task manageable for Year 1 students.

Students photograph an old-fashioned household or school object and use ChatterPix Kids to make it explain how children used it in the past. They record a short voice message that names the object, describes its use and gives a reason it may have changed or been replaced. The class watches the finished talking-object clips and discusses the line of inquiry about reasons for changes to children’s lives over time. The simple mouth-drawing and voice-recording features let Year 1 students produce a clear, shareable clip in one lesson.

Students code a short then-and-now animation showing one part of children’s lives changing over time, such as walking to school in the past and travelling by car or bus today. They create two scenes, add characters and use movement, speech and page-change blocks to show the sequence. The completed animation supports the central idea that understanding history helps us see how the past shapes the future, with students explaining what changed and what might change next. ScratchJr’s picture-based coding blocks and built-in characters make the task practical for Year 1 pairs.

Students use Google Maps to view Street View around Glen Waverley and compare present-day streets, schools, homes and transport with teacher-provided historical descriptions from the unit. In pairs, they navigate along one familiar street and choose two visible details that show how children live and travel today. Each pair presents a short on-screen walkthrough to the class, explaining how one feature connects with ways children’s lives have changed over time. Google Maps’ search, zoom and Street View features allow students to explore and present without logging in or creating a map.

Students make a then-and-now collage about one area of childhood, such as toys, classrooms, clothing or chores. They place past and present pictures side by side, add simple labels and include one sentence explaining why the change may have happened. The finished collage directly addresses the line of inquiry about reasons for changes to children’s lives over time and can be displayed for a class gallery walk. PicCollage’s ready-made layouts, picture placement and text tools help Year 1 students organise and publish their comparison clearly.

Glen Waverley|Year 1|Who We Are.d: Students create a simple digital book about the brain and how it helps us think, feel, remember and make choices. This directly explores the line of inquiry about the function of different parts of the brain. Each pair makes one illustrated page, records a short spoken explanation and combines the pages into a class book to share. Book Creator’s drawing, voice recording and page-making features keep the task manageable for Year 1.

Students complete a short picture-based class survey about situations that cause pleasant and unpleasant feelings, such as joining a game, losing something or receiving help. This directly explores the line of inquiry about situations that cause different feelings. The class views the automatic charts and discusses how people can feel differently in the same situation. Microsoft Forms’ picture questions, large answer choices and automatic charts make the responses easy to collect and compare.

In pairs, students use characters to act out a common relationship problem, such as being left out or disagreeing over a game. They then record a second scene showing actions and values that help the characters connect and collaborate. Each pair presents its short puppet scene to the class and explains the helpful choice it showed. Puppet Pals’ movable characters, backgrounds and voice recording provide a simple way to create and record the role-play.

Students make a personal collage called “Things That Support My Wellbeing” using pictures of actions such as resting, moving, talking, playing and asking for help. This connects directly to the line of inquiry about actions that support wellbeing. They add a few labels or short sentences, then present their finished collage to a partner. PicCollage’s simple photo, sticker, text and layout features help Year 1 students organise their ideas on one shareable page.

Students draw a face showing an emotion, photograph it in ChatterPix Kids and add a moving mouth. They record the character naming the feeling, describing a situation that might cause it and suggesting one helpful response. This links emotions and relationships to the central idea that they guide how we connect and collaborate. ChatterPix Kids’ photo, mouth-line and short voice-recording features turn each drawing into a brief talking feelings presentation.

Glen Waverley|Year 2|How We Express Ours.d: Students use Book Creator to retell a familiar story as part of How We Express Ourselves. They explore the connection between story and illustrations by choosing what each picture should show and how it adds meaning to the words. Each pair publishes a short digital book with drawings, typed sentences and recorded narration, then reads it to the class. The simple page templates, drawing tools and audio recording button make the task manageable for Year 2 students.

Students use ScratchJr to code a short scene for How We Express Ourselves in which two characters communicate an idea or solve a simple problem. This supports the central idea that storytellers use different methods to convey meaning because students combine movement, speech and timing. They make and present a short animated story by selecting characters, creating a setting and joining movement, speech and start blocks. The drag-and-drop coding blocks and play button allow students to test, adjust and debug their scene as they work.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to create a short story for How We Express Ourselves using classroom objects, paper characters or modelling clay. They investigate the mediums and techniques artists use by testing how small changes in position can make a character appear to move. Each group records and presents a 20- to 30-second stop-motion film with a clear beginning, middle and ending. The app’s frame-by-frame camera and playback features let students capture, check and redo their movements easily.

Students use Brushes Redux to illustrate one important moment from a shared story during How We Express Ourselves. They explore the connection between story and illustrations by choosing colours, lines and brush styles that show the setting, action or mood without adding written explanation. Each student creates a finished digital illustration and presents it beside the original story page, explaining one artistic choice. The everyday brush, colour, layer and undo tools allow students to experiment without needing advanced drawing skills.

Glen Waverley|Year 2|How We Express Ours.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
Glen Waverley|Year 2|How We Express Ours.d: Students use Animating a Character with Adobe Express to record a character telling the same short event in a happy, worried or excited way for How We Express Ourselves. This directly explores how ideas and information are communicated through voice, facial expression and character choice. Each student records and shares a brief animated character performance, then classmates identify the feeling or message being conveyed. The character picker and built-in voice recording feature automatically match the character’s mouth movements to the student’s speech.

Glen Waverley|Year 2|How We Organise Our.d: Students use ScratchJr to code a simple animation showing the sequence of a school library borrowing system. They connect their work to the central idea that a sequence of processes enables a system to function by showing choosing, borrowing, scanning and returning in order. Each pair tests and debugs its code, then presents a finished animation that explains what happens if a step is missed. The block coding, character movement and speech bubbles make the sequence clear and manageable for Year 2.

Students use Sphero Indi to build and test a route that represents the school mail delivery system. This explores the purpose of various systems as students decide where the mail starts, which classrooms it visits and where the route finishes. Groups place the coloured tiles, run the car, debug any wrong turns and present a working delivery route to the class. Indi’s colour-sensing movement tiles let students create and change the route without needing advanced coding.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to show how classroom paper moves through a recycling system. They arrange simple paper labels or classroom objects, take one photo at a time and show the sequence from use and collection through sorting and recycling. The finished stop-motion video demonstrates the central idea that a sequence of processes enables a system to function. The app’s frame-by-frame camera and playback features help students check whether each stage is clear and in the correct order.

Students use Freeform to map the parts of a familiar classroom system, such as packing up at the end of the day. They add shapes for jobs, arrows for the order and short labels showing how students, materials and routines depend on one another. This directly explores how systems are made of many interdependent parts, and each group finishes with a clear process map to present. Freeform’s shapes, text boxes, drawing tools and connecting lines make it easy to move, correct and reorder ideas.

Students use Microsoft Forms to collect class data about how people travel to school as an example of a system in their lives. They complete a short teacher-made form, then examine the automatic charts to compare walking, cars, bicycles and public transport. This supports the line of inquiry into the systems in our lives, and the class produces a shareable response summary showing which transport parts are used most. The simple question choices and automatic results charts do the data collection and counting for students.

Glen Waverley|Year 2|How the World Works.d: Students use Book Creator to make a class guide to materials found in everyday objects, such as plastic bottles, metal spoons, paper bags and fabric hats. They photograph each object, label its material and record a short voice explanation of properties such as hard, soft, flexible, waterproof or absorbent. This directly supports the line of inquiry about understanding material properties. The finished digital book uses Book Creator’s page templates, camera, text and audio recording features and can be presented to another Year 2 class.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to record how a material changes when they fold paper, squash foil, stretch dough or reshape modelling clay. They take a series of photos as the change happens, then add simple titles explaining whether the material can be reused in its new form. This explores the line of inquiry about reuse and recycling through physical change. The finished stop-motion clips use the app’s frame-by-frame camera and playback features and can be shown during a class materials discussion.

Students test common materials such as paper towel, foil, fabric and plastic to see how many drops of water each can hold before leaking. With teacher support, they enter their results into a simple Microsoft Excel table and create a column chart. This builds understanding of material properties and how those properties affect the way materials are used. The class presents the chart and uses Excel’s cells and chart button to compare which materials were most and least water-resistant.

Students use PicCollage to create a sorting poster about materials and sustainable choices. They photograph or select images of everyday objects, then arrange them under headings such as reuse, recycle or rubbish and add a short reason for each choice. This directly supports the line of inquiry about sustainably managing materials. The completed poster uses PicCollage’s photo grid, text labels, stickers and drag-and-drop layout and can be displayed for families or another class.

Students use ScratchJr to code a short sequence showing an everyday material being collected, changed and reused, such as a cardboard box becoming a storage container. They choose or draw characters and backgrounds, then connect movement, speech and page-change blocks to show each step in order. This connects to the central idea that changes to materials affect how we use and reuse them in daily life. The finished animation uses ScratchJr’s simple block coding, drawing and speech features and is presented with the student explaining one improvement they made while debugging it.

Students use simple paper models of the Sun and Earth to record a stop-motion sequence showing Earth rotating and orbiting the Sun. This explores Earth's place in the solar system and helps explain observable patterns such as day and night. Pairs create a short labelled animation and present it to the class with a spoken explanation. They use the app’s frame-by-frame camera and playback features to test and improve the sequence.

Students keep a short sky journal about the Solar System by recording what they notice outdoors at the same time over several days. This connects to observable patterns in the sky, such as the Sun appearing in different positions or the Moon changing shape. Each student publishes a set of drawings, photos or voice recordings and adds a simple sentence about the pattern they noticed. They use Seesaw’s built-in camera, drawing, voice recording and journal features.

Students measure the length of a fixed object’s shadow at three times during the school day and enter the class results into Microsoft Excel. This investigation focuses on observable patterns in the sky and how the Sun’s apparent position changes. With teacher support, students create a simple column chart showing the morning, midday and afternoon measurements, then present what changed. They use Excel’s table, number-entry and chart features to organise and display the data.

Students build a simple Solar System model with the Sun in the centre, the planets in the correct order and clear paths to represent their orbits. This directly explores Earth's place in the solar system and its relationship to nearby planets. Small groups create a walk-through model with signs naming each planet, then guide classmates through it and explain where Earth belongs. They use Minecraft Education’s blocks, signs and movement controls to build and present the model without trying to make the sizes or distances exact.

Students watch a teacher-selected Clickview video about the Solar System and pause at key moments to identify planets, day and night, and tools used to observe the sky. This supports the lines of inquiry about Earth's place in the solar system and the tools and methods we use to observe the sky. Students complete the video’s embedded questions, leaving a class set of recorded answers that the teacher can review and discuss. They use Clickview’s video controls, captions and interactive question feature to replay evidence before answering.

Glen Waverley|Year 2|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use Google Maps to view two communities with very different access to water, such as central Melbourne and a remote Australian community. They explore satellite view and Street View to look for rivers, reservoirs, water tanks, taps and the distances between homes and water sources. This directly supports the line of inquiry into unequal access to water. Pairs use the zoom, Street View and distance features to present three visible differences they noticed to the class.

Students complete a short Microsoft Forms survey about everyday water use, including showers, drinking, washing and watering gardens. The class examines the automatic charts to discuss the central idea that water is a limited resource that is essential to life. Students identify one common habit that could save water and explain their choice. The completed survey and its built-in response charts create a simple class record that can be shared with families.

Students code a short ScratchJr animation showing how water travels from a source such as a reservoir to a home, school or garden. They move characters and water symbols across backgrounds, adding simple speech or text to explain each stage. This connects directly to the line of inquiry about the transferral of water from source to use. Students use the block-based movement, timing and scene tools to make, test and debug a clear animated sequence.

Students create a PicCollage poster called “Every Drop Counts” about responsible water use at home and school. They add their own short captions and arrange pictures showing actions such as turning off taps, taking shorter showers and reusing water on plants. This supports the line of inquiry into responsibility as global citizens. The finished posters use PicCollage’s simple photo, text and layout features and can be presented to the class or displayed for families.

Students use Seesaw to explain how limited water access can affect a community’s daily life. They draw a simple scene showing how people collect, carry or store water, then record a short spoken explanation over their picture. This connects to the line of inquiry about communities affected by water access. Seesaw’s built-in drawing and voice-recording tools produce a shareable reflection that teachers can place in each student’s learning journal.

Glen Waverley|Year 3|How We Express Ours.d: Students create a short digital book for How We Express Ourselves showing how they understand a familiar place, event or part of nature. They combine their own drawings, written captions and recorded narration to explore how texts and images work together. Each student publishes a shareable book with a cover and three or four carefully planned pages. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools and audio recording make the task manageable for Year 3 students.

Glen Waverley|Year 3|How We Express Ours.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
Glen Waverley|Year 3|How We Express Ours.d: Students design a character and record it speaking about how creativity helps people express their understanding of the world in How We Express Ourselves. They choose words, tone and movement to explore how technology influences our creativity. Each student produces a short animated message that can be presented to the class. The simple character picker and voice-recording feature automatically match the character’s movement to the student’s speech.

Students make a digital artwork for How We Express Ourselves that shows their personal understanding of Melbourne through colour, shape and line. This directly explores the central idea that creativity allows people to express their understanding of the world. Students present their finished artwork and explain two choices they made while creating it. Brushes Redux’s everyday brush, colour, layer and undo tools let students test and revise ideas without needing advanced drawing skills.

Students create a one-page visual poem for How We Express Ourselves about a place, object or experience that matters to them. They arrange photos, short phrases, colours and shapes to investigate how texts and images work together. Each student produces a finished collage that can be displayed or presented to a partner. PicCollage’s ready-made layouts, text boxes, image tools and stickers make it easy to move and resize each part.

In pairs, students record a two-minute class podcast for How We Express Ourselves about a creative choice they have made in art, writing, music or play. Their conversation connects to the line of inquiry about the ways people use technology to express creativity. Each pair records a clear introduction, an interview question, an answer and a closing statement to share with classmates. The microphones and simple record, stop and playback controls help students capture and review their voices clearly.

Glen Waverley|Year 3|How We Organise Our.d: Students use Microsoft Forms to collect class opinions about a real classroom need, such as choosing new wet-day activities or improving the class library. This shows how needs can be met with digital systems because the form gathers and organises information quickly. Students write suitable multiple-choice questions, submit responses and examine the automatic charts. They present the results and explain how the class could use the information to make a fair decision.

Students code a Micro:bit reminder system that helps meet a classroom need, such as reminding people to use quiet voices or pack away materials. They program button presses to show different words, numbers or symbols, then test and debug their code with a partner. This helps students see that a digital system uses an input, follows instructions and produces an output. Each pair demonstrates its working system and explains the need it was designed to meet.

Students use Padlet to create a shared class space about being a responsible digital citizen. Each student publishes a short post explaining one safe online action, such as protecting personal information, using kind words or asking before sharing a photo. They use Padlet’s post and comment features to organise and share ideas in a safe online environment, with teacher approval turned on. The finished board becomes a practical class guide that students can present and revisit during the unit.

Students use Explain Everything to map how a familiar digital system meets a need, such as an online lunch order, library search or weather service. They draw and label the information going in, what the system does with it and what comes out for the user. Using the recording feature, students talk through their diagram and explain how the parts work together. They finish with a short narrated presentation that directly answers the line of inquiry, “What are digital systems?”

Students use Adobe Express to make a one-page digital citizenship poster for younger students. They choose three clear rules for organising and sharing information safely online, then add simple headings, icons and short explanations. This directly supports the line of inquiry about being a responsible digital citizen. Using Adobe Express templates and drag-and-drop design tools, students publish a polished poster that can be presented to another class.

Glen Waverley|Year 3|Sharing the Planet.d: Students test several soil samples for colour, texture, water drainage and how much water each one holds, then enter their results into Microsoft Excel. This directly explores the line of inquiry about the observable properties of soils, rocks and minerals. Pairs use the table and chart features to create a simple column graph comparing the samples. They present their graph and explain which soil might be most useful for growing plants and why.

Students use Google Maps to view several Victorian quarries, mines and nearby communities through satellite view and Street View where available. They compare how rocks and minerals are used with signs of change to the surrounding land, linking to the line of inquiry that Earth's resources are vital and must be used responsibly. Using the distance and scale features, they estimate the size of one site and its distance from homes, roads or bushland. Small groups present a short on-screen tour, pointing out what they notice and suggesting one way the resource could be managed responsibly.

Students photograph a small set of classroom rock, mineral and soil samples within Explain Everything and place the images onto three labelled pages. They use drawing, text and pointer tools to mark observable properties such as colour, grain size, layers, shine and texture. This addresses the line of inquiry about the observable properties of soils, rocks and minerals. Each student records a short narrated explanation of how they sorted the samples, creating a shareable digital classification presentation.

Students use clay, sand, pebbles and small paper signs to build a simple model showing a resource being taken from the Earth and the land being cared for afterwards. They move the materials a little at a time and capture each change with Stop Motion Studio's frame-by-frame camera feature. This connects to the line of inquiry that Earth's resources are vital and must be used responsibly. Groups publish a short stop-motion film that shows extraction, use, waste reduction and land repair in a clear sequence.

Students use PicCollage's built-in camera option to photograph soil and rock samples, then arrange the images into a one-page class field guide. They add short labels describing visible properties and one everyday use for each resource, linking to the central idea that the diversity of soils, rocks and minerals shapes how people value and use Earth's resources. Students use the layout, text and sticker-arrow features to make links between each sample, its properties and its use. They present the finished collage to a partner and explain which resource should be used most carefully and why.

Glen Waverley|Year 3|How the World Works.d: Students use Stop Motion Studio to photograph an ice cube at regular intervals as it melts. This directly explores how heating and cooling change state and shows that careful observation helps us understand materials. They turn the photographs into a short stop-motion film with simple labels marking solid ice, melting and liquid water. The frame-by-frame camera and playback features make a slow change easy to see and share with the class.

Students code a Micro:bit to measure and log temperature while testing which everyday wrapping keeps a container cool for longest. This connects scientific thinking with solving the everyday problem of keeping food or drinks cool. Each group produces a working temperature logger and a simple graph of its readings, then presents which wrapping worked best. The built-in temperature sensor, block coding and data logging features allow students to collect real evidence without specialist equipment.

Students use Teachable Machine to train a simple model to sort webcam images of classroom materials into solids and liquids.
