This supports the line of inquiry into observable properties of solids and liquids while showing that scientific classifications need reliable evidence. They test the model with new examples, record when it is wrong and add better training images to improve it. The webcam capture, training buttons and live testing window let students build and debug a shareable working classifier.

Students examine a small set of everyday solids and liquids, then enter observations about shape, flow, colour and transparency into Microsoft Forms. This directly addresses observable properties of solids and liquids and helps the class compare evidence from different groups. The class uses the combined response summary to identify patterns and present claims about how solids and liquids behave. Multiple-choice questions and automatically generated charts make collecting and sharing the class data manageable for Year 3.

Students use Book Creator to make a class guide called Changes in Everyday Materials. They photograph safe examples such as ice melting, water freezing or chocolate softening and explain how each example connects with how heating and cooling change state. Each pair publishes two pages containing before-and-after images, a short written observation and a recorded spoken explanation. The built-in camera, page layout, text and voice recording features support a clear digital book that families and classmates can read.

Glen Waverley|Year 3|Where We Are in Pla.d: Students explore Australia and neighbouring regions using the map, satellite view and Street View. They compare borders, distances, landscapes and landmarks to investigate how Australia and nearby countries define places. Each pair presents a short guided walkthrough of two locations, pointing out three similarities or differences visible on screen. The everyday zoom, distance and Street View features make this a manageable virtual field trip for Year 3.

Students create a class book about First Nations connections to Country using information and language shared through approved class resources. Each student makes one page showing that Country can include land, waterways, plants, animals, stories and responsibilities, directly exploring the line of inquiry about First Nations connections to Country. They add a drawing, a short written explanation and a recorded reading, then present the finished book to another class. Book Creator’s simple page templates, drawing tools and audio recording feature allow all students to contribute.

Pairs choose one Australian state or territory and make a visual identity collage about its landscapes, climate, landmarks, symbols and ways people value the place. This directly investigates how Australia’s states and territories have unique identities. Students arrange teacher-provided images, add labels and write a short statement explaining what makes their chosen place distinctive, then present the finished collage. PicCollage’s basic grid layouts, text boxes and image arrangement tools keep the task clear and achievable.

Students contribute to a class wall called “Places We Value” by describing one Australian place that matters to them or their family. Each post includes a short written explanation, a drawing made in Padlet or an audio recording, helping the class explore the central idea that land and place are represented and valued in different ways. Students then read or listen to classmates’ posts and add one respectful comment identifying a shared or different way of valuing place. Padlet’s post, drawing, audio and comment features keep all the class contributions together for a shareable display.

Small groups record a one-minute audio postcard representing the identity of an Australian state or territory. They speak a short script naming its location, important physical features, well-known places and reasons people may value it, directly addressing the line of inquiry about the unique identities of states and territories. Students record, listen back, trim mistakes and add a brief sound effect only where it supports the place being described, then play the finished postcards for the class. GarageBand’s voice recorder, simple editing controls and sound library provide everything needed for the task.

Glen Waverley|Year 3|Who We Are.d: Students create a short digital book about choices that support a healthy mind and body. This directly explores the line of inquiry, actions to maintain a healthy mind and body. Each student publishes pages showing a realistic daily routine, with their own writing, drawings, photos and recorded explanations. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools and voice-recording button make the task manageable for Year 3 students.

Students collect simple class data about health and wellbeing choices, such as sleep, breakfast, active play and screen-free time. They enter anonymous totals into a spreadsheet and discuss the line of inquiry, choices and their impact on health. Students use the data to make a labelled column chart and present one pattern they notice to the class. Excel’s table cells, basic formulas and chart button are the practical features that power the activity.

Glen Waverley|Year 3|Who We Are.d: Students make an animated character explain one everyday choice that can support health and wellbeing, such as drinking water, moving regularly or talking to someone when worried. Each student writes a short script, records their voice and publishes a brief animated explanation for classmates. In pairs, students record a two-minute audio guide for a healthy mind or body routine, such as calm breathing, stretching or preparing for sleep. Pairs produce a finished audio track with spoken instructions, a short introduction and quiet built-in music or sound effects. GarageBand’s voice recorder, loops and simple track controls allow students to record, trim and arrange their guide in one place.

Students keep a short health and wellbeing reflection journal by recording one choice they made each day and its effect on how they felt or functioned. This supports the line of inquiry, choices and their impact on health. At the end of the week, each student selects three entries and records a spoken reflection about a helpful pattern they noticed. Seesaw’s journal posts, built-in camera, drawing tools and voice-recording feature let students capture and share their learning without needing another app.

Glen Waverley|Year 4|How We Organise Our.d: Students use Microsoft Forms to survey classmates about which classroom rules help people feel safe and treated fairly. In pairs, students write clear multiple-choice questions, collect responses and examine the automatic charts. They then present one rule the class strongly supports and one rule that may need changing, using the survey results as evidence. The everyday features powering the task are the question templates, response collection and automatic summaries.

Students use National Geographic MapMaker to map services that help a community function, such as schools, hospitals, fire stations, parks and public transport. This directly explores the central idea that communities create services to help people live together safely and fairly. Students add markers, labels and short notes explaining who each service supports and why its location matters. Each group presents its annotated community service map and identifies an area that may need better access to a service. The task uses MapMaker’s everyday map layers, markers, drawing and measuring features.

Students use Book Creator to make a short class book called Leaders Who Help Communities. This connects directly to the lines of inquiry about effective and influential leadership and the strengths that help leaders guide others. Each student creates one page about a real community leader, adding a picture, a short explanation of the leader’s actions and an audio recording naming two useful leadership strengths. The completed pages are combined into a shareable digital book for the class to read and discuss. The task uses Book Creator’s simple page templates, text, image and built-in audio recording features.

Students use Minecraft Education to build a small community space that includes services and rules designed to keep residents safe and treated fairly. This directly explores how leadership impacts communities and why communities organise shared services. Teams build a realistic area such as a park, transport stop or town centre, then add signs explaining rules, responsibilities and which community leaders would oversee the space. Each team gives classmates a guided walk through its build and explains one decision that improves fairness or safety. The activity relies on Minecraft Education’s familiar building blocks, signs and shared-world presentation features.

Students use Adobe Express to create a one-page public information poster about a local rule, law or service that helps a community live together safely and fairly. This connects directly to the central idea and asks students to consider how leaders communicate decisions to a community. Students include a clear heading, three key facts, a suitable image or icon and a short call to action for Year 4 readers. They publish and present the finished poster, explaining how its message could influence people’s choices. The task uses Adobe Express’s everyday poster templates, text boxes, icons and image tools.

Glen Waverley|Year 4|How the World Works.d: Students use Tinkercad to design a simple reusable container that could replace a single-use classroom product. They choose shapes and wall thicknesses to explore how material properties determine a product’s use. Each student produces a labelled 3D model and presents how the design could reduce harm to the natural world. The everyday drag, resize, align and text features make the design manageable for Year 4 students.

Students create a Microsoft Forms survey about the use and disposal of paper, plastic and reusable products in the classroom. This supports the line of inquiry into material solutions for a sustainable future by showing which everyday choices create the most waste. They collect class responses and present the automatically generated charts, along with one practical change suggested by the data. The simple question builder and built-in response charts power the activity.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to show the life cycle of an everyday product such as a plastic bottle, aluminium can or cardboard box. Their animation explains how the product’s design and use can have an impact on the natural world, from sourcing the material through to reuse, recycling or landfill. Pairs produce a short stop-motion film with titles that clearly identifies one environmental problem and one more sustainable solution. The frame-by-frame camera, playback and title features let students build and check the sequence as they work.

Students use National Geographic MapMaker to explore where materials used in familiar products, such as cotton, timber, aluminium and plastic, come from. They add labels and connecting lines to show the journey from a material source to Melbourne, linking to how research solves problems in the natural world. Each group presents an annotated map that highlights one long journey or environmentally sensitive location and suggests a more sustainable product choice. The map layers, drawing tools, labels and distance measurement features make the material journey visible and easy to discuss.

Students build and code a small Lego Spike Prime sorting machine that moves sample items into reuse or recycling groups. This explores material solutions for a sustainable future by testing how automation could help people sort waste more consistently. Teams test the machine, record where it sorts incorrectly, debug their code and demonstrate a working final version to the class. The motor, colour sensor and block-based coding features are central to making and improving the sorter.

Glen Waverley|Year 4|Where We Are in Pla.d: Students investigate exploration by viewing the routes and places connected with a selected explorer, using the world map and Street View where available. They compare distances, landscapes and landmarks to explore how people have explored over time. Pairs present a short guided map walkthrough to the class, explaining likely challenges and discoveries along the journey. The zoom, distance measurement and Street View features make the route and scale visible without students needing to log in or edit a map.

Students create a digital explorer’s journal about a real journey linked to the unit Where We Are in Place and Time. Each page explains a reason for exploration, an important discovery and one positive or negative consequence of the journey. Students publish a short book containing written diary entries, labelled pictures, maps and recorded narration. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools and voice recording make it manageable for Year 4 students to combine their research in one shareable book.

Students code Sphero BOLT to travel across a simple floor map representing an explorer’s route between key locations. They measure distances, program turns and speeds, then test and debug the route when the robot misses a destination or meets a marked obstacle. This practical task connects to how people have explored over time by focusing on navigation, planning and responding to unexpected conditions. Students finish by running and explaining their coded journey, using Sphero BOLT’s block coding, movement and coloured light features.

Students make a one-page visual timeline showing how exploration has changed from an early sea or land journey to modern space or scientific exploration. They add short captions explaining the reasons for each journey, the discoveries made and the opportunities or consequences that followed. The finished timeline is published and presented as a clear visual summary of how people have explored over time. Adobe Express’s timeline templates, text boxes and built-in image search help students organise the information without complicated design work.

Students record a short class podcast episode discussing whether a chosen exploration brought more opportunities or more harmful consequences. In pairs, one student acts as the interviewer while the other answers as an explorer, local person, scientist or historian using researched facts. They produce a two-to-three-minute episode with an introduction, three questions, balanced viewpoints and a closing conclusion linked to the consequences of exploration. Canva’s audio recording, simple editing timeline and ready-made podcast layouts let students record and arrange the episode in one place.

Glen Waverley|Year 4|Who We Are.d: Students create a short digital book about the unit topic of spiritual or religious beliefs, with one page each for beliefs, practices, celebrations and contributions to community life. This directly explores the line of inquiry about contributions of different religions to human diversity. They combine researched facts, respectful illustrations and recorded narration, then publish the finished book for classmates to read. Book Creator’s simple page templates, drawing, audio recording and page-turning book features make the task manageable for Year 4 students.

Students use Google Maps and Street View to visit several places of worship, such as a church, mosque, synagogue, temple or gurdwara, in Melbourne and other parts of the world. They look closely at visible features and orally compare similarities and differences of spiritual beliefs without making assumptions about the people who attend. Pairs present a short guided Street View walkthrough, pointing out three observations and one respectful question they still have. The search, zoom and Street View features provide the real-world visual evidence for their presentation.

Students build an annotated world map showing selected places where different spiritual or religious traditions began or have important cultural sites. This connects to the central idea that people’s beliefs contribute to the diversity of human life. Each pair adds a small set of clearly labelled markers with brief, researched notes explaining the importance of each place, then presents its map to the class. National Geographic MapMaker’s editable markers, labels, map layers and zoom controls allow students to create and share the map within the one tool.

Students plan and record a two-minute podcast episode about one way a religion contributes to human diversity through music, art, service, celebrations, food traditions or community gatherings. They include accurate information, explain why the contribution matters and avoid speaking as if everyone within a belief group is the same. Each pair publishes a short episode with a spoken introduction, main explanation and closing reflection linked to the unit’s central idea. Canva’s audio recording, simple timeline, title templates and built-in sound controls support the complete task.

Small groups create a short Kahoot about similarities and differences among spiritual beliefs studied in the unit. They write respectful multiple-choice questions based on class learning, add suitable images where helpful and include answers that avoid stereotypes. Each group hosts its finished quiz for classmates, then briefly explains one question that prompted useful discussion. Kahoot’s quiz builder, answer timer and instant class results make the student-created quiz easy to run and share.

Glen Waverley|Year 4|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use Google Maps to explore teacher-selected places connected to several named First Nations communities, including urban, coastal and inland locations. They use zoom, satellite view, Street View and the distance tool to notice physical features and discuss the importance of Country to First Nations people. Pairs then present a short live map tour, explaining how the places differ and why Country cannot be treated as one single type of environment. The everyday map-viewing and Street View features make the locations visible without students creating or saving their own maps.

Students use Book Creator to make a short digital book about the diversity of First Nations people. Using teacher-provided, trusted information, each pair creates pages about one named Nation or language group, its Country, community connections and a living tradition. Their finished book includes written explanations, approved images, a simple map sketch and a recorded reading, and can be shared with classmates. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tool and built-in voice recording keep the task manageable for Year 4.

Students use Minecraft Education to build a small virtual place that shows practical ways a community can care for Country, such as protecting waterways, limiting damage to plants and managing waste. This connects directly to the importance of Country and community for First Nations people, based on examples already studied in class rather than invented cultural practices. Students add signs explaining each choice and then lead classmates through their completed environment. Minecraft Education’s block-building, signs and shared-world features allow students to build and explain a clear model at a realistic scale.

Small groups use Kahoot to create a respectful class quiz about the diversity of First Nations people. They write questions from teacher-approved class material about named Nations, languages, Country, family, community and traditions, avoiding questions about restricted or sacred knowledge. Each group publishes and hosts its quiz, then reviews the answer screen with the class to correct common misunderstandings. Kahoot’s multiple-choice questions, images and instant answer results make the quiz easy to build and run in one or two lessons.

Students use Podcasting using Canva to record a two-minute audio segment explaining why Country, language or community is significant to a named First Nations group studied in class. Working from teacher-approved information, pairs write a short introduction, include two clear facts and finish with a respectful reflection on the central idea. They record their voices, trim mistakes, arrange the audio and publish a finished class podcast episode. Canva’s built-in voice recording and simple audio timeline let Year 4 students produce and present the episode without specialist equipment.

Glen Waverley|Year 5|How We Express Ours.d: Students use Microsoft Forms to survey classmates about a small community need, such as clearer playground signs or a better way to organise shared equipment, as part of How We Express Ourselves. This directly explores how design thinking meets community needs. They write suitable questions, collect responses and study the automatic charts to identify what users want. Each group presents its survey results and a short design brief based on the evidence.

Students use Lego Spike Prime to build and code a simple working solution for an everyday classroom need in the How We Express Ourselves unit, such as a reminder alarm, moving sign or equipment counter. This puts the central idea, People design for purpose, into practice. Using the building pieces, motors, sensors and block coding, they test the design with classmates and debug problems. Each group presents its working model and explains how feedback helped improve it.

Students use Adobe Express to create a digital poster promoting a school event or positive community action during the How We Express Ourselves unit. This focuses on effective ways to engage an audience through purposeful choices. They combine a strong headline, a few key facts, suitable images, colour and layout using the ready-made poster templates and simple editing tools. Students publish and present their finished posters, explaining which design choices should catch the intended audience’s attention.

Students use Book Creator to document how design thinking creates in various ways during the How We Express Ourselves unit. They make a short design journal showing an initial need, labelled sketches, feedback, changes and a final proposal for a useful classroom product. The page templates, drawing tools, text boxes, photo feature and built-in audio recording let students explain each stage clearly. They share the completed digital books with classmates as evidence that people design for purpose.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to make a short advertisement for a simple product they have designed on paper for the How We Express Ourselves unit. This explores effective ways to engage an audience by showing a problem, the product’s purpose and how it helps. They arrange paper shapes or classroom objects, capture small movements frame by frame, and add titles and recorded narration using the app’s built-in features. Each group screens its finished advertisement and gathers audience feedback about which message was most convincing.

Glen Waverley|Year 5|How We Organise Our.d: Students use Microsoft Excel to manage a fictional weekly income and make choices about spending, saving, donating and unexpected costs. This directly explores the line of inquiry that responsibilities come with managing income. They enter amounts into a simple budget table, use formulas to calculate balances and test how changing one choice affects the final result. Each student finishes with a clear budget and a short explanation typed into the spreadsheet about their most responsible decision.

Students use Microsoft Forms to create and complete a class survey about what makes a person wealthy, including money, time, relationships, health, skills and access to services. This connects directly to the line of inquiry that wealth is more than money. They use multiple-choice and ranking questions, then examine the automatic charts to identify patterns and differences in the class responses. The class ends with a shareable survey summary showing its main findings about wealth.

Students use Book Creator to make a short guide showing several ways people earn and manage income in human society. This directly addresses the line of inquiry that income is earned and managed in many ways. Each page can feature a different example, such as wages, running a small business, selling goods or providing a service, with students adding text, drawings and recorded narration. Students publish and present a digital book that explains both earning choices and responsible money decisions.

Students use Minecraft Education to build and run a small class marketplace that models how an economic system works. This makes the central idea that economic systems are an integral part of human society visible through rules, supply, demand and limited resources. Using building blocks, signs and inventory, each group produces a working market and presents what helped or hindered fair trade.

Students use National Geographic MapMaker to investigate how access to schools, health care, transport, water and jobs can shape wealth in different places. Students present an annotated map with a short written conclusion explaining how location can affect people’s economic opportunities and quality of life.

Students write clear survey questions, collect responses and study the automatic charts before presenting two practical recommendations. Students use Lego Spike Prime to build and code a small automated sorting system for the How We Organise Ourselves unit. Students use Minecraft Education to build a compact community precinct for How We Organise Ourselves, including essential organisations such as a council office, health service, transport hub and emergency service. Students use Book Creator to produce a short digital case study of one organisation for How We Organise Ourselves, such as Wesley College, a local council, a charity or a sporting club. Each student publishes a shareable book containing a simple organisation chart, written explanations, images and a recorded spoken reflection. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools, image tools and built-in audio recording keep the task manageable.

Students use Adobe Express to create a one-page public information poster for an imagined community organisation in the How We Organise Ourselves unit. Students combine a clear heading, a simple flow diagram, short role descriptions and contact information, then present the finished poster as if introducing the organisation to local residents. Adobe Express’s ready-made poster templates, text boxes, icons and layout tools provide the practical support.

Canva’s ready-made poster templates and drag-and-drop text and image tools make the task manageable in a few lessons.

Students use IMovie to make a 30-second community announcement about an issue relevant to Year 6 students, such as reducing litter or balancing screen time. Each group records short video clips, adds titles, trims scenes and chooses suitable music before presenting its finished announcement to the class. IMovie’s simple timeline, camera recording and title tools support the whole production in one place.

Students use GarageBand to record a short radio advertisement promoting a fictional event at school. Each group produces a polished 30-second advertisement, then plays it for classmates and collects verbal responses about which techniques were convincing. GarageBand’s voice recorder, sound loops and track editor let students record and refine the advertisement without specialist equipment.

Students use Book Creator to make a short guide called “How to Read Media Messages” for younger students. Each student creates several pages with their own sample media messages, written explanations and recorded audio advice. Book Creator’s page templates, text boxes, drawing tools and built-in audio recording make the guide easy to create and share.

Students use Padlet to examine a teacher-prepared collection of media examples about the same topic, such as advertisements, news headlines and public messages. Padlet’s column layout, post boxes, links and comment feature create a clear, shareable class media-analysis wall.

Glen Waverley|Year 6|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use Microsoft Forms to survey classmates about what influences their consumer choices, such as price, advertising, brand, convenience and environmental impact. They create clear multiple-choice questions, collect anonymous responses and present the automatic charts to the class. The everyday features that make this manageable are the question templates, response collection and built-in summary charts.

Students use Microsoft Excel to analyse a supplied table comparing everyday products by price, packaging, transport distance, worker pay and impact on habitats. This connects to the line of inquiry about how consumer decisions impact living things and their habitats. They sort and filter the data, calculate simple scores and make a chart showing which products appear to be more responsible choices. The familiar spreadsheet cells, formulas, sorting tools and chart button power the task.

Students use Dollar Street to compare food, clothing, household items and shopping habits of families at different income levels around the world. This supports the central idea by showing how human needs, income and natural resources are connected within consumer systems. Pairs select several image comparisons and present a live visual explanation of what is similar, what is different and what assumptions the images challenge. Dollar Street’s country, income and topic filters make the comparison practical for Year 6 students.

Students use Adobe Express to create a one-page responsible shopping guide about the unit topic of consumer choices and sustainability. Each guide explains one realistic action, such as repairing, borrowing, buying second-hand, choosing less packaging or checking how a product was made, and is published for families to view. Students use Padlet to build a class gallery of fairer alternatives to common consumer habits. Padlet’s shared board, post and commenting features make every proposal visible and easy to discuss.

Tinkercad’s everyday circuit simulator, including its drag-and-drop components and virtual multimeter, lets students test safely without needing specialist equipment.

The built-in light sensor, LED display and simple block coding are the key features used in the investigation.

Each pair presents a short live walkthrough showing three observations and one question about who benefited from the development. They sort the figures and create charts to investigate how migration has contributed to nation building. Each student produces one clearly labelled chart and a short written conclusion explaining what the data shows and what it does not show about Indigenous and colonial populations. The table, sort and chart features make the activity manageable for Year 6.

Students use Explain Everything to build a narrated timeline of one Australian development, such as the gold rush, railway expansion or post-war migration. They arrange dates, images, labels and arrows to show the human needs that drove change and the effects on migrants, Indigenous peoples and colonial populations. Each group records a two-minute explanation and publishes the finished timeline for classmates to view. The slide canvas, drawing tools and built-in voice recording are the main features used.

Students use Podcasting using Canva to record a short interview-style episode about the claim that human needs drive the development of nations. Working in pairs, one student takes the role of host and the other presents evidence about migration, settlement and impacts on Indigenous or colonial populations. Each pair produces a three-minute podcast with an opening, two evidence-based questions, a balanced conclusion and a simple title screen. Canva's built-in audio recording, trimming and page design features support the whole task.

Glen Waverley|Year 6|Who We Are.d: Students create a short digital book called “Who We Are”, combining personal stories about the beliefs, values, relationships and experiences that have shaped them. This connects directly to the central idea about the nature of the self and human relationships. Each student publishes a shareable book with written reflections, drawings, photographs they choose to include and recorded narration. They use Book Creator’s simple page templates, audio recording and read-aloud features to bring their reflections together.

Students collect anonymous class data about everyday habits that support physical, mental and social health in the “Who We Are” unit, such as sleep, movement, time outdoors and connecting with others. This investigates the central idea’s focus on personal, physical, mental and social health without asking students to disclose sensitive details. They enter the results in Microsoft Excel, calculate simple totals or averages, and create charts that they present to the class. The activity uses Excel’s table, formula and chart features to help students identify patterns and discuss what the data can and cannot tell us.

Students build a small shared community in Minecraft Education that supports the “Who We Are” focus on wellbeing and human relationships. This connects to the central idea by asking them to show how spaces and agreed behaviours can help people feel safe, included, active and connected. Teams construct places such as a quiet area, community garden, recreation space and meeting place, then guide classmates through their design and explain their choices. They use Minecraft Education’s blocks, signs, books and multiplayer building features to create and present the community.

Students code a Micro:bit wellbeing reminder for the “Who We Are” unit, choosing simple actions such as stretching, breathing slowly, drinking water or checking in with a trusted person. This links directly to the central idea’s focus on personal, physical, mental and social health. They program button presses to display different reminders, test the device with classmates and debug any code that does not work as intended. The activity relies on the Micro:bit’s buttons, LED display and simple block coding, and each student presents a working reminder device with an explanation of the choices they made.

Students design a one-page “Who We Are” wellbeing guide for other Year 6 students, offering practical ways to strengthen relationships, manage everyday stress and care for physical health. This responds directly to the central idea about personal, physical, mental and social health and human relationships. They publish a clear digital page that combines short advice, suitable images and links to trusted school support. Students use Adobe Express’s templates, text boxes, image library and webpage publishing feature to create a polished guide for a real audience.

St Kilda|Prep|How We Express Ourselves.d: Students make one page about an important celebration or tradition in their family, using a drawing, photo or simple typed sentence. They record themselves explaining what happens and why it is important, linking directly to the traditions of our families and communities. The pages are combined into a class celebration book that students can read and listen to together. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools and voice-recording button make this manageable for Prep students.

Students answer a short picture-based class survey about celebrations and traditions, such as whether their family shares special food, wears special clothes, gives gifts or gathers with others. They then look at the automatic charts and talk about the similarities and differences between celebrations. The class presents two or three findings, such as which traditions are common and which are less common. Microsoft Forms’ picture choices and automatic charts power the activity without students needing to type long answers.

In pairs, students choose characters and a background, then record a short puppet scene showing how and why people celebrate an important event. One puppet can ask questions while the other explains a tradition such as sharing food, singing, decorating or giving thanks. Each pair ends with a recorded puppet show that can be presented to the class. Puppet Pals’ movable characters, backgrounds and record button let Prep students create the scene through talk and play.

Students create a short sound piece for a celebration or tradition by choosing a few suitable loops and recording their own voice, clapping or simple percussion. They explain whether the sounds are used for dancing, gathering, remembering, welcoming or another reason, connecting to how and why people celebrate. Each student or pair produces a short audio track for a class listening session about celebration sounds. GarageBand’s loop browser and audio recorder make it easy to arrange and record the sounds.

Small groups use classroom figures and simple paper decorations to show the order of events in a familiar celebration or tradition. They move the pieces a little at a time and take photos to animate actions such as preparing, gathering, sharing food and saying goodbye. The finished stop-motion film shows how people recognise an important event through repeated traditions. Stop Motion Studio’s frame-by-frame camera and playback buttons allow students to capture, test and fix their sequence.

St Kilda|Prep|How We Organise Ourselves.d: Students code a Bee-Bot to travel across a simple floor mat showing places in the school community, such as the classroom, office, library and sick bay. At each place, they name a person’s role and one responsibility, linking directly to the line of inquiry about roles people play. Pairs plan, test and debug their route before presenting the completed journey to the class. The Bee-Bot’s forward, backward, turn and go buttons make the coding manageable for Prep students.

Students make a short digital class book called “Everyone Has a Job” about roles and responsibilities in the community. Each child creates one page about a familiar role, draws the person, adds a simple sentence and records their voice explaining how that person helps others. The finished pages form a shareable class book that supports the central idea that we all have roles and responsibilities in the community. Book Creator’s drawing, text and voice-recording features let Prep students contribute in different ways.

Students use ChatterPix Kids to make a familiar community object speak, such as a library book, rubbish bin, school hat or crossing sign. They photograph the object, draw a mouth and record a short message explaining who looks after it and what people are responsible for doing. The clips connect to the line of inquiry about responsibilities in the community and can be presented as a class guessing game. The simple photo, mouth line and voice-recording features keep the task quick and achievable for Prep.

Students view the St Kilda neighbourhood in Google Maps and use Street View to explore places such as the school, library, shops, park and transport stops. In pairs, they identify people who may work at each place and discuss the roles those people play in the community. Each pair presents a short live Street View walkthrough, naming two places, the people who help there and how their work supports everyone. Google Maps’ search, zoom and Street View features allow students to explore without needing to log in or edit a map.

Students create a short Puppet Pals scene showing people working together in a familiar community situation, such as borrowing a library book or keeping a playground tidy. They choose characters and a background, move the puppets and record simple dialogue about each person’s role and responsibility. The finished puppet scene directly explores the line of inquiry about how working together helps everyone. Puppet Pals’ character movement, backgrounds and built-in voice recording allow Prep pairs to make and present the scene in one tool.

St Kilda|Prep|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use Seek by iNaturalist to photograph and identify plants, insects and other living things in the school grounds while exploring Sharing the Planet. They discuss how people interact with this environment and how actions such as planting, watering or dropping rubbish may affect what lives there. Each pair records three identified living things and presents the photographs and names to the class. The tool’s camera identification feature makes the close observation and recording manageable for Prep students.

Students view Street View images of the St Kilda foreshore and compare cleaner areas with places where roads, buildings or rubbish affect the environment. This directly explores the central idea that human actions change the environment. As a class, they present a simple oral list of things people have changed and actions that could help care for the beach. Google Maps’ Street View feature lets students safely look around a familiar local environment without needing to log in or edit a map.

Students make a short class book about ways Prep children can care for the environment in Sharing the Planet. Each pair creates one page showing an action such as using a bin, saving water or protecting plants, linking to the line of inquiry about ways people can take action and care for the environment. They add a drawing or photo, a short teacher-supported sentence and a voice recording, then share the finished book with another class. Book Creator’s simple page, drawing, photo and audio buttons allow the whole product to be made in one tool.

Students program a Beebot to travel across a simple classroom mat showing a park with paths, plants, bins and areas of rubbish. They choose a route that avoids damaging plants and reaches places where people can take action to care for the environment. Pairs enter commands, test the route, debug any mistakes and then present their successful caring-for-the-park journey. The Beebot’s forward, backward and turn buttons make movement and navigation clear and hands-on for Prep students.

Students photograph one example of people helping or harming the school environment as part of Sharing the Planet. They use the microphone to explain what is happening and suggest one action that would care for the environment, connecting directly to the idea that human actions change the environment. Each student publishes a simple photo-and-voice reflection for classmates and families to view. Seesaw’s built-in camera, voice recording and drawing tools let students circle the important detail and explain their thinking in one place.

St Kilda|Prep|Where We Are in Place and.d: Students use Beebots to explore orientation and movement through a simple floor map of familiar places around St Kilda Campus. This connects to the central idea by helping them understand where places are and how people move between them. In small groups, students program, test and debug a route from one landmark to another, then demonstrate the completed journey to the class. The Beebot’s forward, backward, turn and go buttons make the navigation task manageable for Prep students.

Students view Google Maps and Street View to explore St Kilda Campus and nearby landmarks as part of learning about where we are in place and time. This connects to the central idea through orientation in place and the relationship between people and familiar local places. Pairs follow a teacher-chosen route in Street View, identify two landmarks and present an oral walkthrough explaining what they noticed along the way. The everyday map zoom and Street View arrows allow students to look around and move through the area without needing a login.

Students use ScratchJr to create a simple personal history showing three moments such as being a baby, starting kindergarten and beginning Prep. This directly explores the central idea’s focus on personal histories and changes over time. Students make three pages, add a character to each one and code it to move or speak, then present their finished sequence to a partner. ScratchJr’s page button, picture blocks and simple movement commands make the timeline achievable for Prep students.

Students use PicCollage to compare a familiar place or part of family life in the past and today for the unit Where We Are in Place and Time. This connects to the central idea by showing how personal histories and places can change over time. Using teacher-provided or family-supplied photographs, students arrange a simple then-and-now collage and add short labels such as “past” and “now.” PicCollage’s photo layout, text and sticker features help students create a clear image they can publish and discuss with the class.

Students use Seesaw to record a short story about an important place in their personal history, such as a previous home, a grandparent’s house or a favourite local park. This links directly to the central idea by exploring the connection between individuals, places and memories over time. Each student draws the place, adds one or two labels and records their voice explaining why it matters and whether it has changed. Seesaw’s built-in drawing, labelling and voice-recording tools create a shareable class collection of personal place stories.

St Kilda|Prep|Who We Are.d: Students complete a teacher-made picture survey about sleep, healthy food, water, movement and feeling cared for. This explores the central idea that people's basic needs must be met to be healthy. As a class, they view the automatic charts and talk about which needs help bodies and brains. The simple choice questions and built-in charts make the class data easy for Prep students to collect and present.

Students code a short animation showing a character making a kind choice, such as inviting someone to play or helping someone who is upset. This connects to how our emotions, behaviours and actions promote relationships. They use movement blocks, speech bubbles and two simple scenes to show what happens before and after the kind action. Each pair presents its finished animation and explains how the choice helped the relationship.

In pairs, students create and record a short puppet scene about recognising an emotion and responding helpfully. This directly explores how our emotions, behaviours and actions promote relationships. Students choose characters and a background, move the puppets and record their own voices as the scene plays. They present a finished puppet video showing an everyday response such as listening, sharing, apologising or asking for help.

Students record a short collection of sounds that can help them feel calm, connected or ready to learn. This supports the inquiry into how our emotions, behaviours and actions promote relationships. They use the built-in microphone to record gentle tapping, humming, breathing or positive spoken phrases, then arrange the recordings into a simple sound sequence. The class listens to each finished track and discusses when that calming action might be useful.

Students make a short digital book called What My Body and Brain Need, with one page each for food, water, sleep, movement and care. This connects to how we care for our bodies and the central idea that people's basic needs must be met to be healthy. They draw or add pictures, write a simple sentence and record themselves explaining each need. Book Creator's page templates, drawing tools and voice recording help each child publish a clear book to share with the class.

St Kilda|Prep|How the World Works.d: Students investigate how things move in How the World Works by recording a ball rolling down a low ramp. They test two ramp heights and use slow-motion replay to notice when the ball speeds up, linking directly to the central idea about laws in the natural world. Each pair presents its two short recordings and explains what changed. The tool’s record and slow-motion playback features make movement easy for Prep students to observe.

Students explore change in the natural world for How the World Works by photographing an ice cube as it melts. They take a new frame every few minutes, then play the frames together to show the change from solid ice to water. This connects directly to the central idea about the natural world and its laws, and each group creates a short animation to share with the class. The simple frame-by-frame camera and playback features power the activity.

Students explore the St Kilda foreshore in How the World Works using satellite view and Street View. They look for natural features such as water, sand and trees, then notice human features such as roads, paths and buildings. This connects directly to the central idea about interactions between the natural world and human societies, and pairs present one example by showing the chosen view on screen. The zoom, satellite view and Street View features let students closely examine the place without needing to log in or edit a map.

Students investigate local living things in How the World Works by browsing pictures of Victorian birds, insects or plants. In pairs, they choose one living thing and use its information page to notice where it lives and what helps it survive there. This links directly to the central idea about the natural world, and each pair presents the species page and shares two observations. The tool’s picture galleries, categories and species information pages make the research manageable for Prep students.

Students code a simple How the World Works scene showing how rain affects people, plants or animals. They choose characters and backgrounds, then use movement and start blocks to show clouds arriving, rain falling and a response such as a plant growing or a person opening an umbrella. This connects directly to the central idea about interactions between the natural world and human societies, and each pair creates and presents a short animated project. ScratchJr’s picture-based coding blocks, characters and backgrounds make the sequence realistic for Prep students to build and debug.

St Kilda|Year 1|How We Express Ourselves.d: Students use Book Creator to make a class book about different ways people communicate emotions. Each pair creates a page showing one feeling through a drawing, a short sentence and a recorded voice that matches the emotion, linking to the line of inquiry about different ways to communicate emotions. The finished book becomes a shareable feelings guide that the class can read and listen to together. Book Creator’s drawing, text and audio recording features keep the task simple for Year 1 students.

Students photograph a toy or their own drawing, add a mouth and record it speaking in a happy, worried, excited or frustrated voice. They explore the central idea that people express their emotions through the way they communicate by changing their words, volume and tone. Each student makes a short talking-character clip and presents it while classmates identify the emotion and explain what they heard. ChatterPix Kids’ simple mouth line and voice recording features power the activity.

Students code a character to show an emotion using movement, facial appearance, speech and sound. This connects to the line of inquiry about how movement expresses feelings as students test whether slow, quick, bouncy or drooping movements communicate different emotions. Each pair makes and presents a short coded scene in which one character shows a feeling and another responds appropriately. ScratchJr’s movement blocks, speech bubbles, recorded sounds and character editor let students build and debug the scene.

Students use classroom figures or playdough characters to create a short stop-motion scene about understanding emotions through body language and facial cues. They move the character a little at a time to show a feeling changing, such as calm to surprised or lonely to included. Each group records and presents a short animation, then classmates name the clues that helped them understand the character’s emotion. Stop Motion Studio’s frame-by-frame camera and playback features make the gradual movement visible.

Students record a short feelings performance in Apple Clips, using their face, body and voice to communicate one chosen emotion without naming it. This directly explores the line of inquiry about understanding others’ expressions through body language and facial cues. They add a simple title at the end revealing the emotion, then present the finished clip for classmates to interpret. Apple Clips’ video recording, trimming and built-in title features allow students to make a clear, shareable guessing clip.

St Kilda|Year 1|How We Organise Ourselve.d: Students code a Beebot to move across a simple floor mat showing a product’s journey, such as milk travelling from a farm to a factory, shop and home. This explores the line of inquiry, “The systems products go through.” In small groups, students program, test and debug the route, then present the completed journey to the class. The Beebot’s forward, backward, turn and clear buttons make each step in the system visible and manageable for Year 1 students.

Students use Google Maps to view where familiar products such as bananas, rice or wool can come from. This connects directly to the line of inquiry, “Where products come from.” With the teacher, they zoom out from Melbourne, find each place and use Street View where suitable to compare farms, towns, ports and shops. Pairs then present one product’s possible journey by navigating the map live and explaining the places it passes through, using the search, zoom and Street View features.

Students complete a short picture-based class survey about how they choose between familiar products, such as two lunchbox snacks or two kinds of packaging. This investigates the line of inquiry, “How people choose their products.” They select reasons such as price, taste, appearance, size or less packaging, then view and discuss the class results. The simple choice questions and automatic charts in Microsoft Forms create a shareable record of the class data.

Students make a short stop-motion film showing the stages involved in preparing a simple product for consumers, such as bread moving from grain to flour, bakery, shop and table. This demonstrates the central idea, “Systems are involved in preparing products for consumers.” Pairs move paper pictures or classroom models one small step at a time, take a frame after each movement and play the sequence back to check the order. The frame-by-frame camera and playback features let students create and present a clear film of the product system.

Students code a simple animated sequence showing where a familiar product comes from and how it reaches a consumer. This links the lines of inquiry, “Where products come from” and “The systems products go through.” They create or choose characters for places such as a farm, factory, shop and home, then use movement and message blocks to show the product passing through each stage. The picture-based coding blocks and page backgrounds help Year 1 students build, test, debug and present a short interactive product journey.

St Kilda|Year 1|How the World Works.d: Students collect the St Kilda weather each morning for two weeks and enter simple words or numbers into a shared Microsoft Excel table. This explores types of weather conditions and helps the class notice weather patterns. With teacher support, students use the chart feature to turn their results into a simple column graph and present which weather occurred most often. Excel’s cells and automatic charts make the class data easy to organise and compare.

Students place weather, clothing and activity picture cards on a floor grid, then code a Beebot to travel from a weather condition to a suitable choice. This directly explores how weather impacts our clothing and activities. Pairs test their route, debug any wrong turns and present their successful journey to the class. The Beebot’s forward, backward, turn and go buttons allow Year 1 students to program the route themselves.

Students use Google Maps and Street View to visit several teacher-chosen places with visibly different conditions, such as a snowy town, a tropical beach and central Melbourne. They look closely for clues about how weather affects people’s clothing, homes and activities. Each pair presents two observations from the Street View images and explains what the weather might be like in that place. Google Maps’ search and Street View features let students explore these locations without needing an account.

Students make a short digital book called Our Weather Guide about how weather affects our lives. Each student creates one page for a condition such as sunny, rainy, windy or cold, adding a drawing and a sentence about suitable clothing, food, feelings or activities. They record their voice reading the page, and the pages are combined into a class book to share. Book Creator’s drawing, text and voice-recording features keep the task manageable for Year 1.

Students use ChatterPix Kids to turn a photograph or drawing of a weather symbol into a talking weather reporter. They record a short message naming the weather and explaining how it could affect clothing or activities that day. The finished talking-weather clips are played to the class as a set of simple weather reports. The app’s mouth line and voice-recording features let students create and publish the clip in a few clear steps.

St Kilda|Year 1|Where We Are in Place an.d: Students photograph a classroom or family artefact and make it ‘speak’ about how it was used in the past and how a similar object is used today. This directly explores how stories and artefacts help us understand connections between the past and present. Each student creates a short talking-artefact video to show the class or share with families. The simple photo, mouth-drawing and voice-recording features make the task manageable for Year 1 students.

Students interview an older family member about a toy, game or school experience from their childhood, then record a short retelling in Seesaw. This supports the line of inquiry about how we learn about the past and shows why people preserve stories. Students add a drawing or photograph and record their voice to create a digital oral-history page for a class collection. Seesaw’s camera, drawing and voice-recording features allow students to capture and share their work in one place.

Students code a simple story that moves through three scenes showing an object in the past, present and imagined future. This connects directly to the central idea that stories and artefacts help us understand connections between the past, present and future. Students choose or draw characters and objects, then use movement, speech and page-change blocks to build and debug their story. The finished projects can be played and presented to classmates as short interactive timelines.

In small groups, students use classroom objects or play materials to show how an everyday item has changed over time, such as a telephone, camera or toy. This explores how artefacts give us clues about the past and how they may continue changing into the future. Students move the objects a little at a time, take a sequence of frames and add simple spoken narration to make a short stop-motion film. The frame-by-frame camera and playback features let Year 1 students test, adjust and share their sequence.

As a teacher-guided class activity, students use Google Maps and Street View to explore preserved places around St Kilda, such as Luna Park, the pier or older buildings. This supports the line of inquiry about why people preserve stories and artefacts by helping students notice visible clues from the past in places that still exist today. Pairs take turns directing a short Street View walkthrough, identifying one old-looking feature and presenting what they think it tells us about the place. The search, zoom and Street View features are central to this live class tour, with students only viewing the map and not creating or saving content.

St Kilda|Year 1|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use Tablet Magnifiers to closely examine real leaves, flowers and safe images of bees during the Sharing the Planet unit. They use the zoom control to find and compare structures such as leaf veins, petals, pollen-carrying hairs and wings, linking directly to the physical structure of plants and bees. Students capture a few close-up images and explain how one visible feature helps the living thing survive. The everyday zoom and image-capture features turn their observations into a small class gallery.

Students create a short digital field guide about plants and bees in the Sharing the Planet unit. Each pair makes pages showing a living thing, labels its physical structures and records a simple explanation of how one feature supports survival in its environment. They publish a book with drawings, typed labels and their own voice recordings to share with another Year 1 class. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tool and audio-record button make the task manageable for young students.

Students program Beebots to travel across a simple floor grid showing flowers, water, shelter and hazards as part of the Sharing the Planet unit. They plan and test a route that helps a bee reach the things it needs to survive while avoiding human-made dangers such as sprayed areas or rubbish. Groups debug their commands, then present their successful route and explain how the environment helped or harmed the bee. The Beebot’s forward, backward, turn and clear buttons make the movement and navigation visible and easy to test.

Students build simple paper or modelling-clay plant parts and use Stop Motion Studio to show a flower being visited by a bee in the Sharing the Planet unit. They move the bee a small amount between each photo to demonstrate how its wings, legs and body help it reach a flower and carry pollen. Each group produces a short stop-motion film that explains how physical structures support survival. The app’s frame-by-frame camera and playback button let students test and improve the movement without specialist skills.

Students use PicCollage to compare a healthy habitat with one affected by people during the Sharing the Planet unit. They arrange teacher-provided pictures of plants, bees, water, flowers, litter and pesticides into two clear sections, then add short labels explaining helpful and harmful human actions. The finished comparison poster shows their understanding of human impact on living things and can be presented to the class. PicCollage’s simple photo layout, text and sticker tools allow Year 1 students to make the message clear.

St Kilda|Year 1|Who We Are.d: Students make a class book about ourselves and the games we play, with each pair adding a page about one familiar playground or classroom game. They draw the game, record a short explanation and name one responsibility that helps everyone play safely and fairly, linking directly to our responsibilities when playing games. The finished book becomes a shareable Year 1 guide called Games That Help Us Learn About Ourselves. Book Creator’s simple page templates, drawing tools and voice-recording button make this manageable for young students.

Students use puppet characters to act out a small problem that might happen during a game, such as someone changing the rules or leaving another player out. They create two short scenes showing how different player choices affect relationships, then explain which choice was kinder or fairer. Each pair presents its recorded puppet show to the class for a brief discussion. Puppet Pals’ movable characters, backgrounds and built-in voice recording let students create the whole scene in one place.

Students choose an emotion that can arise during games, such as excitement, disappointment, frustration or pride, and draw a simple face to represent it within ChatterPix Kids. They add a mouth and record the character explaining how to notice and manage that feeling, connecting directly to how to identify and manage emotions. Each student produces a short talking emotion character that can be played during a class reflection. The tool’s draw-a-mouth and voice-recording features keep the task quick and accessible for Year 1.

Students code a Beebot across a simple floor grid showing moments from a familiar game, including waiting for a turn, following a rule, checking on a friend and solving a disagreement. At each stop, they explain how that player choice could affect relationships or show responsibility when playing games. Pairs test their route, clear the code and debug any turns or steps that do not reach the intended square, then present the successful journey. Beebots’ forward, backward, turn and clear buttons make the coding concrete and suitable for Year 1.

Students create a short audio reflection called How a Game Can Feel, based on a game they have played at school. They record three spoken parts describing how they felt before, during and after the game, and add simple built-in sounds to match each emotion, linking to how to identify and manage emotions. The result is a short audio piece that students can play for a partner and explain. GarageBand’s voice recorder and ready-made sound loops allow students to record and arrange their ideas without needing another tool.

St Kilda|Year 2|How We Express Ourselves.d: Students use PicCollage to create a museum-style page about an artefact connected to a family or classroom culture. This directly explores how artefacts capture history and cultural expression. They arrange photos of the artefact, add a title and write short labels explaining what it is, how it is used and what it may tell us about people’s beliefs or values. The simple photo layout, text box and sticker features help each pair produce a shareable digital museum page.

Students photograph a familiar artefact in Seesaw, such as a special piece of clothing, celebration object or family keepsake, with family permission. They use the drawing and label tools to point out important details, then record a short explanation of what the object shows about beliefs and values within a culture. This connects directly to the central idea that artefacts provide a window into the beliefs and values of cultures. Their finished Seesaw post becomes a narrated artefact record that classmates can view and discuss.

Students use GarageBand to make a short sound piece representing a familiar ritual or tradition, such as a birthday, welcome, shared meal or community celebration. This supports the line of inquiry about the importance of rituals and traditions by asking students to explain why particular sounds, words or music matter. They record a spoken introduction, add a few suitable instrument sounds or sound effects, and finish with one sentence about the values the tradition expresses. GarageBand’s voice recorder, instrument buttons and simple track timeline power the finished one-minute audio piece.

Students use Puppet Pals to create a short interview between a museum guide and a character connected to a chosen cultural artefact. Their script explains what the artefact is, when it is used and what it reveals about the culture’s beliefs, values or traditions. This directly explores how artefacts capture history and cultural expression. Using the character, background and voice-recording features, pairs produce and present a simple one-minute puppet interview.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to show the steps of a familiar, non-sacred family or classroom tradition using paper figures and small objects. This connects to the line of inquiry about the importance of rituals and traditions because students must place the actions in order and show which artefacts are used. They take a series of small-movement photos, add brief captions and play the images as a short animation. The frame-by-frame camera and playback features create a shareable visual sequence that classmates can compare with other traditions.

St Kilda|Year 2|How the World Works.d: Students create a short class book showing how electricity, solar energy and fossil fuels help people in daily life. This directly explores the line of inquiry about energy types and how energy helps us each day. Each pair makes one page with a drawing, a simple sentence and a recorded explanation, then the pages are combined and presented as a class book. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tool and audio recording make the task manageable for Year 2 students.

Students code a simple animation showing an energy transformation, such as sunlight helping a plant grow or electricity making a lamp produce light. This connects directly to the line of inquiry about energy transformation. They choose characters and backgrounds, join movement and appearance blocks, test their sequence and debug any parts that play in the wrong order. Each pair presents its finished animation and explains where the energy starts and what it becomes.

Students collect classroom data by counting how many lights, screens and other electrical items are switched on at two set times during the day. This supports the line of inquiry about our responsibility to conserve energy. With teacher support, they enter their counts into a simple Excel table and use the chart button to make a column graph comparing the two checks. The class presents the graph and agrees on one realistic action that could reduce unnecessary electricity use.

Students build a short stop-motion sequence showing one everyday energy transformation, such as sunlight warming water or electricity making a fan turn. This directly explores the line of inquiry about energy transformation and how energy helps us in daily life. They move paper pictures a small amount, take a frame with the built-in camera, replay the sequence and fix any jumps that make it unclear. Each group publishes a brief movie with a title naming the starting energy and the resulting action.

Students use Sphero Indi to investigate how stored electrical energy can be transformed into movement. They build a short route with the coloured tiles, predict what the car will do, then test and debug the route until it reaches an everyday destination such as a paper house or school. This connects directly to the line of inquiry about energy transformation. Groups present their completed route and explain that Indi’s rechargeable battery supplies the electrical energy that makes the wheels move.

St Kilda|Year 2|How We Organise Ourselve.d: Students observe the school grounds and count plants, animals, microorganisms they can see evidence of, and human-made technology such as drains, taps and paths. Back in class, they enter their tallies into a simple teacher-prepared spreadsheet to explore the line of inquiry that an ecosystem has animals, plants and microorganisms. They use Excel’s chart button to turn the class totals into a clear column graph. Pairs present the graph and explain one way technology may help or hinder the school ecosystem.

Students use Google Maps and Street View to explore two places where technology has changed an ecosystem, such as a river near a dam and a river in a less developed area. They look closely for roads, buildings, bridges, vegetation and visible animal habitats, connecting their observations to the line of inquiry that technology can help or hinder ecosystems. Each pair chooses two Street View scenes and prepares a short spoken comparison using what is visible on screen. They present their evidence to the class by navigating between the locations with the search, zoom and Street View features.

Students build a small Minecraft ecosystem containing water, plants, animals and safe places for living things. They then add one piece of technology, such as a road, bridge, farm or water channel, and test how it changes the available food, water and shelter. This directly explores the central idea that technology can influence the way ecosystems survive. Students use Minecraft’s blocks, animals and building tools to create a before-and-after model, then guide classmates through it and explain whether their technology helps or hinders the ecosystem.

Students code a short ScratchJr animation showing an ecosystem before and after a technological change, such as litter entering a pond or a water-cleaning system being added. They choose plant and animal characters, create two backgrounds and program movement to show how living things respond. The task connects to the line of inquiry that technology can cause ecosystems to adapt and evolve. Using simple movement blocks, page changes and recorded voices, students make and present a clear animated explanation of the change.

Students use classroom objects or paper pieces to create a small ecosystem with plants, animals and microorganisms. They photograph one small movement at a time as a piece of technology, such as a road, fence or rubbish collector, changes what happens in the habitat. This explores the line of inquiry that technology can help or hinder ecosystems. Students use Stop Motion Studio’s frame-by-frame camera and playback features to make a short film with a clear beginning, change and result, then show it to the class and explain the ecosystem’s response.

St Kilda|Year 2|Sharing the Planet.d: Students make a short digital book about how a local plant, animal and person depend on one another to sustain life. This directly explores the interdependence of people and environments. Each page combines a drawing or photo, a simple sentence and a recorded voice explanation, ending with one action people can take to protect the connection. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tool and voice-recording button make the finished books easy to create and share.

Students use Google Maps to view Street View images of the St Kilda area and compare places with many trees, gardens or open spaces with places covered by roads and buildings. They discuss how people’s wants and needs affect the land, looking for signs such as car parks, homes, shops, bike paths and green spaces. Pairs choose two locations and give a short presentation explaining what people changed, what living things might need there and one more sustainable choice. The ordinary map, zoom and Street View features allow students to explore and compare real places without logging in or editing the map.

Students collect class data about everyday resource use, such as reusable drink bottles, lunch packaging and sheets of paper used in one day, then enter the totals into a simple teacher-prepared spreadsheet. This supports the line of inquiry about our responsibility to use sustainable resources. Students use the data to make a basic column chart and present one change the class could test during the following week. Excel’s cells, simple totals and chart button turn their observations into a clear, shareable class record.

Students code a short ScratchJr animation showing two ways of travelling, such as a petrol car and walking, cycling or public transport. The animation explores the connection between fossil fuels and environmental impact by showing smoke, energy use or changes to the surrounding environment. Students sequence movement, speech and appearance blocks, test their project and debug any actions that happen in the wrong order. They finish with a playable comparison in which the characters explain which travel choice uses fewer fossil fuels.

Students photograph one example of a natural resource used around the classroom, such as paper, water or electricity, and explain how it helps people and comes from the environment. This connects to the responsibility to use sustainable resources and the central idea that people and environments depend on one another. On the photo, students use the drawing and label tools to show where waste could be reduced, then record a short spoken promise describing one realistic action. Seesaw’s camera, annotation and voice-recording features create a simple post that can be shared with classmates and families.

St Kilda|Year 2|Where We Are in Place an.d: Students use Google Maps to explore a familiar journey around St Kilda and a journey in another part of the world. They view each route and use Street View to identify landmarks, transport, road conditions and possible challenges, linking to the line of inquiry about challenges encountered on journeys. In pairs, students present a live Street View walkthrough and explain one new understanding a traveller might gain. The everyday map, zoom and Street View features make the places and routes easy to explore without students needing to log in or edit a map.

Students program a Beebot to complete a physical journey across a simple floor grid containing landmarks and obstacles. They press the direction buttons, test the route and debug it when the Beebot meets a challenge, connecting directly to the central idea that journeys can lead to challenges and new understandings. Each group presents its completed route and explains what it changed after an unsuccessful attempt. The Beebot’s forward, backward, turn, clear and go buttons provide an age-appropriate way to practise navigation and problem-solving.

Students use Book Creator to make a short book about a physical, learning or cultural journey linked to the unit’s line of inquiry about types of journeys. Each page shows a stage of the journey, a challenge and a new understanding gained along the way. Students publish and share a book containing their own drawings, short sentences and recorded narration. The simple page templates, drawing tools, text boxes and audio recording feature support Year 2 students to explain their ideas clearly.

Students code a character to travel through two or three scenes while completing a journey connected to Where We Are in Place and Time. They add a challenge such as a blocked path, test the program and change the movement blocks so the character can continue, linking to the line of inquiry about challenges encountered on journeys. Each pair presents a working animated journey and explains what the character learns by the end. ScratchJr’s picture-based movement, start, speech and scene blocks let students build and debug the journey without needing to type code.

Students use Puppet Pals to record a short interview between a traveller and someone they meet during a cultural journey. Their conversation explains where the traveller went, a challenge they encountered and a new understanding they gained, directly addressing the unit’s three lines of inquiry. Pairs present a finished puppet scene with spoken dialogue and a clear beginning, middle and end. The character, background, movement and voice-recording features allow students to create the whole performance within the tool.

St Kilda|Year 2|Who We Are.d: Students use Book Creator to make a short “Who We Are” book about their identity, interests and strengths. This directly explores the line of inquiry about personal identity and strengths. Each student creates four pages with drawings, photos, simple sentences and a recorded reading, then shares the finished book with a partner. The easy page templates, drawing tools, camera and audio recording features make the task manageable for Year 2.

Students complete a simple Microsoft Forms class survey about strategies they use when learning feels difficult, such as taking a breath, asking for help or trying a different way. The class examines the automatic charts to discuss how self-regulation supports learning in the Who We Are unit.
