Students compare the responses, identify the most common strategies and present one observation about the class data. The multiple-choice questions and automatic response charts are the key features used in this task.

Students code a short ScratchJr scene showing a character facing a small classroom challenge, managing their response and trying again. This connects to building resilience through knowledge of ourselves in the Who We Are unit. Students choose characters and backgrounds, join movement and speech blocks, test their sequence and debug any parts that do not run clearly. They finish with a playable animation that shows a practical resilience strategy to classmates.

Students create a PicCollage poster called “My Strengths and How I Help Others” for the Who We Are unit. This links personal identity and strengths to the central idea that the way we interact with others is influenced by who we are. Students add a photo or drawing, label three strengths and include examples of how each strength helps them work or play with others. The simple grid layouts, text labels, stickers and image tools support a clear poster that can be presented to the class.

In pairs, students use Stop Motion Studio to make a brief animation about recovering from an everyday setback, such as a block tower falling or a game not working. This explores the line of inquiry about building resilience through knowledge of ourselves in the Who We Are unit. Students move classroom figures a little at a time, capture each frame, test the playback and revise the sequence so the character pauses, chooses a strategy and tries again. The frame-by-frame camera and instant playback features produce a short film the pair can present and explain.

St Kilda|Year 3|How We Express Ourselves.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
St Kilda|Year 3|How We Express Ourselves.d: Students use Animating a Character with Adobe Express to record the same short message twice, changing their pace, volume and tone each time. This explores how the correct verbal form enhances the effectiveness of a message. They publish two short character clips and present which version is clearer, friendlier or more convincing. The simple voice-recording feature automatically matches the character’s movement to each recording.

Students use Book Creator to make a short class guide about verbal, non-verbal and visual methods of communication. Each page communicates one everyday message, such as “Please stop” or “You are welcome,” using recorded speech, a drawing, facial expression or written words. This directly explores the forms of verbal, non-verbal and visual communication and lets students compare their effectiveness. The easy page templates, drawing tools, text boxes and audio-recording button allow each student to publish and share a small digital book.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to create a short wordless scene in which classroom objects or simple paper figures communicate a message through movement and position. Classmates watch the movie and explain what they think the message means, linking to how people interpret messages and bring their own meaning to interactions. The creators then present their intended meaning and discuss which visual clues worked or caused confusion. The frame-by-frame camera and instant playback features make it practical to record, test and improve the movie during one or two lessons.

Students use PicCollage to design two visual notices for the same school message, such as reminding students to return library books. One notice deliberately has crowded text and unclear images, while the other uses a clear heading, a suitable picture and only the most important words. This tests the central idea that methods of communication have different features which impact their effectiveness. Students present both notices and explain their choices, using PicCollage’s simple layouts, text boxes, images and resizing tools.

In small groups, students use Microsoft Forms to build a short survey showing several words, symbols or brief messages that could be interpreted in different ways. Classmates complete the survey by choosing or explaining what they think each message means. This investigates how people interpret messages and bring their own meaning to interactions. Students present the collected responses and built-in charts, using the question builder and automatic results summary to identify which messages were clear and which caused mixed interpretations.

St Kilda|Year 3|How We Organise Ourselve.d: Students use Microsoft Forms to answer short scenarios about online choices, such as receiving an unkind message, sharing a photo or seeing something that feels unsafe. This directly explores how a choice of action and reaction affects others online. The class views the automatic response charts, discusses which choices are safe and ethical, and records a shared set of recommended actions in a final form question. The everyday features powering the task are multiple-choice questions, anonymous responses and automatic charts.

Students use Adobe Express to create a one-page online safety guide for other Year 3 students. Their guide explains our right to feel safe online and our responsibility to make ethical decisions, with practical advice about privacy, kindness and asking a trusted adult for help. Each student publishes or presents a shareable page containing a heading, three clear tips and simple images or icons. The task uses Adobe Express templates, text boxes, image search and page-sharing features.

Small groups use Minecraft Education to build a model online community where everyone should feel safe and included. As they build together, students practise asking permission, sharing resources, responding calmly to mistakes and using the in-game chat respectfully, linking directly to how actions and reactions affect others online. Each group creates labelled buildings or signs that show agreed community rules, then gives the class a guided tour of its world. The shared world, building blocks, signs and in-game chat are the everyday features at the centre of the task.

Pairs use Podcasting using Canva to record a short advice episode about making ethical online choices. They explain one realistic situation, such as pressure to share a password or an unkind comment in a game, and show how an informed choice can make a positive difference. Each pair produces a two-minute podcast with an introduction, a role-play and three clear pieces of advice for Year 3 listeners. The task uses Canva’s built-in audio recording, page timeline and simple sound controls.

Students use Teachable Machine to collect examples of classroom objects and train a simple model to sort them into two groups, without using faces or personal information. They test the model with new objects, record when it makes mistakes and discuss why online systems do not always make fair or accurate decisions, connecting to informed and ethical choices. Each group presents its trained model, test results and one rule about choosing safe, suitable information to share with an online tool. The everyday features powering the activity are webcam image capture, training buttons and live testing.

St Kilda|Year 3|How the World Works.d: Students use small balls of modelling clay to show particles in solids, liquids and gases, then move them frame by frame to model melting, freezing or evaporation. This directly explores how matter changes state when temperature and energy change. They make a short animation with labels explaining what the particles are doing before and after the change. Stop Motion Studio’s frame-by-frame camera and playback features make the movement visible and easy to review.

Students test how the temperature of an ice cube changes as it melts, entering a measurement into Microsoft Excel at regular intervals. This investigation connects to the line of inquiry about how matter changes state depending on temperature and energy. Each group produces a simple table and line graph showing the temperature readings and the point when the ice became liquid water. Excel’s cells and chart button turn the collected measurements into a clear visual record.

Students make a short digital guide about the responsible and ethical use of materials such as glass and plastic. They create pages comparing each material’s useful properties, possible problems and practical choices people can make to reduce waste or reuse items. The finished book includes student drawings, written explanations and a recorded spoken recommendation, ready to present to classmates. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools and audio recording feature keep the task manageable for Year 3.

Students test everyday materials for properties such as flexibility, strength, absorbency or waterproofing, then record each test in Seesaw. This addresses the central idea that materials behave in certain ways, creating both challenges and possible solutions. Each student publishes a short science journal entry with photos, results and a voice explanation of which material would best suit a chosen purpose. Seesaw’s built-in camera, drawing labels and voice recording tools allow students to capture and explain their evidence in one place.

In small groups, students create a short Kahoot quiz about the three states of matter, changes of state and responsible choices involving glass and plastic. They write clear questions, add answer choices, check the science and test the quiz with classmates. The class ends up with a playable review quiz that reveals which ideas are well understood and which need another look. Kahoot’s question builder, images, answer timer and live results make the quiz easy to create and present.

St Kilda|Year 3|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use Google Maps to view places that have experienced earthquakes, floods or bushfires and compare their location, landscape and nearby communities. This supports the line of inquiry into how natural disasters impact the environment and people. In pairs, students use map view, satellite view and Street View to prepare and present a short guided walkthrough showing important features such as rivers, coastlines, roads and open spaces. The everyday zoom, distance and Street View features help them explain why some places may be more exposed and how people could move to safety.

Students code a Micro:bit to act as a simple earthquake shake detector using its built-in movement sensor. They test gentle, medium and strong shaking, then debug the code so the lights or sound give a clear warning when movement passes a chosen level. This connects to the causes and types of natural disasters and to how humans respond with resilience. Each pair presents a working detector, demonstrates its warning signal and explains how monitoring movement can help people respond quickly.

Students build a small community designed to cope with one natural disaster, such as a flood, bushfire or earthquake. They include practical features such as raised buildings, clear evacuation routes, firebreaks, emergency shelters or open meeting areas. This directly explores how humans respond with resilience and connection after natural disasters. Using the ordinary building blocks, signs and camera feature, each group creates and presents a labelled model explaining how its design protects people and the environment.

Students create a short digital book about one natural disaster, covering what causes it, how it affects people and the environment, and how communities respond with resilience. Each page combines simple student-written explanations with drawings, photos from the built-in image search and a recorded voice explanation. This brings together all three lines of inquiry in a format suitable for Year 3 readers. Students publish and share a finished disaster preparedness book using Book Creator’s page templates, audio recording and read-aloud features.

Students watch a teacher-selected Clickview video about a real earthquake, flood, cyclone or bushfire and pause at key moments to answer embedded questions. They identify the cause of the disaster, record evidence of its impact and notice examples of people helping one another. This supports the lines of inquiry into disaster impacts and how humans respond with resilience and connection. Clickview’s pause, replay and interactive question features produce a saved set of student responses that the class can review and discuss together.

St Kilda|Year 3|Where We Are in Place an.d: Students use Google Maps to explore central Melbourne and another city using the map, satellite view and Street View. They identify visible city features such as roads, housing, parks, shops, public transport and public buildings, linking directly to the essential features of a city. Pairs follow a teacher-set route in Street View and record their observations in a simple presentation to the class. The zoom, satellite view, Street View and distance measurement features help students examine how city spaces are organised and used.

Students use Book Creator to make a short digital book showing how Melbourne has developed through time. Each page covers a different stage and explains how factors such as transport, population, work or new buildings helped shape the city, linking to the development of cities through time. Students add drawings, typed captions and short voice recordings, then publish and present their finished books. The simple page templates, drawing tools and audio recording button make the task manageable for Year 3 students.

Students build a simple floor plan of a city area and code Sphero BOLT to travel between places such as homes, a school, a hospital, shops and a park. They test and debug the route while discussing how roads and services help a city function, linking directly to the function of a city. Each group presents its working route and explains why the robot visits the places in that order. The block coding, movement controls and adjustable speed feature allow students to create and improve a realistic city journey.

Students use Stop Motion Studio to show a small model settlement developing into a city over time. They add one change at a time, such as roads, housing, transport, shops, parks and public services, and photograph each stage. Their finished stop-motion film explains the central idea that many factors shape the development of cities. The frame-by-frame camera, playback and simple title features let students record and share the changes clearly.

Students use Microsoft Forms to collect class opinions about which city features are most essential, such as public transport, parks, schools, hospitals and shops. They write clear multiple-choice questions, gather responses and examine the automatic charts, linking their findings to the essential features and function of a city. Each group presents one chart and explains what the class data suggests about people’s needs in cities. The question templates, response collection and automatic graph features power the whole investigation.

St Kilda|Year 3|Who We Are.d: Students create a short digital book about how the digestive, respiratory and circulatory systems connect and function. Each pair makes one page for each system, then adds a final page showing how exercise, food, sleep or hydration can affect the body. They publish and present a clear body systems guide for other Year 3 students. Book Creator’s simple page templates, drawing tools, text boxes and voice recording make it easy to combine labelled diagrams with spoken explanations.

Students use Microsoft Forms to collect class data about everyday health choices such as sleep, movement, breakfast, water and screen-free relaxation. This directly explores how our choices affect physical, emotional and mental wellbeing. They study the automatic charts, identify patterns and present two findings without naming individual students. The ready-made question types and automatic response charts do the main work, so no spreadsheet setup is needed.

Students code a Micro:bit to act as a simple movement counter using its built-in motion sensor. They test it during the same short classroom movement routine, record the count shown on the display and debug the code if it misses movements or counts too many. This supports the line of inquiry about strategies to measure and maintain the health of the human body, while making it clear that movement count is only one simple measure. Students finish by demonstrating their working counter and explaining one healthy way it could be used.

Students make a short stop-motion animation showing what happens to food as it moves through the digestive system. They move simple paper shapes a little at a time, photograph each stage and add labels explaining the job of the mouth, stomach and intestines. The finished animation helps the class explore how body systems connect and function and can be screened with student narration. Stop Motion Studio’s frame-by-frame camera, playback and built-in text tools keep the task manageable for Year 3.

Students record a two-minute guided wellbeing audio about a realistic strategy such as slow breathing, stretching or preparing for sleep. They explain how the chosen strategy may support physical, emotional or mental wellbeing, then lead listeners through the steps using calm, clear instructions. Each student or pair produces a finished audio track that can be played during a class wellbeing routine. GarageBand’s voice recorder, trimming controls and simple sound loops allow students to record, edit and balance their audio in one place.

St Kilda|Year 4|How We Express Ourselves.d: In How We Express Ourselves, students paint two versions of the same scene using different colour choices to communicate contrasting moods. This directly explores how colour communicates character and mood. They present the finished images side by side and play the recorded painting process to explain how their ideas changed as they worked. The simple brushes, colour palette, layers and automatic playback make the creative process easy to see and discuss.

In How We Express Ourselves, small groups use paper characters and coloured backgrounds to create a short stop-motion scene showing a clear change in mood. This explores how colour and movement communicate character and mood. Students take and review frames, adjust movements that look unclear, and publish a short animation with a title. The frame-by-frame camera, playback and simple editing controls let them test and improve the scene during one or two lessons.

St Kilda|Year 4|How We Express Ourselves.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
St Kilda|Year 4|How We Express Ourselves.d: In How We Express Ourselves, students write and record a short character monologue that communicates an emotion through words, voice, colour and movement. This connects directly to how colour, movement and music communicate character and mood. Each student chooses a character and background, records their voice, and publishes a short animated performance to share with the class. The everyday record button and automatic character animation turn the spoken recording into a finished scene without complex animation work.

In How We Express Ourselves, groups build a digital production journal for a short multi-disciplinary presentation that combines visual art, movement and music. This supports the line of inquiry about the creative process of making a multi-disciplinary presentation. Students add planning pages, drawings, rehearsal photos, short audio samples and reflections, then present the completed book as evidence of how their performance developed. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools, camera, audio recording and page-turning presentation mode keep all parts of the process in one place.

In How We Express Ourselves, students record short rehearsal check-ins across several lessons to show the effort and commitment needed to produce a live performance. This directly addresses the line of inquiry about the effort and commitment required for live performance. After each rehearsal, they upload a brief video, identify one successful choice and explain one improvement they will test next time, finishing with a final performance reflection. Seesaw’s video recording, voice recording, drawing and portfolio features create a clear, shareable record of growth over time.

St Kilda|Year 4|How the World Works.d: Students use Tinkercad to design a simple 3D model of a beam, arch or suspension bridge. They focus on the line of inquiry about different bridge types and the features that make each structure strong and fit for purpose. Using the basic shape, resize, rotate and duplicate tools, students add a deck, supports and reinforcing features. They finish with a labelled digital bridge model that they can rotate and present to the class.

Students test small classroom bridge models by gradually adding equal weights and recording how much each bridge can hold before bending or failing. This directly explores how materials and engineering features contribute to structural strength and stability. They enter their results into a simple Microsoft Excel table and use the chart button to compare bridge designs or materials. Each group produces a clear results chart and uses the data to recommend one improvement to its bridge.

Students use Google Maps and Street View to examine real bridges around Melbourne, such as West Gate Bridge, Bolte Bridge and Princes Bridge. They look closely for arches, towers, cables, beams, piers and other design features, linking their observations to the line of inquiry about different types of bridges. The everyday zoom, distance and Street View controls let students compare each bridge’s size, surroundings and purpose without needing to log in. Pairs present a short on-screen tour of two bridges and explain which visible features help each one remain stable and fit for purpose.

Students use Explain Everything to create a narrated explanation of how a chosen bridge design carries weight safely to the ground. This connects to the line of inquiry about engineering principles that contribute to strength and stability. Using the drawing, shape, arrow and voice-recording features, they label the deck, supports and places where pushing, pulling or bending may occur. They publish a short shareable presentation that explains why their bridge is strong and identifies one possible weak point.

Students use Book Creator to keep a digital design journal while building, testing and refining a model bridge. This directly addresses the line of inquiry about improving designs through experimentation. With the built-in camera, text boxes, drawing tools and audio recording, they capture the first design, test results, any failure points and the changes they make. Each group produces a short before-and-after book showing what changed and whether the revised bridge became stronger or more stable.

St Kilda|Year 4|How We Organise Ourselve.d: Students use Microsoft Forms to create a short survey about needs in the St Kilda community, such as food support, animal welfare, homelessness or care for the environment. This explores how not-for-profit organisations respond to community needs. They collect responses from classmates or families and examine the automatic response charts. Using the question templates and built-in charts, each group presents one community need that respondents believe deserves more support.

Students use National Geographic MapMaker to locate and mark not-for-profit organisations that serve the St Kilda area. This supports the line of inquiry into the function and purpose of not-for-profit organisations. They add simple labels explaining the need each organisation addresses and use colours or symbols to group similar services. The map's markers, drawing tools and editable labels help students produce a shareable community support map.

Students use Book Creator to make a class guide to not-for-profit organisations and the needs they address. This directly explores the central idea that not-for-profit organisations exist to respond to a variety of needs within our community. Each pair creates a page with the organisation's purpose, who it helps, how it works and one responsible action children could take. They combine text, images and voice recording using Book Creator's simple page templates, then present the finished digital book to another class.

Students use GarageBand to record a 60-second community message supporting a chosen not-for-profit organisation. This connects with our responsibility to take action and make a difference. They write and record a clear explanation of the community need, the organisation's response and one realistic action listeners can take. GarageBand's voice recorder, trimming controls and built-in music loops help each group publish a short radio-style announcement for the class.

Students use PicCollage to design an action poster for a real not-for-profit organisation connected to a community need studied in the unit. This addresses our responsibility to take action and make a difference. Their poster includes the need, what the organisation does and one safe, realistic way Year 4 students or families could help. Using the built-in text, image, sticker and layout tools, students create a clear poster and present their design choices to the class.

St Kilda|Year 4|Who We Are.d: Students use Microsoft Forms to survey classmates about the strengths and qualities they value in a leader during the Who We Are unit. They write clear multiple-choice and short-answer questions, collect responses and examine the automatic charts. This directly explores the line of inquiry about the strengths and qualities of a leader. Each group presents a short evidence-based leadership profile using the survey results and built-in response charts.

Students use Canva to create a one-page guide called “Helping Our Group Function Effectively” for the Who We Are unit. They explain the roles and responsibilities of a group leader and include practical examples such as listening, sharing jobs and resolving disagreements. Canva’s templates, text boxes, icons and drag-and-drop layout help students organise their ideas clearly. Students publish and present their finished guides to the class before they are displayed for future group work.

Students use IMovie to record and edit a short role-play showing a group completing a classroom task with effective leadership. Their scenes demonstrate the central idea that leaders can help a group to function effectively, including how a leader assigns roles, listens and keeps the group focused. Students use the built-in camera recording, clip trimming, titles and voice-over features to shape the film. Each group screens its finished video and explains which leadership actions made the biggest difference.

Students use Explain Everything to work through a leadership problem from the Who We Are unit, such as a group in which one person makes every decision or nobody accepts responsibility. They place pictures and short notes on the canvas, move them into a sensible plan and record themselves explaining how an effective leader could respond. This explores the purpose of leadership and the roles and responsibilities that help a group function effectively. Each pair produces a narrated problem-and-solution presentation that can be played for the class.

Students use Freeform to build a shared map of the roles needed for an effective classroom team during the Who We Are unit. They add sticky notes for roles, connect each role to its responsibilities with lines and sort leadership qualities beside relevant examples. This directly explores the roles and responsibilities of effective leadership while showing how different contributions help a group function. Each group presents its completed board and uses the zoom and linking features to explain how the roles work together.

St Kilda|Year 4|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use Google Maps to view places connected to several First Nations communities, using a teacher-provided list of suitable locations. They compare distance, landscape and visible features through the map, satellite view and Street View, while noting that Google Maps does not show the full cultural boundaries or meaning of Country. This supports the line of inquiry into the diversity of language and culture across First Nations communities in Australia. Pairs present a short guided map walkthrough to the class, explaining two observations and one question they still have.

Students use Adobe Express to create a one-page digital profile of a teacher-approved First Nations community, focusing on Country, language and culture. This connects directly to the central idea that First Nations people have a deep connection to Country, language and culture. They publish a page containing a simple map image, carefully sourced facts, captions and a list of where their information came from. The ready-made page layouts and text-and-image blocks make the task manageable for Year 4 students.

Students use GarageBand to record a two-minute audio explanation of custodial responsibility after learning from a teacher-selected First Nations source. They explain one example of caring for Country, clearly naming the community and source rather than speaking as if the perspective is their own. This addresses the line of inquiry about the significance of connection to Country as custodial responsibility. Students use the voice recorder, audio tracks and trim controls to produce a clear recording that can be played to classmates.

Students use Explain Everything to make a short narrated presentation showing how caring for Country can involve land, water, plants, animals and community responsibilities. This helps them explore the significance of connection to Country as custodial responsibility without treating all First Nations communities as the same. They create three or four slides, draw and label connections, record their explanation and include the name of the teacher-approved community or source they learned from. The simple drawing, text, slide and voice-recording features allow students to explain their thinking in one place.

Students use Padlet to build a class listening wall based on teacher-selected videos, texts or visits that share Indigenous perspectives. Each student posts one important idea they heard, one respectful question and the name of the speaker, community or source, then responds thoughtfully to a classmate. This directly supports the line of inquiry about listening to and learning from Indigenous perspectives. Padlet’s short posts, comments and audio-recording feature create a shareable class collection that can be revisited throughout the unit.

St Kilda|Year 4|Where We Are in Place an.d: Students map one voyage from the age of exploration, adding the starting point, key stops, destination and major geographical challenges. This directly explores the line of inquiry about the age of exploration and the reasons explorers set out on their journeys. They create an annotated route map with short notes explaining motives such as trade, wealth, knowledge or competition. MapMaker’s markers, drawing tools and map layers let students build and label the map themselves. Pairs can present their finished map and explain how geography shaped the journey.

Students use Google Maps to view places connected with European arrival in Australia, such as London, Botany Bay and Sydney Cove, and compare their locations and distances. This supports the line of inquiry about how Australia changed through European arrival. They use the world map, distance tool and Street View to prepare a short guided walkthrough showing the journey and what these places look like today. Each pair presents the route on screen and explains two observations about distance, location or landscape. Students only view and explore the map, without creating pins or saving a custom map.

Students create a short book showing different perspectives on one consequence of European exploration and arrival in Australia. This directly addresses the line of inquiry about different perspectives on the consequences of exploration. Each book includes carefully researched pages representing an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander perspective and a European perspective, followed by a page explaining where the views differ. Students use Book Creator’s page templates, text boxes, drawing tools and built-in voice recording to combine words, images and spoken explanations. They publish the book to the class library for a partner reading session.

Students build two small versions of the same Australian coastal place, one representing the area before European arrival and one showing selected changes after settlement. This connects with the line of inquiry about how Australia changed through European arrival. Groups use blocks, signs and labelled characters to show changes such as buildings, land use, transport and access to resources without trying to recreate an entire city. Their finished world includes a clear pathway between the two scenes and signs explaining at least three changes and who was affected. Students lead classmates through the build and answer questions about the choices they made.

Students make a simple visual timeline about the age of exploration, including why selected explorers travelled, what they encountered and one lasting change linked to each journey. This supports the central idea that exploration and discovery have led to changes that shape the world we live in. Each student produces a one-page timeline with dates, short captions, images and a final statement about a consequence of exploration. Adobe Express’s timeline templates, image search, text boxes and drag-and-drop layout tools keep the task manageable for Year 4. Students publish the finished timeline and present one event they believe had the greatest impact.

St Kilda|Year 5|How We Organise Ourselve.d: Students use Tinkercad to design a simple product, such as a reusable lunch container, and identify the raw materials it would need. This directly explores the production of goods from raw materials through manufacturing to the consumer. Each student makes a labelled 3D model and presents how its shape, materials and useful features could affect production choices. They use Tinkercad’s basic shapes, resizing, grouping and text tools to build the model.

Students use Microsoft Excel to track the journey and changing price of a familiar product, such as a chocolate bar, from raw materials to shop shelf. This connects to the exchange of currency for goods and services in a functioning economy. They enter estimated costs for ingredients, manufacturing, transport, packaging and retail, then produce a table and chart showing how the final price is formed. Excel’s cells, simple formulas and chart button make the costs easy to calculate and compare.

Students use Microsoft Forms to collect class opinions about what makes a marketplace decision fair and responsible. This directly supports the line of inquiry into ethics and responsible decision-making in the marketplace. In groups, they create a short consumer survey about issues such as price, packaging, worker treatment and environmental impact, then present the response charts and explain the strongest patterns. They use Forms’ multiple-choice questions and automatic response summaries to collect and display the data.

Students code a Micro:bit to act as a simple checkout for a classroom marketplace, showing a product price and confirming a purchase when a button is pressed. This explores the exchange of currency for goods and services in a functioning economy. Pairs build, test and debug their code, then demonstrate a working checkout that displays prices and keeps a basic count of sales. They use the Micro:bit’s buttons, LED display, variables and block coding to create the system.

Students use Adobe Express to create a short visual explanation of how one everyday good moves from raw material through manufacturing to the consumer. This directly addresses the production of goods from raw materials through manufacturing to consumer. They publish a one-page presentation with ordered stages, brief captions, images and a final note about one responsible choice a producer or buyer could make. Adobe Express’s page templates, image search, text boxes and simple layout tools support the finished explanation.

St Kilda|Year 5|How We Express Ourselves.d: Students create a short anonymous class survey about everyday social norms and stereotypes, using neutral questions such as who people expect to lead, play certain sports or do particular jobs. This connects directly to how stereotypes and social norms form and persist in society. They collect responses, examine the automatic charts and present two patterns that surprised them without naming individual students. The simple question types and built-in response charts make the task manageable in two lessons.

Students use Teachable Machine to explore how limited examples can cause unfair assumptions about who looks like a scientist, athlete or leader. They first train an image model with a narrow set of poses and props, test where it makes mistakes, then add more varied examples and test it again. This directly shows how stereotypes can form and persist when a system repeatedly sees the same narrow picture. Students present their working model and its before-and-after results using the camera capture and confidence scores.

Students design a digital campaign poster that challenges a familiar stereotype about hobbies, jobs, appearance or leadership. This addresses how people overcome stereotypes to express themselves and inspire change. Each student publishes a clear poster containing a short slogan, one strong image and a practical action the audience can take. They use Adobe Express templates, stock images and drag-and-drop text tools to create a polished message in one or two lessons.

In pairs, students record a one-minute audio segment called “More Than an Assumption” about the impact of prejudice or stereotypes on an individual. One student voices an unfair assumption, while the other explains its effect and offers a more respectful response. They produce a shareable audio piece with a spoken introduction, the short scene and a closing message that encourages change. GarageBand’s voice recording, simple trimming and built-in music loops let students shape the mood without needing advanced audio skills.

Students create a short digital book showing how a character experiences and then challenges a social norm or stereotype. This connects directly to the line of inquiry about the impact of discrimination, prejudice and assumptions on individuals and communities. Their finished book includes a title page, the character’s experience, the effect on others, a turning point and a final message about self-expression. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools, text boxes and built-in voice recording allow students to combine writing, pictures and narration in one place.

St Kilda|Year 5|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use National Geographic MapMaker to explore how communities interact with forests, rivers and coastlines in Australia. They turn on map layers, compare land use and conservation areas, then add drawings and labels showing places where the natural environment is protected or under pressure. This connects directly to how community values shape the management of the natural environment. Each group presents its annotated map, using the layer, drawing and text tools to explain two different management choices.

Students carry out a simple classroom waste audit linked to the need for conservation and environmental stewardship. They count one lesson's paper, food scraps, soft plastics and reusable items, then enter the results into Microsoft Excel. Using the table, total and chart features, they make a column graph and test how the totals might change if the class adopted two realistic waste-reduction actions. Each group presents its graph and a short evidence-based recommendation for managing the classroom environment more responsibly.

Students code a Micro:bit to measure light or temperature in several parts of the school grounds as they investigate how communities interact with the environment. They test their program, take readings in shaded, planted and paved areas, and debug it if the displayed values do not update correctly. This supports discussion about the need for conservation and environmental stewardship, including how trees and built surfaces affect local conditions. Students present a labelled set of readings and use the Micro:bit's built-in light or temperature sensing and LED display to recommend one achievable improvement for the campus.

Students use Adobe Express to create a one-page visual explainer about a researched First Nations land management practice, such as cultural burning or caring for waterways. They explain how the practice can drive positive environmental change and include the Country, community or First Nations organisation connected with the example rather than treating all practices as the same. Each student publishes a clear page containing a heading, short factual sections, images and a source list. The ready-made page layouts, text boxes and image tools help Year 5 students organise and share their learning clearly.

Pairs use Podcasting using Canva to record a three-minute community meeting about how a local natural area should be managed. One student presents the view of a community group while the other presents a conservation concern, helping the class examine how community values shape the management of the natural environment. They finish by agreeing on one practical action and explaining how it supports environmental stewardship. Students use Canva's built-in audio recording, timeline and simple sound controls to produce and present a finished podcast episode.

St Kilda|Year 5|How the World Works.d: Students use Microsoft Forms to survey classmates about a changing need at school, such as reducing waste, saving water or improving access to shared spaces. This directly explores the central idea that inventions and initiatives respond to the changing needs of society. They create clear multiple-choice and short-answer questions, collect responses and use the automatically generated charts to identify the strongest need. Each group presents its Forms results and a simple design brief for an innovation that could address the need.

Students use National Geographic MapMaker to investigate global problems addressed by the UN Sustainable Development Goals. They choose one goal, explore relevant map layers and add markers with short notes showing where the problem is especially visible. This directly supports the line of inquiry about the Sustainable Development Goals and the global problems they address. Each group shares an annotated digital map and explains how an invention or community initiative could respond in one selected place.

Students use Tinkercad to create a simple three-dimensional model of an invention that responds to a real-world need, such as a water-saving tap attachment or an easy-grip classroom tool. This follows the design thinking process by asking them to define a need, make a model, seek feedback and improve it. They build with Tinkercad’s everyday shape, resize, align, group and text tools rather than attempting complex engineering. Each student presents a shareable digital model with labels explaining the invention’s purpose and the change made after testing it with a partner.

Students use Sphero BOLT to test how an automated delivery invention could move safely through a school or community space. They code a short route between floor-tile landmarks, including turns, pauses and a safe stop, then test and debug the program when the robot misses its destination. This connects to the design thinking line of inquiry because students repeatedly improve an innovation in response to a real need. Each team presents a successful live route and its saved block-code program, explaining how speed, timing and direction were adjusted.

Students use Canva to create a visual timeline showing how one invention, such as the telephone, bicycle or washing machine, changed as society’s needs changed. This directly addresses the line of inquiry about how inventions have changed over time to meet the demands of society. They use a timeline template, text boxes, images and arrows to show at least four stages and explain the need behind each change. Students publish and present a one-page timeline that finishes with a realistic suggestion for the invention’s next improvement.

St Kilda|Year 5|Where We Are in Place an.d: Students use Google Maps to explore Street View and satellite views of places shaped by colonisation, such as Melbourne, Cape Town and Mumbai. They compare street layouts, place names, ports, monuments and surviving cultural landmarks to investigate how colonisation transformed society and culture. Pairs present a short live map tour showing three visible signs of lasting impact and explain the evidence they noticed. The everyday search, satellite view, Street View and distance tools make the comparison manageable for Year 5.

Students use Book Creator to make a short evidence-based book about colonisation from the perspectives of colonisers and people who were colonised. Each pair adds pages explaining a reason for colonisation, a method used and two lasting impacts, directly addressing the reasons, methods and impact of colonisation. Their finished book includes brief written explanations, sourced images, captions and a recorded reflection about the responsibility of colonisers. The simple page templates, image import, text boxes and voice-recording button support the whole task in one place.

Students enter a small teacher-provided set of historical data into Microsoft Excel, such as changes in First Nations population, land control, migration or language use following colonisation. They create two charts and discuss what the numbers reveal about the central idea that colonisation has had a lasting impact on countries and their people. Each group presents its charts with a short written conclusion that states what the data shows and what it cannot explain on its own. Excel’s basic tables, sorting and chart buttons are the practical features at the centre of the task.

Students use Minecraft Education to build two small versions of the same place: one representing land use before colonisation and one showing changes made during or after colonisation. They include features such as waterways, food sources, roads, fences, farms, ports or government buildings to explore how colonisation transformed society and culture. Groups guide classmates through their paired builds and explain which changes affected movement, land access and daily life. Minecraft’s block building, signs and shared-world features allow students to create and present a clear spatial comparison without complicated coding.

Students use Podcasting using Canva to record a three-minute class podcast episode about the responsibility of colonisers and the perspectives of those colonised. In pairs, they present a host discussion that uses researched facts and clearly labels any quoted words, rather than pretending to speak as a historical person. Their finished episode includes an introduction, two contrasting perspectives, supporting evidence and a closing statement about a lasting impact of colonisation. Canva’s script pages, voice recording, audio trimming and simple publishing controls make the podcast realistic to complete across two lessons.

St Kilda|Year 5|Who We Are.d: Students create a short digital book called “What Shapes Who I Am” about the values, beliefs, people and experiences that influence their identity. This directly explores how our values and beliefs shape our identity and interactions. Each student publishes a shareable book with written reflections, drawings, photos and a recorded explanation of one value they try to show through their actions. Book Creator’s simple page templates, drawing tools and audio recording make the task manageable in a few lessons.

Students respond to a teacher-made set of everyday scenarios about friendship, strong emotions, online messages and asking for help. The class examines the anonymous response charts to explore our responsibility to manage emotions and be safe online and in person. Small groups then present one chart, explain the different choices classmates made and suggest a safe and respectful response. Microsoft Forms’ multiple-choice questions and automatic charts provide the evidence for the discussion.

In pairs, students make a short stop-motion film showing a character facing a disagreement, online problem or setback and responding with resilience and respect. This connects directly to the importance of resilience, respect and positive relationships in a diverse community. Each film must show the problem, an unhelpful reaction, a pause or reset, and a safer action that repairs the relationship. Stop Motion Studio’s frame-by-frame camera, playback and simple titles let students build and revise the scene within two or three lessons.

Students record a two-minute “Resilience Radio” segment explaining a realistic Year 5 challenge and helpful ways to manage the emotions involved. The task explores our responsibility to manage emotions and be safe online and in person, while showing how actions affect relationships. Each student produces a finished audio segment with a spoken introduction, practical advice, a short example and a closing message. GarageBand’s voice recorder, basic editing and built-in music loops allow students to record and polish the segment in one place.

Small groups build a compact community space where people with different values, beliefs and needs can feel welcome and safe. This applies the central idea that values, beliefs and actions contribute to a diverse society. Students add signs or in-game books explaining at least four design choices, such as a quiet area, accessible paths, shared meeting places or clear community agreements, and then lead classmates through the finished world. Minecraft Education’s block building, signs, books and shared worlds make the group design and presentation practical for Year 5.

St Kilda|Year 6|How We Express Ourselves.d: Students choose a global issue and create a one-page awareness poster that encourages a realistic action by the school community. This directly explores how design choices contribute to the effectiveness of a message and how communication can inspire action. They test two versions with different headlines, images, colours and layouts, then publish the clearer version for a class campaign gallery. Adobe Express templates, image library and simple text and layout controls make the task manageable in a few lessons.

Students investigate how two media sources present the same global issue from different viewpoints. This connects directly to the line of inquiry that presentations in the media can reflect the perspective of the author rather than the truth. Each pair makes a short digital book showing selected claims, missing information, persuasive choices and a final page explaining which source they consider more trustworthy and why. Book Creator's page templates, text boxes, image tools and built-in audio recording let students combine evidence and spoken explanation in one shareable book.

Students use National Geographic MapMaker to explore the interconnected causes and effects of a global issue such as plastic pollution, deforestation or access to clean water. This addresses the line of inquiry that global issues are caused by interconnected factors that require collective solutions. They add labelled points, lines, shapes and relevant data layers to build an annotated map showing affected places, contributing factors and possible responses. MapMaker's map layers, drawing tools, labels and measurement features allow students to create and present the finished map within the one tool.

Small groups record a four-minute podcast episode about a global issue, with students taking the roles of host, expert, affected community member and action advocate. This supports the central idea that understanding global issues and using effective communication empowers us to raise awareness and inspire action. The finished episode includes an opening hook, contrasting perspectives, checked facts and one practical action listeners could take. The microphones, headphones and recorder allow students to capture clear voices, monitor sound levels and produce a shareable class podcast recording.

Students create a short stop-motion public service announcement about making responsible choices when creating or responding to media about a global issue. This directly addresses the line of inquiry that we must make responsible choices when responding to and creating media. Using paper cut-outs or classroom objects, they animate an example of a misleading post, show a student checking the claim, and finish with a clear responsible action. Stop Motion Studio's frame-by-frame camera, playback, titles and voice recording features let students test timing and produce a concise video message.

St Kilda|Year 6|How We Organise Ourselve.d: Students use Microsoft Excel to examine a teacher-provided set of data showing how a fictional government budget is divided among services such as health, education, transport and parks. They calculate percentages and compare how different funding decisions could impact citizens, directly exploring the line of inquiry about government decisions at federal, state and local levels. Each group changes one part of the budget and records which citizens may benefit or be disadvantaged. Using the everyday table, formula and chart features, students create a labelled budget chart and present their funding decision to the class.

Students use Google Maps to view Parliament House in Canberra, Parliament House in Melbourne and the City of Port Phillip offices in St Kilda. They explore Street View, identify visible features and use the distance tool to compare where federal, state and local decisions are made. This supports the line of inquiry about the key institutions and functions of Australia's democratic system of government. Pairs present a live guided walkthrough in Google Maps, explaining one responsibility handled at each level and how it affects citizens.

Students use Padlet to take part in a class civic forum about a realistic local issue, such as improving safety around the school or deciding how a public park should be used. They post a proposal, explain which level of government should respond, and comment respectfully on two classmates' ideas. This directly explores citizens' rights and responsibilities and how government decisions impact the community. The simple post, comment and reaction features create a shareable class forum that can be reviewed before students vote on the strongest proposal.

Students use Book Creator to make a short guide called “How Australian Government Affects My Life”. They create one page each for federal, state and local government, showing a service, the institution responsible and an everyday impact on citizens. A final page explains one right and one responsibility of Australian citizens, linking directly to the unit's citizenship line of inquiry. Students use the familiar page templates, text, drawing and built-in audio recording features to publish and present their illustrated guide.

Students use Podcasting using Canva to record a three-minute interview about a fictional government decision, such as changing public transport fares or funding a new community facility. One student takes the role of a government representative and another takes the role of a citizen who is affected by the decision. Their questions and answers must explain the government's function, the reasons for the decision and its impact, connecting clearly to the unit's central idea. Using Canva's recording, trimming and audio timeline features, pairs produce a polished podcast episode to play for the class.

St Kilda|Year 6|How the World Works.d: Students use models of the Earth, Moon and Sun to photograph a frame-by-frame demonstration of day and night, moon phases or seasons. This directly explores how the movement of the Earth, Moon and Sun causes predictable patterns. Each group produces a short labelled animation that they can play for the class and explain. The tool’s simple frame capture, playback and text features let students check and correct their model as they work.

Students enter a teacher-provided week of local tide times and heights into Microsoft Excel, then look for repeating changes linked to the Moon. This supports the line of inquiry about how Earth, Moon and Sun movements cause predictable patterns such as tides. They create a line graph, add clear labels and write a short conclusion in the spreadsheet about the pattern they found. The everyday table, formula and chart features make the data easy to organise, calculate and compare.

Students build a simple three-dimensional model showing the Sun, a tilted Earth and the Moon in their relative positions. They animate the Earth moving around the Sun and add short labels explaining how its tilt and position relate to seasons, addressing the line of inquiry about structures, positions and relationships represented through models and simulations. Each pair presents a working virtual model and explains one limitation of it, such as objects not being to scale. Delightex’s ready-made shapes, movement controls and text labels keep the building manageable for Year 6.

Students create a world map showing several places connected with teacher-provided, carefully checked cultural interpretations of the night sky, including an appropriate Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander example. This addresses the line of inquiry that different cultures and Indigenous knowledge systems interpret the night sky in unique and meaningful ways. They add markers with brief summaries, relevant locations and a note about similarities or differences between perspectives, then present their map to classmates. MapMaker’s editable markers, map layers and text notes allow students to build and share the geographic comparison within the tool.

Students use Padlet to build a class evidence wall answering the question, “How do relationships between the Earth, Moon and Sun shape life on our planet?” Each group posts one explanation about day and night, moon phases, tides, seasons or a teacher-provided cultural perspective, linking directly to the central idea. They add a labelled diagram or recorded spoken explanation, then respond to another group with one question or suggested correction. Padlet’s post, image, audio and comment features make the finished wall easy to review and present as a class.

St Kilda|Year 6|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use National Geographic MapMaker to investigate an ecosystem such as Port Phillip Bay and identify habitats, waterways, human activity and protected areas. This directly explores what the environment is comprised of and how ecosystems function, as well as the interdependence between humans, animals and the environment. They create an annotated map showing key ecosystem features, examples of human impact and two places where protection is important. The map layers, drawing tools, labels and markers make the task manageable for Year 6 students.

Students collect simple data about waste produced in the classroom over five school days, sorting items into categories such as food scraps, paper, soft plastic and reusable materials. They use the results to examine the consequences of human actions on the balance of nature. In Microsoft Excel, they build a clear table, calculate totals and create a column or pie chart to present the class waste pattern and suggest one realistic change. The spreadsheet cells, simple formulas and chart button are the main features used.

Students create a short digital field guide about a local ecosystem and the relationships between its plants, animals, non-living features and people. This connects directly to the interdependence between humans, animals and the environment. Each student or pair publishes a book with labelled drawings, brief explanations, a food web page and a final page describing how people can protect the ecosystem. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools, text boxes and voice-recording button allow students to combine written and spoken explanations in one shareable book.

Students use Teachable Machine to build a simple image model that sorts common classroom waste into compost, recycling and landfill groups. The task supports the line of inquiry about our responsibility to care for and protect the natural world by testing how accurately waste can be identified before disposal. Students capture examples with the built-in camera, train the model, test unfamiliar items and record which objects confuse it during a live class demonstration. Teachable Machine’s image classes, training button and live prediction display are central to the activity.

Students create a one-page public awareness poster showing how one everyday human action affects the balance of nature, such as littering, wasting water or using single-use plastic. This directly addresses the central idea that peoples’ actions affect the balance of nature and the line of inquiry about consequences. Their finished poster includes a clear cause-and-effect explanation, one relevant image, a supporting fact and two realistic actions for the Wesley community. Adobe Express’s poster templates, text tools, image library and download or share option make the finished work easy to present to classmates or display around the school.

St Kilda|Year 6|Where We Are in Place an.d: Students explore a real migration journey connected to Australia by viewing the place of origin, destination, route and distance in Google Maps. They use Street View to compare everyday features such as housing, transport, shops and public spaces in both locations. This directly explores the central idea that human migration is a response to challenges, risks and opportunities. Pairs finish by presenting a live map walkthrough, using the search, distance and Street View features to explain what a migrant might encounter along the journey.

Students use a teacher-provided Excel table showing migration to Australia from several countries across different decades. They sort the figures, calculate simple changes and create column or line charts to investigate changes in society as a result of migration. Each pair produces one clearly labelled chart and adds a short written conclusion explaining an important pattern. The everyday sorting, formula and chart features make the data visible without requiring advanced spreadsheet skills.

Students create a one-page case study about a real person or family who migrated, using information provided by the teacher. Their page explains the causes of the migration and its positive and negative impact on the individual. Students combine a short timeline, quotations, images and a balanced summary, then present the finished page to a small group. Canva’s templates, text boxes, image tools and timeline elements help students publish a clear visual account.

Students build and record a narrated timeline showing one migration story, from the decision to leave through to settlement in a new place. They explain how challenges, risks and opportunities shaped key decisions and how the move affected the individual. Students place teacher-provided maps and images on slides, draw arrows, add dates and record a three-minute explanation. Explain Everything’s slide canvas, drawing tools and built-in voice recording produce a shareable narrated timeline.

Students work in small groups to sort teacher-provided migration examples under challenges, risks, opportunities and consequences. They then connect examples to changes in Australian society, such as new foods, languages, businesses, celebrations or community groups, linking directly to migration resulting in a more diverse society. Each group creates a completed thinking board and presents two connections they can support with evidence from the examples. Freeform’s sticky notes, movable cards, connectors and shared canvas make it easy to organise and revise the group’s thinking.

St Kilda|Year 6|Who We Are.d: Students create a short decision-making form about staying safe online and in person, using realistic Year 6 situations such as an unkind group chat, an unknown message or pressure from friends. This directly explores the line of inquiry about the tools and skills we use to stay safe. They add multiple-choice responses and simple branching so each choice leads to feedback or a sensible next step, then invite classmates to complete the form. The everyday question, branching and response-summary features produce a shareable safety check and class discussion data.

Students make a short Who We Are handbook showing practical strategies for building and maintaining positive relationships. This connects directly to the line of inquiry about strategies for positive relationships and can include listening, setting boundaries, repairing harm and asking for help. Each pair creates pages with a realistic scenario, suggested words to use and a recorded explanation, then publishes the finished book for classmates to read. Book Creator’s simple page templates, text, drawing and voice-recording features keep the task manageable.

Students map the connections between emotions, behaviour, learning, interactions and goals as part of the Who We Are unit. They begin with a familiar situation, such as receiving difficult feedback, and use sticky notes and arrows to show several possible reactions and outcomes. Each group ends with a visual connection map that they present, including places where a helpful strategy could change what happens next. Freeform’s ordinary sticky notes, shapes, connectors and shared canvas make these links easy to move, test and revise.

Students record a two-minute wellbeing audio guide for a common Year 6 moment, such as preparing for a presentation, settling after conflict or refocusing during study. This supports the line of inquiry about the active role we play in achieving and maintaining our wellbeing. They script and record clear instructions for one realistic strategy, add a brief music introduction, edit out mistakes and play the finished recording to the class. GarageBand’s voice recording, trimming and built-in music loops allow students to produce a polished, shareable audio track without specialist equipment.

Students create and present a short interactive scenario about the recognisable features of safe and healthy interactions. They show a realistic friendship or playground situation, annotate the warning signs and protective signs, and explain how different responses could affect everyone involved. The finished narrated presentation includes a final slide with useful words a student could say and trusted people they could approach. Explain Everything’s slides, drawing tools, movable objects and built-in voice recording let students demonstrate their thinking step by step.

Elsternwick|Prep|Where We Are in Place a.d: Students create a simple three-page book about their own past: baby, when I was little, and now. This supports the line of inquiry about reflecting on and recording our past, showing that discovering our past helps us know ourselves today. On each page, students draw a picture, add a short sentence with teacher help, and record themselves explaining the memory. Book Creator’s page templates, drawing pen and voice-recording button make the finished digital life story easy to share with families.

Students work with a teacher to record a short question-and-answer video about how they have changed since they were babies. This directly supports the central idea that discovering our past helps us know more about ourselves today. Each child answers one class question, such as “What can you do now that you could not do as a baby?”, and the clips are joined into a class time capsule. Apple Clips’ large record button, simple trimming and text titles keep the recording process manageable for Prep.

Students code a character to travel through three parts of a simple life timeline: baby, little and now. This connects to the line of inquiry about recording our past and helps students practise putting personal events in order. Students choose or draw three backgrounds, program the character to move between them, and record a short spoken sentence for each stage. ScratchJr’s picture-based movement blocks and built-in voice recorder allow students to make a short, playable timeline.

Students use three drawings or classroom figures to show a person changing from baby to child to Prep student. This supports the line of inquiry about personal stories and histories by making the order of change visible. In pairs, students move the figures a small amount, photograph each step, and play back their short animation for the class. Stop Motion Studio’s frame-by-frame camera and playback button make it possible to create the sequence in one lesson.

Students view places connected to their family stories, such as Melbourne, another Australian town or a country named by their family. This supports the inquiry into where families come from and helps children see that everyone has a different history that contributes to who they are today. With the teacher entering each place, students use the world map and Street View to notice a landmark, building or landscape, then give a short live presentation about what they saw. Google Maps’ search, zoom and Street View features provide a clear visual journey without students creating accounts, pins or custom maps.

Glen Waverley|Year 2|Who We Are.d: Pairs create a short digital book about the difference between needs and wants. On each page, they add a picture of an everyday item, label it as a need or a want, and record a sentence explaining their choice. Their finished book shows that everybody has rights and responsibilities, including helping others access basic needs. Book Creator’s simple page templates, drawing tools and voice-recording button make the task manageable for Year 2 students.

Students code two characters to act out a respectful relationship, such as taking turns, listening or including someone in a game. They use movement, speech and wait blocks to show how each person has a responsibility to value the rights of the other person. Students test and debug their code, then present the finished animation to the class and explain the respectful choice. ScratchJr’s drag-and-drop coding blocks and speech bubbles power the activity.

The teacher creates a picture-based class survey about needs and wants, rights and responsibilities, and respectful choices. Students select answers to everyday situations, such as whether clean water is a need or want and what to do when someone else is speaking. The class views the automatic response charts and discusses where answers were similar or different. Microsoft Forms’ picture questions, large choice buttons and automatic charts make the class data easy for Year 2 students to read.

Students make a poster showing what a respectful relationship looks and sounds like at school. They add photos or stickers for actions such as sharing, listening and giving others space, then write short captions that connect these actions to rights and responsibilities. Each student presents the completed poster and names one responsibility they will practise. PicCollage’s ready-made layouts, image tools and simple text boxes support the task.

Small groups record a short role-play about an everyday friendship problem, such as two people wanting the same toy or one person being left out. They show the problem, pause to explain each person’s rights and responsibilities, and then act out a respectful solution. Groups edit the clips into a short film and present it as an example of a respectful relationship. IMovie’s built-in recording, clip trimming, titles and voice-over tools allow students to create the whole film in one place.

Glen Waverley|Year 2|Where We Are in Pla.d: Students explore Glen Waverley in Google Maps and use Street View to closely examine local landmarks, streets and older buildings. They look for visible evidence of the past and discuss the line of inquiry, “Evidence and its significance in a place.” In pairs, students present a short live Street View walkthrough showing two landmarks and explaining what each one tells us about the place. The everyday zoom, search and Street View features let students investigate the local area without needing to log in or edit a map.

Students use Book Creator to make a short book about their personal history and how it shapes their present. Each page shows one important event, person or place from their life, with a drawing, simple sentence and recorded explanation. Students publish and share a clear personal timeline that connects directly to the line of inquiry, “Personal history shapes the present.” The page templates, drawing tools and voice-recording button make the task manageable for Year 2 students.

Students program a Beebot to travel across a teacher-prepared floor map showing a familiar place at different points in time. They code routes between picture cards such as an old house, a newer school, a former shop and a present-day park, then explain what changed and what stayed the same. Each pair presents and tests one route linked to the line of inquiry, “Connections between the past and present within a place.” The arrow buttons, clear button and go button allow students to code, test and debug the route directly on the map.

Students photograph a classroom object or supplied historical item connected to life in the past, then use ChatterPix Kids to make it speak. They write and record a short first-person explanation of what the object was used for and why it is useful evidence about a place. The finished talking-object video is shared with the class as part of the line of inquiry, “Evidence and its significance in a place.” The built-in camera, mouth-line tool and short voice recorder keep the activity simple and focused.

Students use blocks, paper figures or classroom objects to show how one local place changed from the past to the present. They move the pieces a little at a time and take frame-by-frame photos, creating a short transformation such as a paddock becoming a neighbourhood. The completed stop-motion film demonstrates the central idea, “Exploring the past helps us to understand the present,” and students present it with a brief spoken explanation. The camera button, frame timeline and playback feature let pairs capture, check and improve their sequence as they work.

Glen Waverley|Year 4|How We Express Ours.d: Students use Stop Motion Studio to create a short animation for How We Express Ourselves, moving paper shapes or classroom objects to communicate a feeling or message without dialogue. This explores the line of inquiry about ways forms of expression convey messages. They test the sequence, adjust movements and publish a 20–30 second animation with a title for classmates to interpret. The frame-by-frame camera and simple playback features make it easy to check whether the intended message is coming through.

Students use Sketchbook to make a digital artwork for How We Express Ourselves that communicates an idea such as belonging, change or courage through colour, line and shape. This supports the line of inquiry about creative and critical thinking skills as students try alternatives and explain their choices. They produce a finished artwork with a short written artist statement naming the message and two artistic choices they made. The drawing brushes, colour picker, layers and text tool allow students to experiment and revise without needing advanced skills.

Students use Podcasting using Canva to record a short response to a chosen painting, sculpture, dance or piece of music in How We Express Ourselves. This directly develops the language used to respond to The Arts, with students describing what they notice, what they think it may mean and what evidence shaped their response. Pairs plan, record and publish a two-minute art discussion that can be played for the class. Canva’s audio recording, simple timeline and ready-made podcast layout help students organise their voices and add a clear title.

Students use Minecraft Education to build a small virtual art installation for How We Express Ourselves that conveys a clear message, such as caring for nature or welcoming others. This explores the line of inquiry about ways forms of expression convey messages because students must choose blocks, colours, scale and space deliberately. They build and test their installation, add signs explaining key choices, then guide classmates through the finished space. The familiar block-building tools, signs and in-game camera make the installation practical to construct and present within a few lessons.

Students use Explain Everything to create a narrated response to an artwork for How We Express Ourselves. This connects to the central idea that responding to different artistic expressions can promote thinking, as students record an initial interpretation and then revise it after looking more closely. They make a short presentation containing the artwork, spoken observations, arrows or circles showing evidence, and a final reflection on how their thinking changed. The slide canvas, drawing tools and built-in voice recording let students point to details while explaining their ideas.

Glen Waverley|Year 5|How the World Works.d: Students test how water changes trays of sand, soil and small stones, then enter measurements of the erosion caused by each test into Microsoft Excel. This directly explores how weathering and erosion cause change to Earth’s surface. Pairs use simple tables, formulas and column charts to compare how much material moved under different conditions. They finish with a labelled chart and a short conclusion written in the spreadsheet about which surface resisted erosion best.

Students use National Geographic MapMaker to investigate places where coastlines, rivers, wind or ice have shaped Earth’s surface. This connects directly to how weathering and erosion cause change to Earth’s surface. They add labelled points and short notes to a map showing at least four examples and the likely cause of each change. The everyday map layers, search and annotation features help them create a shareable erosion evidence map.

Students use sand, small stones and water to create a short stop-motion sequence showing erosion changing a model landscape over time. This directly demonstrates how weathering and erosion cause change to Earth’s surface. They take a frame after each small change, then add titles explaining processes such as movement, wearing away and deposition. Stop Motion Studio’s frame-by-frame camera and playback tools turn their model into a clear science explanation they can present to the class.

Students use Tinkercad to build a simple three-dimensional model of a living thing with one enlarged structural feature, such as a bird’s beak, a cactus stem or a webbed foot.
