This supports the line of inquiry about how structural features and adaptations help living things survive. They add basic shapes and text labels to show how the feature helps the organism find food, conserve water, move or stay safe. The drag-and-drop shapes, resizing and rotate tools let students produce a shareable digital model without specialist design skills.

Students use Explain Everything to show how light travels and is reflected in a simple technology such as a periscope, mirror or bicycle reflector. This directly explores how light is used in science and technology. They draw light rays, move arrows to show direction, and record a spoken explanation of what happens when light meets each surface. The drawing, animation and voice-recording features produce a short narrated explanation that classmates can watch and discuss.

Glen Waverley|Year 5|Sharing the Planet.d: Students use National Geographic MapMaker to investigate how the Glen Waverley community interacts with local parks, waterways and built areas. They add markers, labels and simple drawings to show places needing conservation, areas already protected and possible sites for improvement. This directly explores the need for conservation and how communities manage the natural environment. Each group presents its annotated digital map and explains one realistic stewardship action the community could take.

Students create a short Microsoft Forms survey about how people value and use a local natural area, with questions about wildlife, recreation, rubbish, water and native plants. They collect responses from classmates and use the automatic charts to identify common values and different viewpoints. This directly explores how community values inform management of the natural environment. Each group presents a results chart and recommends one management decision supported by its survey data.

Students use Google Maps and Street View to compare how two communities interact with beaches, rivers, forests or urban parks. They examine visible features such as walking tracks, bins, fences, signs, revegetation and nearby buildings, then use the distance and scale tools to compare the size and location of managed areas. This supports the central idea that communities interact with the environment in different ways. Pairs present a guided Street View walkthrough, pointing out evidence of conservation and explaining which management choices seem effective.

Students use Book Creator to make a short digital field guide about environmental stewardship in the local community. Each page explains one practical action, such as protecting habitat, reducing litter, conserving water or planting native species, and connects it to the need for conservation. Students combine typed explanations, drawings, photographs from Book Creator’s built-in camera option and recorded narration. They publish and present the finished books as practical guides showing how environmental stewardship can drive change.

Students use Adobe Express to design a one-page conservation campaign for a local habitat or species. They explain the environmental issue, show how community choices affect it and propose one realistic action people can take, directly addressing how environmental stewardship can drive change. Students use the ready-made poster templates, text boxes, icons and image tools to organise their message clearly for a Year 5 audience. The finished posters are published as digital campaign pieces and presented to the class with a brief explanation of the intended community impact.

Glen Waverley|Year 5|Where We Are in Pla.d: Students explore the Victorian goldfields and Melbourne using the world map, satellite view and Street View, looking for evidence of how places grew around resources. They compare distances between goldfield towns, ports and Melbourne to investigate the significance of resource discovery in the development of societies. Pairs present a live map walkthrough showing three locations and explaining how transport, settlement and access to gold shaped each place. The familiar search, distance-measuring and Street View features make the investigation manageable for Year 5 students without requiring student logins.

Students enter a small teacher-provided set of historical data about gold production, population growth and migration during the Victorian gold rush. They use the data to examine the central idea that the discovery of resources has impacted the growth and development of nations. Each pair creates a labelled column or line chart and adds a short written conclusion explaining one pattern they notice. Excel’s simple table, formula and chart features allow students to organise evidence and present a clear data-based finding.

Students build a small model of a gold rush settlement, including a resource site, housing, shops, transport routes and an area representing the continuing presence of First Nations peoples. Their model explores the effects of exploration and settlement on Indigenous and colonial populations, rather than showing settlement as empty land. Teams add signs and a short in-game book explaining who benefited, who faced harm and how the town changed as people arrived. Minecraft Education’s block-building, signs and book-and-quill features let Year 5 students create and explain a manageable spatial model.

Students create posts about people who migrated during a resource boom, using teacher-provided accounts from miners, merchants, workers, families and First Nations people. They sort their posts into columns for cultural, social and economic growth, directly investigating the impact of migration on societies. Each post includes a short summary, a piece of evidence and a captioned image, and students comment on one connection between two different experiences. Padlet’s columns, post cards, image upload and comment features produce a class evidence wall that can be displayed and discussed.

Students create a short digital timeline showing how the discovery of a resource, such as gold in Victoria, changed population, work, transport and settlement. The timeline addresses the significance of resource discovery in the development of societies and includes both colonial and First Nations perspectives. Students publish a one-page visual story with five dated events, brief explanations, images and a final statement about the most important impact. Adobe Express’s ready-made page layouts, text boxes, image library and simple publishing feature make the finished timeline easy to build and share.

Glen Waverley|Year 5|Who We Are.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
Glen Waverley|Year 5|Who We Are.d: Students write and record a short message from an animated character explaining how to respond to a tricky group chat, gaming or messaging situation. This directly explores managing behaviours in digital situations and shows how knowledge and practical strategies can help people manage change. Each student produces a short animated safety message that can be presented to the class. They use the tool’s character choice, voice recording and automatic mouth movement features.

Students create a short, age-appropriate guide about managing changes associated with puberty, using teacher-provided facts and trusted support options. The guide connects to the central idea that managing change requires acceptance, knowledge and strategies. Pairs publish a digital book with clear headings, illustrations, helpful advice and a final page listing trusted adults students can approach. They use Book Creator’s page templates, drawing tools, text boxes and built-in voice recording to explain their ideas.

Students respond to teacher-posted relationship scenarios, such as joining a new group, resolving a disagreement or supporting a friend through change. This addresses establishing, managing and maintaining relationships by asking students to suggest respectful words and practical next steps. The class builds a shared wall of useful relationship strategies, then students comment on which responses are likely to help and why. They use Padlet’s post, comment and reaction features to collect and discuss their ideas.

Small groups create questions about safe and respectful choices in digital situations, including privacy, unkind messages, group chats and asking an adult for help. This directly supports managing behaviours in digital situations by helping students identify useful strategies and explain the reasons behind them. The class plays the finished quiz, with each group briefly presenting the thinking behind one answer. Students use Kahoot’s multiple-choice questions, images, timer and results screen to build, test and review the quiz.

Students record a two-minute podcast offering practical advice for someone experiencing a change in friendships, family routines or puberty. This connects to the central idea that managing change requires acceptance, knowledge and strategies. Each pair produces a short episode with an introduction, three realistic strategies and a closing reminder about seeking support from a trusted adult. They use GarageBand’s voice recorder, simple editing controls and built-in music loops to record and assemble the episode.
